author: hannah-whitall-smith
fields.title: The God of All Comfort
fields.description: Why do so many Christians carry their faith like a heavy burden rather than a source of rest? In this timeless classic, Hannah Whitall Smith strips away the exhausting layers of religious effort to reveal the true character of God. She invites you to move beyond a “rollercoaster” spiritual life and settle into the quiet, steady confidence that comes from simply taking God at His word. Discover a peace that remains unshaken.

qa.question: What is The God of All Comfort about?
qa.answer: It is Hannah Whitall Smith's warm answer to a searching question: why do so many Christians carry their faith like a heavy burden rather than a source of rest? Stripping away the exhausting layers of religious effort, she sets out the true character of God as good, loving, and utterly trustworthy, and invites the anxious believer into the comfort and rest that flow from knowing him as he really is.

qa.question: Who was Hannah Whitall Smith?
qa.answer: An American author and speaker of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, raised a Quaker, who became one of the most influential voices of the higher Christian life. Best known for The Christian's Secret of a Happy Life, she wrote this later book, published in 1906, on the comfort and rest available to the believer who truly trusts God's goodness.

qa.question: What is the book's central message?
qa.answer: That God's own character — his goodness, love, and faithfulness — is the ground of all real comfort, and that many Christians are burdened simply because they do not know him as he is. Smith presses the reader to rest not in their feelings or performance but in the settled truth of who God is, and so to exchange anxious religion for peace.

qa.question: Why do so many Christians lack rest, in Smith's view?
qa.answer: Because they misunderstand God, picturing him as harsh or hard to please, and so treat their faith as a wearying effort to satisfy him. Smith argues that this false picture is the root of much Christian anxiety, and that seeing God's true, unfailing goodness dissolves the burden and lets the believer rest in his care.

qa.question: How does this book relate to The Christian's Secret of a Happy Life?
qa.answer: It is a companion to that famous book and presses the same heart-truth from another angle. Where The Christian's Secret sets out the life of trust and surrender, The God of All Comfort dwells on the character of the God we are to trust — grounding the life of rest in the goodness of the One in whom we rest.

qa.question: Is this book only about feelings of comfort?
qa.answer: No — the comfort Smith describes rests on truth, not mood. It comes from knowing God's real character, so it holds firm even when feelings fail or circumstances darken. She is concerned to move the reader off shifting emotions onto the solid ground of who God is, so that their peace has a foundation that does not move.

qa.question: Who is this book for?
qa.answer: For any Christian who finds their faith a burden rather than a rest, who is anxious, weary, or troubled by a fearful picture of God. Smith writes with unusual warmth and directness for such readers, and the book has brought relief to many by turning their eyes from their own effort to the goodness of the God of all comfort.

qa.question: Where should a reader begin?
qa.answer: At the beginning, letting Smith address the burdened, joyless religion so many carry, before she unfolds the true character of God that answers it. The book builds its case warmly and in order, and is best read slowly and applied, since its comfort is meant to be entered into and rested in, not merely understood.

fields.title: Why This Book Has Been Written
fields.body_html:
“My heart overflows with a pleasing theme; I address my verses to the king.” Psalm 45:1 I was once talking on the subject of religion with an intelligent agnostic, whom I very much wished to influence, and after listening to me politely for a little while, he said, “Well, madam, all I have to say is this. If you Christians want to make us agnostics inclined to look into your religion, you must try to be more comfortable in the possession of it yourselves. The Christians I meet seem to me to be the most uncomfortable people anywhere around. They seem to carry their religion as a man carries a headache. He does not want to get rid of his head, but at the same time it is very uncomfortable to have it. And I, for one, do not care to have that sort of religion.” This was a lesson I have never forgotten, and it is the primary reason for my writing this book.

I was very young in the Christian life at the time of this conversation and was still in the first joy of entering into it, so I could not believe that any of God’s children could be as uncomfortable in their religious lives as my agnostic friend had claimed. But when the early glow of my conversion had passed, and I had come down to the dullness of everyday duties and responsibilities, I soon found from my own experience, and also from the similar experiences of most of the Christians around me, that there was far too much truth in his statement, and that the religious life of most of us was full of discomfort and unrest. In fact, it seemed, as one of my Christian friends said to me one day when we were comparing our experiences, “as if we had just enough religion to make us miserable.”

I confess that this was very disappointing, for I had expected something altogether different. It seemed to me extremely inconsistent that a religion, whose fruits are declared in the Bible to be love, joy, and peace, should so often work out in practice in exactly the opposite way, and should produce doubt, fear, unrest, conflict, and discomfort of every kind; and I resolved, if possible, to find out what was wrong. Why, I asked myself, should the children of God lead such completely uncomfortable religious lives when He has led us to believe that His yoke is easy and His burden is light? Why are we troubled with so many spiritual doubts, and such heavy spiritual anxieties?

Why do we find it so hard to be sure that God really loves us, and why is it that we never seem able to believe for long in His kindness and His care? How is it that we can allow ourselves to suspect Him of forgetting us and forsaking us in times of need? We can trust our earthly friends and feel at ease in their companionship, so why is it that we cannot trust our heavenly Friend, and that we seem unable to be at ease in His service?

I believe I have found the answer to these questions, and I would like to say frankly that my purpose in writing this book is to try to bring a little real and genuine comfort into some troubled Christian lives around me. My own understanding of the religion of the Lord Jesus Christ is that it was meant to be full of comfort. I am sure that any unbiased reader of the New Testament would say the same, and I believe that every newly converted person, in the first joy of their conversion, fully expects it. And yet, as I have said, it seems that for a large number of Christians, their religious lives are the most uncomfortable part of their existence. Does the fault of this situation lie with the Lord? Has He promised more than He is able to give?

A writer has said, “We know what over-advertising is. It is a modern disease from which we all suffer. There are posters on every billboard, exaggerations on every blank wall, representations and misrepresentations without number. What visions we have seen of impossible fruits and flowers grown from so-and-so’s seeds. Everything is over-advertised. Is it the same with the kingdom of God? Do the fruits we produce from the good seed of the kingdom match the description given by Him from whom we received that good seed? Has He misled us? There is a feeling around that Christ has offered in His Gospel more than He has to give. People think that they have not quite experienced what was promised as the portion of the children of God. But why is this so? Has the kingdom of God been over-advertised, or has it simply been under-believed? Has the Lord Jesus Christ been overestimated, or has He only been under-trusted?”

What I want to do in this book is to show, in my small way, what I firmly believe: that the kingdom of God cannot possibly be over-advertised, nor can the Lord Jesus Christ be overestimated, for “what no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love him”; and that all the difficulty arises from the fact that we have under-believed and under-trusted.

I want, therefore, to show as clearly as I can the reasons there are in the religion of the Lord Jesus Christ for that deep and lasting peace and comfort of soul, which nothing on earth can disturb, and which is said to be the portion of those who embrace it. And I also want to explain, if this is indeed our rightful portion, how we are to make use of it, and what things stand in the way. There is God’s part in the matter, and there is man’s part, and we must look carefully at both.

A wild young man, who was brought to the Lord at a mission meeting, and who afterwards became a joyful Christian and lived a good life, was asked by someone what he did to be converted. “Oh,” he said, “I did my part, and the Lord did His.”

“But what was your part,” asked the questioner, “and what was the Lord’s part?”

“My part,” was the quick reply, “was to run away, and the Lord’s part was to run after me until He caught me.”

A very meaningful answer; but how few can truly understand it!

God’s part is always to run after us. Christ came to seek and to save that which is lost. “What man of you, having a hundred sheep, if he has lost one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the open country, and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it? And when he has found it, he lays it on his shoulders, rejoicing.” This is always the divine part; but in our foolishness we do not understand it, and instead think that the Lord is the one who is lost, and that our part is to seek and find Him. The very expressions we use show this. We urge sinners to “seek the Lord,” and we talk about having “found” Him. “Have you found the Saviour?” asked an overly zealous mission worker of a happy, trusting little girl.

With a look of amazement, she replied in a tone of wonder, “Why, I did not know the Saviour was lost!”

It is our ignorance of God that causes all this. Because we do not know Him, we naturally form all sorts of wrong ideas about Him. We think He is an angry Judge watching for our slightest faults, or a harsh Taskmaster determined to demand the utmost service from us, or a self-centred Deity requiring His full measure of honour and glory, or a distant Sovereign concerned only with His own affairs and indifferent to our welfare. Who can wonder that such a God can neither be loved nor trusted? And who could expect Christians, with such ideas of Him, to be anything other than full of discomfort and misery?

But I can say with confidence, and without fear of contradiction, that it is impossible for anyone who truly knows God to have such uncomfortable thoughts about Him. There may be many outward discomforts, and many earthly sorrows and trials, but through them all the soul that knows God must dwell inwardly in a place of perfect peace. “Whoever listens to me will dwell secure and will be at ease, without dread of disaster.” And this is a statement no one can question. If we would truly listen to God—which means not only hearing Him but believing what we hear—we could not fail to know that, because He is God, He cannot do anything other than care for us as the apple of His eye, and that everything that tender love and divine wisdom can do for our good will surely be done. Not a single opening for worry or fear is left to the soul that knows God.

“Ah, yes,” you say, “but how am I to know Him? Other people seem to have some kind of inward revelation that makes them know Him, but I never do; and no matter how much I pray, everything seems dark to me. I want to know God, but I do not see how to manage it.”

Your difficulty is that you have a wrong idea of what knowing God is, or at least of the kind of knowing I mean. For I do not mean any mystical inward revelations. Such experiences are delightful when they occur, but they are not always under our control, and they can be uncertain and inconsistent. The kind of knowing I mean is the simple, practical knowledge of God’s nature and character that comes from believing what is revealed about Him in the Bible.

The apostle John, at the end of his Gospel, says concerning the things he had written: “Now Jesus did many other signs in the presence of the disciples, which are not written in this book; but these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.” (John 20:30). It is believing what is written, not what is inwardly revealed, that gives life; and the kind of knowing I mean is the knowing that comes from believing what is written.

I mean, in practical terms, that when I read in the Bible that God is love, I am to believe it simply because it is written, not because I have had any inward experience proving it to be true; and when the Bible says that He cares for us as He cares for the lilies of the field and the birds of the air, and that even the hairs of our head are all numbered, I am to believe it simply because it is written, whether or not I have any inward sense of it.

It is very important for us to understand that the Bible is a statement, not of theories, but of actual facts; and that things are not true because they are in the Bible, but they are in the Bible because they are true. A little boy, who had been learning at school about the discovery of America, said to his father one day, “Father, if I had been Columbus, I would not have taken all that trouble to discover America.”

“Why, what would you have done?” asked his father.

“Oh,” replied the little boy, “I would have just gone to the map and found it.”

This little boy did not understand that maps are only representations of places already known, and that America did not exist because it was on the map, but that it could only be on the map because it already existed. And it is the same with the Bible. It is, like the map, a simple statement of facts; so that when it tells us that God loves us, it is only telling us something that is already true, and that would not be in the Bible if it were not a fact.

It was a great discovery to me when I understood this. It seemed to remove all uncertainty and speculation from the revelation given to us in the Bible about the salvation of the Lord Jesus Christ, and to make everything written about Him a simple statement of undeniable facts. And facts are something we can believe—and indeed, we do believe them as soon as we recognise them as facts. Inward revelations are not something we can control, but anyone in their right mind can believe what is written. And although this may seem rather plain and simple at first, if it is steadily followed, it will result in deeply blessed inward assurance, and will eventually lead us into such a knowledge of God as will transform our lives.

This kind of knowing brings conviction; and in my view, conviction is far superior to inward experiences, as delightful as those may be. An inward experience may be affected by one’s health or by many other disturbances, but a conviction remains. Once a person is convinced that two and two make four, no amount of illness, discomfort, or external influence can shake that conviction. He knows it just as well when he is unwell as when he is in good health. Convictions come from knowledge, and no change in feelings or physical condition can alter knowledge.

It is to help my readers come to this kind of practical knowledge of God, and to the convictions that come from it, that this book is written. I will first try to show what God is—not in a theological or doctrinal sense, but simply what He is in real, everyday life, as the God and Father of each one of us. I will also point out some of the things that seem to me to be the main obstacles to truly knowing Him.

I am completely certain that coming to know Him as He truly is will bring unfailing comfort and peace to every troubled heart, and I deeply long to help everyone within my reach to come to this knowledge. One of Job’s friends said, in response to Job’s distress, “Agree with God, and be at peace; thereby good will come to you.” (Job 22:21) And our Lord, in His last recorded prayer, said: “And this is eternal life, that they know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.” (John 17:3). It is not a matter of knowing ourselves—what we are, what we do, or what we feel—but simply a matter of becoming acquainted with God, and knowing what He is, what He does, and what He feels. Comfort and peace never come from what we know about ourselves, but always from what we know about Him.

We may spend our days performing what we call religious duties, and fill our devotions with enthusiasm, and still be miserable. Nothing can truly bring rest to our hearts except a real knowledge of God; for in the end, everything in our salvation depends on Him. Our comfort depends entirely on whether He is worthy of our trust. If we were planning a dangerous voyage, our first concern would be the kind of captain we would have. Common sense would tell us that if the captain were untrustworthy, no amount of trustworthiness on our part could make the voyage safe. It would be his character, not ours, that mattered most.

If I can only say this often enough, and in enough different ways, to bring conviction to some troubled hearts, and lift them out of their unhappy and uncomfortable religious lives into the kingdom of love, joy, and peace—which is their rightful inheritance—I will feel that my purpose in writing this book has been fulfilled. And I will be able to say, “Lord, now you are letting your servant depart in peace, according to your word; for my eyes have seen your salvation”; and my pen has tried to describe it.

It must, however, be clearly understood that this book does not attempt to deal with the critical or theological aspects of religion. It does not address questions about the authenticity of the Bible.

Others, far more capable, can deal with such matters. This book is written for people who, like myself, profess to believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and who accept the Bible simply as His revelation.

Setting aside all critical questions, therefore, I seek only to explain what seems to me to be the natural result of such belief, and how believers can personally experience it.

There may be mistakes in how I express these things, and for that I ask the understanding of my readers. But the truth I want to communicate—and to communicate in such a way that no one can fail to understand—is not a mistake. And that truth is this: our religious lives ought to be full of joy, peace, and comfort, and if we come to know God better, they will be.

fields.title: What is His Name?
fields.body_html:
“And Moses said to God, ‘If I come to the people of Israel and say to them, “The God of your fathers has sent me to you,” and they ask me, “What is his name?” what shall I say to them?’”

Exodus 3:14 The vital question of all ages and of every human heart is expressed here: “What is his name?”

The whole fate of humanity depends on the answer to this question. As we know, the condition of a country depends upon the character of its rulers. The state of an army depends upon the officers who command it. And the more absolute the government, the more this must be the case.

We can see, therefore, that everything in a universe depends upon the kind of creator and ruler who has brought that universe into existence, and that the whole well-being of the human beings placed in it is necessarily bound up with the character of their Creator. If the God who created us is a good God, then everything must ultimately be right for us, since a good God cannot ordain anything but what is good. But if He is a bad God, or a careless God, or an unkind God, then we cannot be sure that anything is right, and we can have no real peace or comfort anywhere.

The true foundation for peace and comfort is found only in the kind of God we have. Therefore, we must first find out what His name is—that is, what His character is—in short, what kind of God He is.

In Bible language, a name always means character. Names there are not given arbitrarily, as they often are with us, but are always given in relation to the character or work of the person named.

Creden, in his Concordance, says that the names of God signify what He truly is, and are used throughout the Bible to express His attributes, His purposes, His glory, His grace, His mercy, His love, His wisdom, His power, and His goodness. A careful study of His names makes this clear.

When, therefore, the children of Israel asked, “What is his name?” they meant, “Who and what is this God of whom you speak? What is His character? What are His attributes? What does He do?

In short, what kind of being is He?”

The psalmist says, “Those who know your name put their trust in you, for you, O Lord, have not forsaken those who seek you.” (Psalm 9:10) And again he says, “The name of the Lord is a strong tower; the righteous man runs into it and is safe.” (Psalm 18:10) “Those who know your name put their trust in you.” They cannot do otherwise, because in knowing His name they know His character and His nature—that He is a God who is completely trustworthy.

There can be no doubt that a large part of the unrest and discomfort in many Christian hearts comes simply from the fact that they do not yet know His name. “Some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the Lord our God. They collapse and fall, but we rise and stand upright.” (Psalm 20:7-8) In all that we read about Israel in the past, we find this constant truth: everything they were and everything they had depended on the fact that their God was the Lord. “Blessed is the nation whose God is the Lord, the people whom he has chosen as his heritage.” (Psalm 33:12) “Therefore you are great, O Lord God. For there is none like you, and there is no God besides you, according to all that we have heard with our ears. And who is like your people Israel, the one nation on earth whom God went to redeem to be his people, making himself a name and doing for themd great and awesome things by driving out before your people,e whom you redeemed for yourself from Egypt, a nation and its gods? And you established for yourself your people Israel to be your people forever. And you, O Lord, became their God.” (Psalm 7:22-24) “Happy are the people whose God is the Lord!” (Psalm 144:15) Blessed is that nation; happy are those people whose God is the Lord. All the blessing and happiness of Israel came from the fact that their God was the Lord. Nothing else was important enough to mention when recounting their advantages. The fact that their God was the Lord was enough to explain every good thing they possessed.

The question above all questions for each one of us, therefore, is this: “What is his name?”

To the Israelites, God Himself answered this question. God said to Moses, “I AM WHO I AM.”

(Exodus 3:14) And He said, “Say this to the people of Israel: ‘I AM has sent me to you.’” God also said to Moses, “Say this to the people of Israel: ‘The Lord, the God of your fathers, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, has sent me to you.’ This is my name forever, and thus I am to be remembered throughout all generations.” (Exodus 3:15) In the Gospel of John, Christ takes this name “I am” for Himself. When the Jews questioned Him about His authority, He said to them, “Truly, truly, I say to you, before Abraham was, I am.”

(John 8:58) And in the Book of Revelation He declares again: “I am the Alpha and the Omega… who is and who was and who is to come, the Almighty.” (Revelation 1:8) These simple words, “I am,” express eternity and unchangeableness of existence, which is the first essential quality of a God who can be relied upon. No one could place confidence in a changeable God. He must be the same yesterday, today, and forever if we are to have any peace or comfort. But is this all His name means—simply “I am”? I am what? we ask. What does this “I am” include? I believe it includes everything the human heart longs for and needs. This unfinished name of God seems like a blank cheque signed by a wealthy friend, given to us to fill in with whatever amount we require. The whole Bible tells us what it means.

Every attribute of God, every revelation of His character, every proof of His unfailing love, every declaration of His watchful care, every assurance of His tender mercy, every expression of His loving kindness—all are the filling out of this unfinished “I am.”

God tells us throughout His Word what He is. “I am,” He says, “all that my people need. I am their strength. I am their wisdom. I am their righteousness. I am their peace. I am their salvation.

I am their life. I am their all in all.”

This seemingly unfinished name is therefore the most comforting name the human heart could imagine, because it allows us to add to it, without limit, whatever we need—even “far more abundantly than all that we ask or think.”

But if our hearts are full of our own miserable “I ams,” we will have no ears to hear His glorious, soul-satisfying “I am.” We say, “I am such a weak person,” or “I am so foolish,” or “I am so useless,” or “I am so helpless,” and we give these poor “I ams” as the reason for the misery and discomfort of our religious lives, and even feel that we deserve sympathy because things are so difficult for us. Meanwhile, we completely ignore the blank cheque of God’s magnificent “I am,” which gives us permission to draw from Him an abundant supply for every need.

If you are an uncomfortable Christian, then the only thing that can give you a truly comfortable religious life is to know God. The psalmist says that those who know God’s name will trust in Him, and I am convinced it is impossible to truly know Him and not trust Him. A trustworthy person naturally inspires trust—not by demanding it, but by winning it through their character.

What our Lord declares is eternally true: “And I, when I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” Once you truly know Him, Christ is irresistible. You cannot help trusting Him any more than you can help breathing. And if the whole world could know Him as He truly is, the whole world—sinners and all—would fall at His feet in worship. They simply could not help it. His surpassing beauty would overcome everything.

How then can we come to know God?

Two things are necessary: first, God must reveal Himself; and second, we must accept His revelation and believe what He reveals.

The apostle John tells us that “no one has ever seen God; the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known.” (John 1:18) Christ, therefore, is the revelation of God. None of us has seen God, nor can we see Him in our present state, because we do not have the ability to do so. But He has revealed Himself in Christ, and we can see Christ, since He became a man like us.

A man who wanted to speak with ants might stand over an anthill and talk all day, yet not a single word would reach them. They would move about, completely unaware of him. As far as we know, ants have no ability to understand human speech. But if a man could become an ant, live among them, and speak their language, he would immediately make himself understood.

When a higher form of life wants to communicate with a lower, incarnation is necessary.

Christ revealed God by what He was, by what He did, and by what He said. From the cradle to the grave, every moment of His life revealed God. We must go to Him, then, to know God, and we must refuse to believe anything about God that is not shown to us in Christ. All other revelations are incomplete and therefore not fully reliable. Only in Christ do we see God as He truly is, for Christ is “the exact imprint of his nature.”

Whatever God would have said or done in any situation, Christ said and did. “I do nothing on my own authority… the Father who dwells in me does his works” (John 14:10) “I and the Father are one” (John 10:30) “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” (John 14:9) Nothing is stated more clearly in the New Testament than this truth: that we are to see “the light of the knowledge of the glory of God in the face of Jesus Christ,” (2 Corinthians 4:6) and that we cannot see it fully anywhere else.

If we want to know the full meaning of what God meant when He gave Moses that seemingly unfinished name, “I am,” we will find it revealed in Christ. He alone explains God. He alone is the image of the invisible God.

It is clear, therefore, that we must never accept any idea of God that contradicts what we see in Christ, and we must completely reject any view of His character, His actions, or His relationship with us—no matter how strongly it is taught—if it does not agree with what Christ has revealed.

We are all aware that the Old Testament revelation of God sometimes seems to differ from the revelation given in Christ, and the question arises as to which we are to accept as the truest. In view of the fact that God Himself tells us that in these last days He has spoken to us by His Son, who is “the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature,” we cannot reject Christ’s testimony. Instead, we must regard the Old Testament revelation, where it differs from the revelation in Christ, as partial and incomplete, and accept as a true picture of God only what we find in Christ.

Christ alone tells us the true and real name of God. In His final and wonderful prayer He says: “I have manifested your name to the people whom you gave me out of the world… I have given them the words that you gave me, and they have received them and have come to know in truth that I came from you; and they have believed that you sent me.”

Could we ask for greater authority than this?

In the whole life of Christ, nothing is clearer or more emphatic than the fact that He continually claimed to be a complete revelation of God. “The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works.” (John 14:10) Again and again He declares that He speaks only what the Father gives Him to speak. “I declare to the world what I have heard from him.” (John 8:26) “I do nothing on my own authority, but speak just as the Father taught me.” (John 12:49) The apostle also declares most plainly that it pleased the Father that in Christ “all the fullness of God was pleased to dwell.” (Colossians 1:19) And although we may not fully understand all that this means in a theological sense, we cannot fail to see that if we want to know God, we only need to become familiar with Christ’s ways and Christ’s character in order to know God’s ways and God’s character. “Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.” And again He declares that “no one knows the Father except the Son and anyone to whom the Son chooses to reveal him.”

(Matthew 11:27) This settles the matter completely. We may have many thoughts about God; we may imagine or speculate—but it is all in vain. We simply cannot know Him except through the revelation given in Christ.

We may know many things about God, but that is very different from knowing Him as He truly is in nature and character. Other witnesses may tell us about His outward acts, but from these we often form very wrong impressions of His true character. No one but Christ can reveal the true inner nature of God, for only of Him can it be said that “the only God, who is at the Father’s side, he has made him known.” (John 1:18) It makes all the difference in our Christian lives whether or not we believe this to be true. If we do believe it, then the stern Judge and hard Taskmaster we have feared—even while trying to follow Him—and whose service we have found so difficult and uncomfortable, will disappear. In His place will come the God of love revealed to us in “the face of Jesus Christ,” the God who cares for us as He cares for the sparrows and the flowers of the field, and who tells us that even the hairs of our head are all numbered.

No one could be afraid of a God like this.

If we have been used to approaching God with any doubt about His kindness towards us; if our religious life has been poisoned by fear; if unworthy thoughts of His character and will have filled our hearts with suspicion of His goodness; if we have imagined Him as a harsh ruler or a self-seeking tyrant; if, in short, we have thought of Him in any way other than what has been revealed to us in “the face of Jesus Christ,” we must go back, in simplicity of heart, to the record of that beautiful life lived among people, and bring our understanding of God into full agreement with the character and ways of Him who declares that He came to make known the name of God.

In answer, then, to the question, “What is His name?” I have only this to say: ask Christ. We are told that He was “God manifested in the flesh,” and that whoever sees Him sees the God who sent Him. Therefore, it is perfectly clear that if we want to know the name, we must look at the manifestation. This simply means that we must study the life, words, and actions of Christ, and say to ourselves, “Whoever has seen Christ has seen God,” and that what Christ was on earth, God is in heaven. All the confusion that surrounds the character of God will disappear if we accept the light Christ has given and believe the “manifestation of His name” that Christ has shown us, and refuse to believe anything else.

When Nicodemus came to Jesus by night to ask how these things could be true, Jesus told him that whether he understood them or not, they were still true, and said very clearly: “Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen.” (John 3:11) No one who believes in Christ can doubt that He knew God; and no one can question whether we ought to accept His testimony. He repeatedly assured us that He knew what He was speaking about, and that His words are to be accepted as absolute truth, because He came down from heaven and therefore knows heavenly things.

None of us would openly question this; yet in practice many of God’s people ignore Christ’s testimony and instead listen to their own doubting hearts, which tell them that it cannot be true that God is as loving, as tender, or as ready to forgive as Christ has shown Him to be. Yet I must repeat again and again, even at the risk of repetition, what so few seem to understand: if there is one truth taught more clearly than any other in the Bible, it is that the name—that is, the character—of the Father, as revealed by Christ, is His true character. Christ continually declares that He is the living expression of the Father, and that in everything He said and did, He was simply saying and doing what the Father would have said and done if He had acted directly from heaven.

In the face of such clear statements from our Lord Himself, it becomes not only our privilege but our responsibility to remove from our understanding of God anything that does not agree with the life, character, and teaching of Christ. If we want to know the true name of God, we must accept the name Christ has revealed and listen to no other.

Whatever qualities we see in Christ, these fill out the meaning of God’s “I am.” As we look at Christ’s life and listen to His words, we hear God saying, “I am rest for the weary; I am peace for the troubled; I am strength for the weak; I am wisdom for the foolish; I am righteousness for the sinful; I am everything the neediest soul can desire; I am far more abundantly than all you can ask or think, in blessing, help, and care.”

But here someone may say, “Yes, this may all be true, but how can I take hold of it? I am such an unworthy person that I dare not believe such grace belongs to me.”

How can you take hold of it? You cannot take hold of it at all—but you can let it take hold of you. It is good news declared to you in the Bible, and you only need to treat it as you would any trustworthy news told to you by a reliable source. If the person speaking is trustworthy, you believe what they say and act on it. And you must do the same here. If Christ is trustworthy when He says He is the revelation of God, then you must believe Him and act accordingly.

You must take your stand on His trustworthiness. You must say to yourself, and if necessary to others, “I am going to believe what Christ says about God. No matter what things seem like, no matter what my own thoughts or feelings say, no matter what anyone else says, I know that what Christ says must be true, because He knows and no one else does. I will believe Him completely.

He says that He is one with God; therefore, everything He is, God is. I will not be afraid of God any longer. I will not think of Him as a stern lawgiver angry with me, or as a harsh master demanding impossible things, or as a distant and unapproachable being who is indifferent to my struggles and fears. All such ideas are impossible now that I know Christ reveals God.”

If we firmly hold to this truth—that Christ and God are one—and refuse to accept any idea of God that contradicts what Christ has shown, our lives will be transformed.

We may often need to stand firm in this, because old doubts and fears will return and try to take hold again. But we must turn away from them decisively and declare that we now know the name—that is, the character—of our God, and that such things are impossible for Him.

Therefore, we refuse to listen to any suggestion that misrepresents His character or His ways.

It is impossible to think that when God said to Moses, “I AM,” He meant, “I am a harsh lawgiver,” or “I am a hard master,” or “I am indifferent to the suffering of my people.” If we tried to fill in His “I am” with such meanings, Christians everywhere would be shocked. Yet do not the fears and doubts of many believers say exactly these things quietly in their hearts every day?

May God grant that what we learn as we consider His name will make such doubts and fears impossible for us from now on.

Jesus is God! Oh, if I could Travel land and sea, To teach and tell this single truth, How happy I would be!

Oh, if I had an angel’s voice, I would proclaim aloud— Jesus, the good, the beautiful, Is the image of our God!

This simply means that we must study the life, words, and actions of Christ, and say to ourselves, “Whoever has seen Christ has seen God,” and that what Christ was on earth, God is in heaven. All the confusion that surrounds the character of God will disappear if we accept the light Christ has given and believe the “manifestation of His name” that Christ has shown us, and refuse to believe anything else. When Nicodemus came to Jesus by night to ask how these things could be true, Jesus told him that whether he understood them or not, they were still true, and said very clearly: “Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen.” (John 3:11) No one who believes in Christ can doubt that He knew God; and no one can question whether we ought to accept His testimony. He repeatedly assured us that He knew what He was speaking about, and that His words are to be accepted as absolute truth, because He came down from heaven and therefore knows heavenly things. None of us would openly question this; yet in practice many of God’s people ignore Christ’s testimony and instead listen to their own doubting hearts, which tell them that it cannot be true that God is as loving, as tender, or as ready to forgive as Christ has shown Him to be. Yet I must repeat again and again, even at the risk of repetition, what so few seem to understand: if there is one truth taught more clearly than any other in the Bible, it is that the name—that is, the character—of the Father, as revealed by Christ, is His true character. Christ continually declares that He is the living expression of the Father, and that in everything He said and did, He was simply saying and doing what the Father would have said and done if He had acted directly from heaven. In the face of such clear statements from our Lord Himself, it becomes not only our privilege but our responsibility to remove from our understanding of God anything that does not agree with the life, character, and teaching of Christ. If we want to know the true name of God, we must accept the name Christ has revealed and listen to no other. Whatever qualities we see in Christ, these fill out the meaning of God’s “I am.” As we look at Christ’s life and listen to His words, we hear God saying, “I am rest for the weary; I am peace for the troubled; I am strength for the weak; I am wisdom for the foolish; I am righteousness for the sinful; I am everything the neediest soul can desire; I am far more abundantly than all you can ask or think, in blessing, help, and care.” But here someone may say, “Yes, this may all be true, but how can I take hold of it? I am such an unworthy person that I dare not believe such grace belongs to me.” How can you take hold of it? You cannot take hold of it at all—but you can let it take hold of you. It is good news declared to you in the Bible, and you only need to treat it as you would any trustworthy news told to you by a reliable source. If the person speaking is trustworthy, you believe what they say and act on it. And you must do the same here. If Christ is trustworthy when He says He is the revelation of God, then you must believe Him and act accordingly. You must take your stand on His trustworthiness. You must say to yourself, and if necessary to others, “I am going to believe what Christ says about God. No matter what things seem like, no matter what my own thoughts or feelings say, no matter what anyone else says, I know that what Christ says must be true, because He knows and no one else does. I will believe Him completely. He says that He is one with God; therefore, everything He is, God is. I will not be afraid of God any longer. I will not think of Him as a stern lawgiver angry with me, or as a harsh master demanding impossible things, or as a distant and unapproachable being who is indifferent to my struggles and fears. All such ideas are impossible now that I know Christ reveals God.” If we firmly hold to this truth—that Christ and God are one—and refuse to accept any idea of God that contradicts what Christ has shown, our lives will be transformed. We may often need to stand firm in this, because old doubts and fears will return and try to take hold again. But we must turn away from them decisively and declare that we now know the name—that is, the character—of our God, and that such things are impossible for Him. Therefore, we refuse to listen to any suggestion that misrepresents His character or His ways. It is impossible to think that when God said to Moses, “I AM,” He meant, “I am a harsh lawgiver,” or “I am a hard master,” or “I am indifferent to the suffering of my people.” If we tried to fill in His “I am” with such meanings, Christians everywhere would be shocked. Yet do not the fears and doubts of many believers say exactly these things quietly in their hearts every day? May God grant that what we learn as we consider His name will make such doubts and fears impossible for us from now on. Jesus is God! Oh, if I could Travel land and sea, To teach and tell this single truth, How happy I would be! Oh, if I had an angel’s voice, I would proclaim aloud— Jesus, the good, the beautiful, Is the image of our God!

fields.title: The God of All Comfort
fields.body_html:
“Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of mercies and God of all comfort, who comforts us in all our affliction, so that we may be able to comfort those who are in any affliction, with the comfort with which we ourselves are comforted by God.” (2 Corinthians 1:3-4) Among all the names that reveal God, this one—“the God of all comfort”—seems to me one of the most beautiful and deeply reassuring. The words all comfort allow no limits and no exceptions; and one might expect that, however many outward difficulties the followers of such a God may face, their inward spiritual life would always be full of comfort.

But in reality, it often seems to be exactly the opposite, and the spiritual lives of many of God’s people are filled, not with comfort, but with deep discomfort. This discomfort comes from anxiety about their relationship with God, and doubts about His love. They trouble themselves with the thought that they are too unworthy to deserve His care, and they suspect Him of being indifferent to their struggles or of abandoning them in times of need.

They are anxious and troubled about everything in their spiritual life—their attitudes and feelings, their lack of interest in the Bible, their lack of fervour in prayer, their coldness of heart.

They are weighed down by regret over the past and filled with fear about the future. They feel unworthy to come into God’s presence and cannot believe that they truly belong to Him. They can feel happy and at ease with their earthly friends, but they cannot feel at ease with God.

And although He declares Himself to be the God of all comfort, they continue to say that they cannot find comfort anywhere; and their sorrowful expressions and discouraged voices show that they are speaking honestly, speaking the truth.

Such Christians, although they profess to follow the God of all comfort, spread gloom and uneasiness wherever they go. It is impossible for them to convince anyone that this beautiful name—by which God has revealed Himself—is anything more than a religious phrase without real meaning. And I am very much afraid that the visibly uncomfortable lives of so many Christians are responsible for a large part of the unbelief in the world.

The apostle tells us that we are to be “letters… known and read by all.” What people read in us is far more important for the spread of Christ’s kingdom than we often realise. It is not what we say that matters most, but what we are. It is easy to speak many beautiful words about God being the God of all comfort; but unless we ourselves know what it is to be truly comforted, our words are empty. People must see in our lives what they hear in our words, or else all our speaking does more harm than good. It would be wise for us to ask what others are reading in us. Is it comfort or discomfort that shows itself in our daily life?

But at this point someone may ask what I mean by the comfort God gives. Is it a kind of religious feeling that may prepare us for heaven but is not strong enough for the realities of daily life with all its trials and pains? Or is it a real and genuine comfort—the kind we understand— that brings peace even in the middle of life’s difficulties? With all my heart, I believe it is the latter.

Comfort, whether human or divine, is simply comfort—nothing less. We do not care for empty phrases; we want something real. And the reality of being comforted seems to me one of the most precious experiences in life. We all know what it is. As children, when we have run to our mother after being hurt or frightened and felt her arms around us and her gentle care, we have known comfort. As adults, after a long day, when we rest and feel at ease, we have known comfort. When illness begins to pass and strength returns, we have known comfort. When someone we love has been close to death but is restored, we have known comfort.

Many times in life we have said with relief, “This is comfortable,” and in that word there is a sense of rest, relief, and quiet joy that is hard to express in any other way. We understand, therefore, what it means when God is called the “God of all comfort.”

And yet, sadly, we have failed to believe it. It has seemed too good to be true. The joy of it has been more than our doubtful hearts could accept. We may sometimes hope for small moments of comfort, but we shrink back from believing in the fullness of the “all comfort” that is ours in the salvation of the Lord Jesus Christ.

And yet what more could God have said than this: “As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you; you shall be comforted”? (Isaiah 66:13) Notice the comparison—as… so. It is real comfort that is meant here—the kind a child feels when held and cared for by its mother. Yet how many of us have truly believed that God’s comfort is as real and tender as a mother’s, or even nearly so? Instead of seeing ourselves as held close to His heart, we have often thought of Him as a strict and distant judge, demanding respect and watching for our faults. Is it any wonder that our religion has made us uncomfortable instead of bringing comfort? Who could feel at ease before such a judge?

But I am glad to say that such a judge does not exist. The God who truly exists is like a loving mother. He says plainly, “As one whom his mother comforts, so I will comfort you.”

Again and again He says this. “I, I am he who comforts you,” He says to His people. And then He asks why they are still afraid: why should anything terrify you when your Maker Himself is ready and willing to comfort you? Why fear the power of others and forget the One who created all things?

The God who is real is the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ—the God who loved the world so much that He sent His Son, not to condemn it, but to save it. He is the God who sent Christ “to bind up the brokenhearted… to comfort all who mourn.” (Isaiah 61: 1-3) Notice that word all. Not just a few, but every single one. Every sorrowing heart, every struggling soul, is included. If even one were left out, it would not be “all.” I have often been grateful that even the weak and troubled are specially included in Scripture. We are told not to criticise such people, but to comfort them. Those who need comfort most are the very ones God most desires to comfort—not the strong, but the weak.

This is the glory of a religion of love. Christ was sent to comfort all who mourn. The God of all comfort sent His Son to bring comfort to a world full of sorrow. And throughout His life, Christ fulfilled this mission.

When His disciples wanted Him to call down judgement on those who rejected Him, He rebuked them and said that He had not come to destroy lives but to save them. He welcomed sinners. He showed mercy where others showed condemnation. To the woman caught in sin, He said, “Neither do I condemn you; go, and from now on sin no more.” (John 8:11) Everywhere, He stood on the side of those in need. That was His purpose—to save sinners.

Two young girls were once talking about God, and one said, “I don’t think God loves me. I am too small and unimportant.”

The other replied, “But that is exactly who God cares for—people like us who cannot manage on our own.”

“Is that true?” said the first. “Then I do not need to worry anymore.”

If anyone reading this feels afraid or troubled, let me say clearly: this is exactly what the Lord Jesus Christ is for—to care for and comfort all who mourn. All—every single one, including you. It would not be “all” if you were left out. Even if you feel completely cast down, He is described as the One “who comforts the downcast.”

What a beautiful mission—to bring comfort into a world full of sorrow. And how I long for every troubled heart to experience this comfort from God.

And our Comforter is not distant. He is near. He remains with us. When Christ was about to leave this world, He told His disciples He would not leave them alone, but would send “another Helper” to be with them forever. This Comforter would teach them and remind them of all truth.

Then He added: “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you… Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid.” (John 14:27) How can we remain fearful in the light of such words?

“Comforter”—what a wonderful word, if only we truly understood it. Let us dwell on it until it becomes real to us. And not just a comforter who comes and goes, but one who remains—always present, always ready to bring joy in place of sorrow.

An abiding Comforter—what an extraordinary truth. Even having a human friend stay with us in difficulty is a great help. But here is a divine Comforter who is always with us and whose ability to comfort never fails. There should never be a moment when we are without comfort.

And yet many do not realise this. If they did, there would not be so many troubled Christians.

You may ask whether this Comforter also corrects us, and whether that can truly be comforting.

In fact, this is one of the ways He comforts us. What would we be like without someone to show us our faults and help us change?

If I were walking with a fault in my appearance that I did not know about, it would be a kindness for a friend to point it out. In the same way, it is a comfort to know that the Spirit gently shows us our faults so that we are not left unaware of them.

There is comfort even in correction, because it leads to healing. God “comforts all our waste places” by showing us what needs to be restored and then restoring it.

You may feel unworthy of such comfort. That may be true—but that is exactly why you need it.

Christ came to save sinners, not those who think themselves worthy. Your need is your qualification.

The path to receiving God’s comfort often comes through recognising our need for it. This is why God sometimes allows sorrow. In difficult places, we are able to hear His voice more clearly. It is often in the wilderness that we hear His words of comfort.

God knows that it is better for us to receive His comfort, even through trials, than never to experience it at all. What He gives is far greater than what we lose. Earthly things may pass, but what He gives is eternal.

Like Paul, we can come to see that everything is loss compared to knowing Christ.

And yet, strangely, when life is easy, we believe God is the God of all comfort—but when we truly need comfort, we struggle to believe it exists. It is as if we change the meaning of Scripture in our hearts. Instead of believing “Blessed are those who mourn, for they shall be comforted,” we begin to think only the already happy will receive comfort.

We may even twist words like “God who comforts the downcast” into something entirely different, as though He forgets or ignores those who are struggling. And in doing so, we lose the very comfort offered to us.

But God says He will comfort us on every side. Nothing is left out. And yet, in times of trouble, we often believe there is no comfort exactly where we need it most. This is not because God has failed, but because we have doubted.

It is like Israel of old. God declared His comfort, yet they said, “The Lord has forgotten me.”

And His answer came full of tenderness: can a mother forget her child? Even if she could, God will not. We are always before Him.

So be comforted.

But you may still ask, how can you receive this comfort? The answer is simple: you must accept it. God is continually giving His comfort—but unless you receive it, you cannot experience it.

Divine comfort does not come to us in a mysterious or arbitrary way. It comes through a clear and simple process. The indwelling Comforter brings to our remembrance comforting truths about our Lord, and if we believe them, we are comforted.

A verse of Scripture may come to mind, or a line from a hymn, or a quiet reminder of Christ’s love and tender care. If we receive that in simple faith, comfort naturally follows. But if we refuse to listen to the voice of the Comforter and instead give attention to discouragement or despair, then no comfort can reach our souls.

Even a mother can pour out all her love in vain on a child who refuses to be comforted. The child may sit stubborn and unmoved, rejecting every word. In the same way, comforting words can only comfort us if we believe them.

God has spoken enough comforting words to soothe an entire world, yet many Christians remain anxious, burdened, and restless. Why? Because they do not allow those words to enter their hearts. Some even believe it is wrong to feel comfort—they feel too unworthy. And when comfort begins to rise within them, they push it away, refusing it, just as Scripture says, “they refused to be comforted.” (Jeremiah 31:15) We are told that everything written in Scripture is given so that, through endurance and the comfort it provides, we might have hope. But this comfort can only come through belief.

Nothing God says can bring peace to a heart that doubts its truth.

If a ship captain assures us the vessel is safe, we must believe him before we can relax. If a train conductor tells us we are on the right train, we must trust his word before we sit at ease. This is obvious in everyday life—yet in spiritual matters, we often ignore it.

Some people even try to feel comfort before they believe God’s promises. But that reverses the order entirely. Just as a traveler cannot feel secure before trusting the guide, so we cannot feel comfort before believing God.

God’s order is simple: believe first, then feel.

We often reverse it: feel first, then believe.

This reversal is the root of much of our struggle.

Consider this: when we are overwhelmed with anxiety, God tells us not to be anxious, but to cast our cares upon Him because He cares for us. He points us to the birds of the air and the lilies of the field, assuring us that we are far more valuable than they.

What greater comfort could there be than this—that the Creator of Heaven and earth takes responsibility for our care?

And yet, many are not comforted. Why? Because they do not believe it. They admire the words, wish they were true, but hesitate to accept them personally. They wait for a feeling to confirm the truth, instead of trusting the truth itself.

We say, “If only I could feel that it is true.”

God says, “If only you would believe that it is true.”

At the root of our lack of comfort is simply unbelief.

The remedy is clear. If we desire comfort, we must choose to believe every word of comfort God has spoken. We must refuse to entertain the voices of doubt—whether they come from our circumstances or from our own thoughts.

This requires determination. We must set our hearts firmly—like flint—to believe, even when everything around us seems contrary. Being comforted is not passive; it involves the will. We must choose it.

When life feels uncertain, we must say: “God has said it. Therefore, it is true. I will believe it, no matter how it appears.”

And having chosen to believe, we must refuse to turn back into doubt.

Whoever lives this way will, sooner or later, enter into deep and lasting comfort.

The psalmist said, “In the multitude of my thoughts within me, Your comforts delight my soul.”

Yet often our minds are filled more with our troubles than with God’s comforts. If we want to be comforted, we must intentionally dwell on His promises.

It may be helpful to examine our thoughts: How often do we think about God’s comfort compared to our worries?

The answer might surprise us.

Finally, a word to those who preach the Gospel.

What is your message?

It is this: “Comfort My people.”

Not rebuke them, not burden them—but comfort them.

The true Gospel is good news—pure, undiluted good news. Yet often it is mixed with conditions, warnings, and human additions that strip away its comfort.

Christ comforts.

Man often complicates.

The true Gospel is like the angel’s message to the shepherds: “Do not be afraid. I bring you good news of great joy for all people.” (Luke 2:10) These are the words that bring real comfort.

If every preacher proclaimed such words clearly, and every listener believed them, there would be no more restless, anxious Christians. Instead, hearts everywhere would be strengthened and filled with peace.

And this prayer would be fulfilled: May our Lord Jesus Christ Himself, and God our Father—who has loved us and given us eternal comfort and good hope—comfort your hearts and establish you in every good word and work.
