If all who used this name truly understood its meaning, it would have been impossible for the misrepresentations of His character and the doubts about His love and care, which have troubled the hearts of His children throughout history, to take hold. Tyranny, unkindness, and neglect might perhaps be attributed to a God whose name was only king, judge, or lawgiver; but of a God who is first and foremost a Father, and necessarily, since He is God, a good Father, such ideas cannot rightly be held. Moreover, since He is an “everlasting Father,” He must, by His very nature, always act as a good Father should, under all circumstances, and never otherwise. It is unthinkable that a good father would forget, neglect, or act unjustly toward his children. A wicked or careless father might, but a good father never would. And in calling our God by the blessed name of Father, we must recognise that, if He is a Father at all, He must be the very best of fathers, and His fatherhood must represent the highest ideal of fatherhood we can conceive. It is a fatherhood that includes the highest ideals of both father and mother combined, encompassing all the love, tenderness, compassion, longing, and self-sacrifice that we rightly associate with parenthood, even though we do not always see these perfectly expressed in earthly parents. But you may ask about the other names of God—do they not suggest more fearful ideas? They only seem to do so because this blessed name of Father is not understood as underlying them all. This name must be the foundation of every other name by which He is known. Has He been called a Judge? Yes, but He is a Father-Judge, judging as a loving father would. Is He a King? Yes, but He is a King who is also the Father of His people, ruling them with a father’s tenderness. Is He a Lawgiver? Yes, but He is a Lawgiver who gives laws as a father would, mindful of the weakness and ignorance of his children. “As a father shows compassion to his children, so the Lord shows compassion to those who fear him. For he knows our frame; he remembers that we are dust.” (Psalm 103:13–14) We must never, never think of God in any other way than as “our Father.” All other attributes we associate with Him must be grounded in and shaped by this truth of “our Father.” What a good father could not do, God, who is our Father, cannot do either; and what a good father ought to do, God, who is our Father, will certainly do. In our Lord’s final prayer in John 17, He says that He has made known to us the name of the Father so that we may discover the wonderful truth that the Father loves us as He loved His Son. Now, which of us truly believes this? We may have read this chapter many times, perhaps more than almost any other in the Bible, and yet do we actually believe that it is literally true that God loves us as much as He loved Christ? If we truly believed this, could we ever again have an anxious or rebellious thought? Would we not be completely and entirely confident in every circumstance that the divine Father, who loves us as much as He loved His only begotten Son, our Lord Jesus Christ, would care for us in the best possible way, and would therefore clearly instruct us not to be anxious or troubled about anything, because He knows His Father and knows that it is completely safe to trust Him entirely? It is very striking that He so often said, “Your Father in heaven,” not only mine, but yours as well. “Your Father in heaven” cares for the birds of the air and the lilies of the field, and therefore will certainly care for you, who are of far greater value than many birds. How foolish it is, then, for us to be anxious and troubled about things, when Christ has told us that our heavenly Father knows that we need all these things! For being a good Father, He must, by His very nature, provide for us when He knows our needs. What is the matter with us that we do not understand this? Again, our Lord compares earthly fathers with our heavenly Father, not to show how much less good and loving our heavenly Father is, but how much more. “Or which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? ... how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!” (Matthew 7:9–11) Can we imagine a good earthly father giving a stone or a serpent to a hungry child instead of bread or fish? Our hearts would recoil at such a thought. Yet many of God’s children seem to believe that their heavenly Father acts in such ways toward them, giving them stones when they ask for bread, or hardship when they ask for blessing. And some of these very people may belong to organisations that exist to protect children from cruelty—yet they have not considered the seriousness of accusing their heavenly Father of the very things they would condemn in earthly fathers. But our heavenly Father is not only willing to give us good things—He is far more than willing. Our Lord says, “Fear not, little flock, for it is your Father’s good pleasure to give you the kingdom.” (Luke 12:32) There is no reluctance in His giving; it is His good pleasure to give. He delights in doing so. He desires to give you the kingdom far more than you desire to receive it. Those of us who are parents understand how eager we are to give good things to our children, often more eager than they are to receive them; and this helps us understand how it is God’s good pleasure to give us the kingdom. Why then do we approach Him with fear and hesitation, and why do we trouble ourselves with anxiety as though He might fail to provide what we need? There can only be one answer: we do not truly know the Father. We are described as being part of the “household of God.” Scripture teaches that if anyone does not provide for his own household, he has “denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever.” (1 Timothy 5:8) Since we belong to the household of God, this principle applies to Him; and if He were to fail to provide for us, His own words would stand against Him. I say this with reverence, but also with clarity, because so few seem to have grasped it. In my own experience, there came a defining moment when I first understood this truth about the responsibility of my Father in heaven. It was as though, in a single instant, the burden of life was lifted from my shoulders and placed upon His, and all my fears, anxieties, and uncertainties were surrendered into the depth of His loving care. I realised that the natural human instinct which expects parents to care for their children is not merely cultural, but divinely implanted. It is meant to teach us that the Creator, who has made human parents responsible for their children, is Himself equally responsible for His children. I could have rejoiced greatly. From that moment, my burdens were turned into rest. For when this understanding comes to a person, that person must, by necessity, enter into rest. With such a God, who is at the same time a Father, there is no place for anything but rest. And whenever, since that joyful discovery, temptations to doubt, anxiety, or fear have arisen, I have refused to listen to them in light of what I have learned, because I recognise that to do so would be to question the reliability of my Father in heaven. We may have been used to thinking that our doubts and fears come from our own unworthiness and are a sign of humility. We may even have taken them as evidence of special piety and thought they were in some way pleasing to God. But if children, in their relationship with their earthly parents, allowed doubts about their parents’ love and feared that their care might fail, would those doubts and fears show true love and respect? Would they be pleasing to their parents? If God is our Father, the only thing we can do with doubts, fears, and anxious thoughts is to cast them behind us completely and refuse to entertain them again. We can do this. We can give up our doubts just as we would urge someone to give up a harmful habit. If we truly see that our doubts are a sin against God and question His trustworthiness, we will be eager to abandon them. We may have held on to our doubts before because we thought they were part of our faith and a fitting attitude for someone who feels unworthy. But if we now see that God truly is our Father, we will reject every doubt with horror, recognising it as a slander against His love and care. What more could any soul want than to have a God whose name is “our Father,” and whose character matches that name? As Philip said, “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us” (John 14:8). And indeed, it is enough—far beyond what words can express. A friend of mine once went to visit a poor woman living in one of the poorest parts of Philadelphia, whose situation had been reported as one of great need. She found things even worse than expected. The woman was old, crippled with rheumatism, and lived alone in a small, poor room, receiving only occasional help from a kind neighbour. Yet she was cheerful and full of gratitude. My friend was amazed that such joy could exist under such circumstances and asked, “Do you never feel afraid when you think about what might happen to you, living here alone and in such a condition?” The woman looked at her with surprise and said, “Afraid? Why, don’t you know I have a Father, and don’t you know He takes care of me all the time?” Then, seeing my friend’s confusion, she added gently, “Surely my Father is your Father too, and you know Him, and you know He always takes care of His children.” It was a lesson my friend never forgot. “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are” (1 John 3:1). The love given to us is the love of a father for his child—a tender, protective love that understands our weakness and our needs and cares for us accordingly. He treats us as children, and all He asks in return is that we treat Him as a Father whom we can trust without anxiety. We must take the place of children—dependent and trusting—and allow Him to take the place of Father—caring and responsible. Because we are the children and He is the Father, we must let Him do the Father’s part. Too often, we take that role upon ourselves and try to care for and provide for our own needs. But no good earthly father would want his children to carry his responsibilities, and certainly our heavenly Father would not want us to carry His. No wonder we are told, “casting all your anxieties on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). Of course He cares for us—it is His role as Father. He would not be a good Father if He did not. All He asks is that we tell Him what we need and then leave the provision to Him. He promises that if we do this, “the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus” (Philippians 4:7). Children of a good earthly father are at peace because they trust their father’s care. Yet the children of the heavenly Father often have no peace because they are afraid to trust Him. They may tell Him their needs, but only as a routine. They do not truly believe He will take care of them. And so they continue to carry their burdens as though they had no Father in heaven at all. What foolishness this is. If any earthly father is worthy of his children’s trust, how much more is our heavenly Father worthy of ours. The reason so few trust Him is either that they have not realised He is truly their Father, or that, although they call Him Father, they have never understood what that really means. The answer to your unrest is to become truly acquainted with the Father. “For you did not receive the spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15). Is this spirit of adoption ruling in your heart, or is it the spirit of fear? Your peace depends entirely on this. No effort, struggle, or prayer can bring you rest while the spirit of adoption is absent. But you may ask how to receive this spirit. It is not something you obtain by effort. It comes naturally when you discover that God truly is your Father. When you realise this, you cannot help but think and act like a child—and that is what the spirit of adoption means. It is not mysterious; it is simply the natural result of finding a Father where you once thought there was only a Judge. The great need, therefore, is to make this discovery. To do this, we must listen to what Christ says about the Father and believe it. “Truly, truly, I say to you, we speak of what we know, and bear witness to what we have seen, but you do not receive our testimony” (John 3:11). “The words that I say to you I do not speak on my own authority, but the Father who dwells in me does his works” (John 14:10). “Whoever receives his testimony sets his seal to this, that God is true” (John 3:33). If we accept Christ’s testimony, we declare that God is true. If we reject it, we make Him a liar. “If you had known me, you would have known my Father also. From now on you do know him and have seen him” (John 14:7). We must decide that from now on we will believe His testimony and truly know the Father. For us, there must be “one God, the Father, from whom are all things and for whom we exist, and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things and through whom we exist” (1 Corinthians 8:6).

fields.title: Jehovah
fields.body_html:
“That they may know that you alone, whose name is the LORD, are the Most High over all the earth” (Psalm 83:18).

Among all the names of God, perhaps the most complete is Jehovah. This name means the self-existing One, “I AM.” It reveals what God is. At times, additional names are given to show specific aspects of His character: Jehovah-jireh — The Lord will provide.

Jehovah-nissi — The Lord is my banner.

Jehovah-shalom — The Lord is our peace.

Jehovah-tsidkenu — The Lord is our righteousness.

Jehovah-shammah — The Lord is there.

These names were discovered in times of need. When Abraham was about to sacrifice his son and saw no way out, God provided a lamb. Abraham then understood that God provides for His people.

This truth is repeated in the New Testament: “Your heavenly Father knows that you need them all” (Matthew 6:32).

If God sees and knows our needs, He will certainly provide for them.

Over and over our Lord urges us not to be anxious, because God cares for us. “Your heavenly Father knows,” He says, “that you need them all.” (Holy Bible, Matthew 6:32). If the Lord sees and knows our need, it will naturally follow that He will provide for it.

Being our Father, He could not do otherwise. As soon as a good mother sees that her child needs anything, she immediately sets about supplying that need. She does not even wait for the child to ask; the sight of the need is enough. Being a good mother, she could not act differently. When God, therefore, says to us, “I am he who sees your need,” He is in reality also saying, “I am he who provides,” for He cannot see and fail to provide.

“Why do I not have everything I want, then?” you may ask. Only because God sees that what you want is not really what you need, but probably the exact opposite. Often, in order to give us what we need, the Lord must keep from us what we want. “Your heavenly Father knows what you need before you ask him.” (Matthew 6:8). You do not know; and if all your wants were granted, it might be that all your real needs would be left unmet. It ought surely to be enough for us that our God is Jehovah-jireh, the Lord who sees and therefore provides.

But I am afraid that many Christians today have never made Abraham’s discovery, and do not know that the Lord is truly Jehovah-jireh. They may trust Him to save their souls in the future, but they never imagine that He wants to carry their cares for them here and now. They are like a man I have heard of, with a heavy load on his back, who was given a lift by a friend and gladly accepted it. He climbed into the carriage but kept his burden on his back, sitting there bent under its weight. “Why do you not put your burden down on the floor of the carriage?” his friend asked.

“Oh,” replied the man, “it is already a great deal for you to carry me, and I could not ask you to carry my burden as well.” You may wonder how anyone could be so foolish, and yet are you not doing the same? Are you not trusting the Lord to take care of you, while still carrying your burdens yourself? Which is more foolish—that man or you?

Jehovah-nissi, that is, “The Lord my banner,” was a discovery made by Moses when Amalek came to fight against Israel at Rephidim, and the Lord gave Israel a great victory. Moses realised that the Lord was fighting for them, and he built an altar and called its name, “The Lord Is My Banner” (Exodus 17:15). The Bible is full of expressions of this truth. “The LORD is a man of war; the LORD is his name.” (Exodus 15:3). “The LORD your God who goes before you will himself fight for you.” (Deuteronomy 1:30). “The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent.” (Exodus 14:14). “Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed at this great horde, for the battle is not yours but God’s.” (2 Chronicles 20:15). “God himself has been with us as our head.”

(2 Chronicles 13:12).

Nothing is more clearly shown in the Bible than this: the Lord will fight for us if we will only let Him. He knows that we have no strength against our spiritual enemies; and, like a tender mother when her helpless children are attacked, He fights for us. All He asks is that we remain still and allow Him to act. This is the only kind of spiritual conflict that ever succeeds. But we are slow to learn this. When temptations come, instead of handing the battle over to the Lord, we gather all our strength to fight them ourselves. We may believe that the Lord is nearby and will help if things become desperate; but for the most part, we feel that we must do all the fighting ourselves.

Our way of fighting usually consists of repeated repentance, making resolutions and promises, struggling hard for victory, and then failing again; followed by more repentance, more resolutions, more promises, and renewed struggle—over and over again. Each time we tell ourselves that now we will surely succeed, and each time we fail, often worse than before. This may continue for weeks, months, or even years, without any real or lasting deliverance.

But you may ask, “Are we not to fight at all?” Of course we are to fight, but not in this way. We are to fight “the good fight of the faith” (1 Timothy 6:12), and the fight of faith is not a struggle of effort, but a struggle of trust. It is like the fight of King Hezekiah, when he and his people faced their enemy and found that “when they began to sing and praise, the LORD set an ambush… so that they were routed” (2 Chronicles 20:22). Our part is to hand the battle over to the Lord and trust Him for the victory.

There is nothing here about promises or resolutions; nothing about hours or days of agonising struggles or bitter remorse. “In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one” (Holy Bible, Ephesians 6:16). Above all, faith.

Faith is the one essential thing, without which everything else is useless. It means that we must not only hand the battle over to the Lord, but also leave it with Him, and have complete confidence that He will win.

This is where the real struggle lies. It feels unsafe to be still and simply trust the Lord, and the temptation to take the battle back into our own hands is often very strong. Keeping our hands off in spiritual matters is as difficult for us as it is for a drowning person to stop struggling against the one trying to rescue them. We all know how impossible it is to save someone who is drowning if they fight their rescuer, and it is just as impossible for the Lord to fight our battles for us when we insist on trying to fight them ourselves. It is not that He is unwilling, but that He cannot. Our interference hinders His work. Spiritual forces cannot operate while earthly efforts are taking over.

Our Lord tells us, “apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5), and we have read and repeated these words many times; but does anyone truly believe them? If we were honest about our hidden thoughts, would we not find something like this: “When Christ said those words, He surely meant that we cannot do much on our own, or at least nothing great. But nothing at all— that cannot be right. We are not helpless children, and we are surely meant to use all the strength we have to fight our enemies; and when that strength fails, then we can ask the Lord for help.”

Despite all our failures, we still tend to think that if we just tried harder and persevered more, we could succeed in any situation. But we completely overlook the crucial truth that our natural abilities are of no use in spiritual matters or against spiritual enemies.

The grub of a dragonfly, living at the bottom of a pond, may be strong and well developed for its environment; but when it becomes a dragonfly, the abilities that helped it crawl through the mud are useless for flying in the open air. In the same way, just as our ability to walk on the ground would be useless if we needed to fly, our natural abilities are of no use in spiritual warfare. In fact, if we rely on them, they become real obstacles—just as trying to walk would hinder us if we were meant to float or fly.

We can see, then, that trusting in ourselves when facing spiritual enemies has serious consequences. It not only leads to failure, but ultimately leads to rebellion. Much of what is called “spiritual conflict” would be more accurately described as “spiritual rebellion”. God has told us to stop relying on our own efforts and to hand our battles over to Him, yet we refuse to obey. We do fight, but it is not a fight of faith; it is a fight of unbelief. The “wrestling” we are often proud of is not wrestling for God against His enemies, but wrestling against Him alongside His enemies. We allow doubts and fears to grow, and as a result we fall into darkness, turmoil, and inner struggle. Then we label this “spiritual conflict” and consider ourselves a special or unusual case. But the single word that explains this condition is unbelief, and the simple cure is faith.

You may ask about Jacob’s wrestling—did he not gain victory through struggle? In fact, he gained victory by becoming too weak to struggle any longer. It was not Jacob wrestling with the angel, but the angel wrestling with Jacob. Jacob was the one who needed to be overcome. When the angel saw that Jacob’s resistance was too strong to overcome, he touched his hip and put it out of joint; and then the victory was achieved. As soon as Jacob was too weak to resist, he prevailed with God. He gained strength when he lost it. He overcame when he could no longer fight.

Jacob’s experience reflects our own. The Lord wrestles with us to bring us to complete dependence on Him. We resist as long as we have strength, until at last He brings us to a place of helplessness where we must yield; and then we conquer through that very surrender. Our victory is always a victory of weakness. Paul understood this when he wrote: “But he said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.’ Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me… For when I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12:9–10).

Who could ask for a more glorious victory than this?

And this victory will be ours if we take the Lord as our Banner and commit all our battles to Him. The name Jehovah-shalom, meaning “The Lord is peace,” was discovered by Gideon when the Lord called him to a task for which he felt completely unqualified. He said, “Please, Lord, how can I save Israel? Behold, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house” (Judges 6:15). And the Lord said to him, “But I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man” (Judges 6:16)… “Peace be to you. Do not fear; you shall not die” (Judges 6:23). Then Gideon believed the Lord; and although the battle had not yet been fought and no victory had yet been seen, by faith he saw peace already secured. He built an altar to the Lord and called it “The LORD Is Peace” (Judges 6:24).

Of all the needs of the human heart, none is greater than the need for peace, and none is more fully promised in the gospel. “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you… Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid” (John 14:27). And again, “I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).

We often think peace must come from outward calm—that all enemies must disappear and all troubles must end. But the Lord speaks of an inner peace that can exist even in the middle of turmoil and rise above it. The foundation of this peace is not that we have overcome the world, or ever could, but that Christ has overcome it. Only the conqueror can declare peace, and those for whom He has fought can only enter into it. They cannot create it or destroy it. But they can refuse to believe it, and so fail to let it rule in their hearts. You may hesitate to believe that Christ has made peace for you, and so continue in a restless state of conflict; yet He has already done it, and your continued struggle is unnecessary.

The Bible tells us that Christ Himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14). Therefore, whether I feel peaceful or not, peace is already mine in Him, and I must take hold of it by faith. Faith simply believes and declares what God has said. If He says there is peace, faith affirms it and enters into it. If He has declared peace in Scripture, I must declare it in my own heart, regardless of appearances. “For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14:17), and anyone who has not entered into peace has not yet fully entered into this kingdom.

In practice, we can always enter into peace by simply obeying Philippians 4:6–7: “do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus”. The steps are very clear, and there are only two: first, give up all anxiety; second, hand your cares over to God. Then remain firmly there— peace must come. It must, because nothing else can take its place.

The name Jehovah-tsidkenu, meaning “The Lord our righteousness,” was revealed by the Lord through the prophet Jeremiah when he spoke of the coming of Christ: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch… And this is the name by which he will be called: ‘The LORD is our righteousness’” (Jeremiah 23:5–6).

Greater than any other need is our need for righteousness. Most of the struggles and conflicts in our Christian life come from our battles with sin and our efforts to become righteous. And it hardly needs to be said how often we fail. As long as we try to overcome sin or gain righteousness by our own efforts, we are bound to fail. But if we discover that the Lord is our righteousness, we will have found the secret of victory.

In the Lord Jesus Christ we have a fuller revelation of this wonderful name of God. The apostle Paul, speaking as an ambassador for Christ, declares that “for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (Holy Bible, 2 Corinthians 5:21). And again he says, “And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30).

I am afraid that very few Christians truly understand what this means. We repeat these words as part of our religious language, and in a vague way think of them as belonging to Christ’s salvation; but what they really mean, or how they apply in daily life, we scarcely understand.

To me, this name of God—“The Lord our righteousness”—is of such practical importance that I want, if possible, to make it clear. It is not easy, and I cannot explain it theologically. But in experience, it seems to be like this: we are not meant to store up righteousness within ourselves, as if we could draw from it when needed. Instead, we are to receive a continual fresh supply as we need it from the righteousness that is stored up for us in Christ.

In other words, if we need any kind of righteousness—patience, humility, love—it is useless to look within ourselves, hoping to find it there, for we never will. Instead, we must simply take it by faith, as something already given to us in Christ, who is our righteousness. I may not be able to explain exactly how this works, but I know from experience that it does, and that the results are real and powerful. I have seen gentleness and kindness poured like sunlight into hearts that were once bitter and dark, when faith reached out to take them as a present possession in Christ. I have seen harsh words become gentle, anxious hearts become calm, and restless spirits become quiet through this simple act of faith—taking the righteousness that is ours in Christ.

The apostle, after showing in Romans chapter 3 that it is impossible for us to gain righteousness through the law—that is, through our own efforts—goes on to say: “But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law… the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. For there is no distinction” (Romans 3:21–22).

It is faith, and faith alone, that receives this righteousness that is ours in Christ. Just as we receive forgiveness by faith, so we must also receive patience, gentleness, meekness, long-suffering, or any other virtue we need—by faith. Our own efforts cannot produce righteousness any more than they can produce forgiveness. And yet, how many Christians still try!

Paul describes such people when he says: “For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God’s righteousness. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:2–4).

If only all such earnest souls could discover this wonderful name of God—“The Lord our righteousness”—and would stop trying to establish their own righteousness, and instead submit to the righteousness of God. The prophet tells us that even our best righteousness is like “a polluted garment” (Isaiah 64:6). And Paul expresses his desire to “be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith” (Philippians 3:9).

Do we truly understand what this means? And are we ready to embrace it with all our hearts? If so, our struggle to become righteous will come to an end. Jehovah-tsidkenu will meet every need.

The name Jehovah-shammah, meaning “The Lord is there,” was revealed to the prophet Ezekiel when he was shown in a vision, in the twenty-fifth year of the captivity, what would be the future home of the children of Israel. He described the land and the city of Jerusalem, and ended by saying: “And the name of the city from that time on shall be, The LORD Is There” (Ezekiel 48:35).

To me, this name includes all the others. Wherever the Lord is, everything must be right for His children. Where a good mother is, things go well for her children, as far as she is able to provide.

How much more is this true of God. His presence alone is enough.

We can all remember how, as children, the simple presence of our mother was enough for us. All the comfort, rest, and help we needed seemed assured just by her being there—sitting in her usual place with her work or her book—while we came to her with our troubles. If we could only realise that God’s presence gives the same assurance—only infinitely greater—a deep well of joy would open in our spiritual lives, driving out every trace of fear and distress.

All through the Old Testament, the Lord’s answer to the fears and anxieties of Israel was simply this: “I will be with you” (Exodus 3:12). Nothing more needed to be said. His presence was a complete guarantee that all their needs would be met; and once they were sure of it, they were no longer afraid to face even the fiercest enemy. You may say, “Ah, yes, if the Lord would only say the same thing to me, I should not be afraid either.” Well, He has said it, and He has said it in unmistakable terms. When the “angel of the Lord” announced to Joseph the coming birth of Christ, he said: “‘Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel’ (which means, God with us)” (Matthew 1:23). In this short sentence is revealed to us the grandest fact the world can ever know—that God, the Almighty God, the Creator of Heaven and earth, is not a far-off God, dwelling in a Heaven of unapproachable glory, but has come down in Christ to dwell with us right here in this world, in the midst of our poor, ignorant, helpless lives, as close to us as we are to ourselves. If we believe in Christ at all, we are forced to believe this, for this is His name, “God with us.”

Both these names then, Jehovah-shammah and Emmanuel, mean the same thing. They mean that God is everywhere present in His universe, surrounding everything, and sustaining everything, and holding all of us in His safe and blessed keeping. They mean that we can find no place in all His universe of which it cannot be said, “The Lord is there.” The psalmist says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there! If I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me” (Psalm 139:7-10).

We cannot drift from the love and care of an ever-present God. And those Christians who think He has abandoned them, and who cry out for His presence, are crying out in ignorance of the fact that He is always and everywhere present with them. In truth, they cannot get out of His presence, even if they tried. Oh, that they knew this wonderful and satisfying name of God!

Speak to Him, for He hears; and spirit may meet with spirit; He is closer than breathing, and nearer than hands and feet.

Let us sum up, once more, the teaching of these five names of God. What is it they say to us?

Jehovah-jireh, i.e., “I am he who sees your need, and therefore provides for it.”

Jehovah-nissi, i.e., “I am the captain, and your banner, and he who will fight your battles for you.”

Jehovah-shalom, i.e., “I am your peace. I have made peace for you, and my peace I give to you.”

Jehovah-tsidkenu, i.e., “I am your righteousness. In me you will find all you need of wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption.”

Jehovah-shammah, i.e., “I am with you. I am your ever-present, all-encompassing God and Saviour. I will never leave you nor forsake you. Wherever you go, I am there, and there shall my hand hold you, and my right hand lead you.”

All this is true, whether we know it and recognise it or not. We may never have dreamed that God was such a God as this, and we may have gone through our lives until now starved, and weary, and wretched. But all the time we have been starving in the midst of plenty. The fullness of God’s salvation has awaited our faith; and “the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness” (Romans 5:17) have awaited our receiving.

I wish I could believe that for some of my readers all this was ended, and that from now on they would see that these all-embracing names of God leave no tiny corner of their need unsupplied.

Then they would be able to testify with the prophet to everyone around them: “Behold, God is my salvation; I will trust, and will not be afraid; for the Lord God is my strength and my song, and he has become my salvation. With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation” (Isaiah 12:2-3).
fields.body_text: “That they may know that you alone, whose name is the LORD, are the Most High over all the earth” (Psalm 83:18). Among all the names of God, perhaps the most complete is Jehovah. This name means the self-existing One, “I AM.” It reveals what God is. At times, additional names are given to show specific aspects of His character: Jehovah-jireh — The Lord will provide. Jehovah-nissi — The Lord is my banner. Jehovah-shalom — The Lord is our peace. Jehovah-tsidkenu — The Lord is our righteousness. Jehovah-shammah — The Lord is there. These names were discovered in times of need. When Abraham was about to sacrifice his son and saw no way out, God provided a lamb. Abraham then understood that God provides for His people. This truth is repeated in the New Testament: “Your heavenly Father knows that you need them all” (Matthew 6:32). If God sees and knows our needs, He will certainly provide for them. Over and over our Lord urges us not to be anxious, because God cares for us. “Your heavenly Father knows,” He says, “that you need them all.” (Holy Bible, Matthew 6:32). If the Lord sees and knows our need, it will naturally follow that He will provide for it. Being our Father, He could not do otherwise. As soon as a good mother sees that her child needs anything, she immediately sets about supplying that need. She does not even wait for the child to ask; the sight of the need is enough. Being a good mother, she could not act differently. When God, therefore, says to us, “I am he who sees your need,” He is in reality also saying, “I am he who provides,” for He cannot see and fail to provide. “Why do I not have everything I want, then?” you may ask. Only because God sees that what you want is not really what you need, but probably the exact opposite. Often, in order to give us what we need, the Lord must keep from us what we want. “Your heavenly Father knows what you need before you ask him.” (Matthew 6:8). You do not know; and if all your wants were granted, it might be that all your real needs would be left unmet. It ought surely to be enough for us that our God is Jehovah-jireh, the Lord who sees and therefore provides. But I am afraid that many Christians today have never made Abraham’s discovery, and do not know that the Lord is truly Jehovah-jireh. They may trust Him to save their souls in the future, but they never imagine that He wants to carry their cares for them here and now. They are like a man I have heard of, with a heavy load on his back, who was given a lift by a friend and gladly accepted it. He climbed into the carriage but kept his burden on his back, sitting there bent under its weight. “Why do you not put your burden down on the floor of the carriage?” his friend asked. “Oh,” replied the man, “it is already a great deal for you to carry me, and I could not ask you to carry my burden as well.” You may wonder how anyone could be so foolish, and yet are you not doing the same? Are you not trusting the Lord to take care of you, while still carrying your burdens yourself? Which is more foolish—that man or you? Jehovah-nissi, that is, “The Lord my banner,” was a discovery made by Moses when Amalek came to fight against Israel at Rephidim, and the Lord gave Israel a great victory. Moses realised that the Lord was fighting for them, and he built an altar and called its name, “The Lord Is My Banner” (Exodus 17:15). The Bible is full of expressions of this truth. “The LORD is a man of war; the LORD is his name.” (Exodus 15:3). “The LORD your God who goes before you will himself fight for you.” (Deuteronomy 1:30). “The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent.” (Exodus 14:14). “Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed at this great horde, for the battle is not yours but God’s.” (2 Chronicles 20:15). “God himself has been with us as our head.” (2 Chronicles 13:12). Nothing is more clearly shown in the Bible than this: the Lord will fight for us if we will only let Him. He knows that we have no strength against our spiritual enemies; and, like a tender mother when her helpless children are attacked, He fights for us. All He asks is that we remain still and allow Him to act. This is the only kind of spiritual conflict that ever succeeds. But we are slow to learn this. When temptations come, instead of handing the battle over to the Lord, we gather all our strength to fight them ourselves. We may believe that the Lord is nearby and will help if things become desperate; but for the most part, we feel that we must do all the fighting ourselves. Our way of fighting usually consists of repeated repentance, making resolutions and promises, struggling hard for victory, and then failing again; followed by more repentance, more resolutions, more promises, and renewed struggle—over and over again. Each time we tell ourselves that now we will surely succeed, and each time we fail, often worse than before. This may continue for weeks, months, or even years, without any real or lasting deliverance. But you may ask, “Are we not to fight at all?” Of course we are to fight, but not in this way. We are to fight “the good fight of the faith” (1 Timothy 6:12), and the fight of faith is not a struggle of effort, but a struggle of trust. It is like the fight of King Hezekiah, when he and his people faced their enemy and found that “when they began to sing and praise, the LORD set an ambush… so that they were routed” (2 Chronicles 20:22). Our part is to hand the battle over to the Lord and trust Him for the victory. There is nothing here about promises or resolutions; nothing about hours or days of agonising struggles or bitter remorse. “In all circumstances take up the shield of faith, with which you can extinguish all the flaming darts of the evil one” (Holy Bible, Ephesians 6:16). Above all, faith. Faith is the one essential thing, without which everything else is useless. It means that we must not only hand the battle over to the Lord, but also leave it with Him, and have complete confidence that He will win. This is where the real struggle lies. It feels unsafe to be still and simply trust the Lord, and the temptation to take the battle back into our own hands is often very strong. Keeping our hands off in spiritual matters is as difficult for us as it is for a drowning person to stop struggling against the one trying to rescue them. We all know how impossible it is to save someone who is drowning if they fight their rescuer, and it is just as impossible for the Lord to fight our battles for us when we insist on trying to fight them ourselves. It is not that He is unwilling, but that He cannot. Our interference hinders His work. Spiritual forces cannot operate while earthly efforts are taking over. Our Lord tells us, “apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5), and we have read and repeated these words many times; but does anyone truly believe them? If we were honest about our hidden thoughts, would we not find something like this: “When Christ said those words, He surely meant that we cannot do much on our own, or at least nothing great. But nothing at all— that cannot be right. We are not helpless children, and we are surely meant to use all the strength we have to fight our enemies; and when that strength fails, then we can ask the Lord for help.” Despite all our failures, we still tend to think that if we just tried harder and persevered more, we could succeed in any situation. But we completely overlook the crucial truth that our natural abilities are of no use in spiritual matters or against spiritual enemies. The grub of a dragonfly, living at the bottom of a pond, may be strong and well developed for its environment; but when it becomes a dragonfly, the abilities that helped it crawl through the mud are useless for flying in the open air. In the same way, just as our ability to walk on the ground would be useless if we needed to fly, our natural abilities are of no use in spiritual warfare. In fact, if we rely on them, they become real obstacles—just as trying to walk would hinder us if we were meant to float or fly. We can see, then, that trusting in ourselves when facing spiritual enemies has serious consequences. It not only leads to failure, but ultimately leads to rebellion. Much of what is called “spiritual conflict” would be more accurately described as “spiritual rebellion”. God has told us to stop relying on our own efforts and to hand our battles over to Him, yet we refuse to obey. We do fight, but it is not a fight of faith; it is a fight of unbelief. The “wrestling” we are often proud of is not wrestling for God against His enemies, but wrestling against Him alongside His enemies. We allow doubts and fears to grow, and as a result we fall into darkness, turmoil, and inner struggle. Then we label this “spiritual conflict” and consider ourselves a special or unusual case. But the single word that explains this condition is unbelief, and the simple cure is faith. You may ask about Jacob’s wrestling—did he not gain victory through struggle? In fact, he gained victory by becoming too weak to struggle any longer. It was not Jacob wrestling with the angel, but the angel wrestling with Jacob. Jacob was the one who needed to be overcome. When the angel saw that Jacob’s resistance was too strong to overcome, he touched his hip and put it out of joint; and then the victory was achieved. As soon as Jacob was too weak to resist, he prevailed with God. He gained strength when he lost it. He overcame when he could no longer fight. Jacob’s experience reflects our own. The Lord wrestles with us to bring us to complete dependence on Him. We resist as long as we have strength, until at last He brings us to a place of helplessness where we must yield; and then we conquer through that very surrender. Our victory is always a victory of weakness. Paul understood this when he wrote: “But he said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.’ Therefore I will boast all the more gladly of my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest upon me… For when I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12:9–10). Who could ask for a more glorious victory than this? And this victory will be ours if we take the Lord as our Banner and commit all our battles to Him. The name Jehovah-shalom, meaning “The Lord is peace,” was discovered by Gideon when the Lord called him to a task for which he felt completely unqualified. He said, “Please, Lord, how can I save Israel? Behold, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father’s house” (Judges 6:15). And the Lord said to him, “But I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man” (Judges 6:16)… “Peace be to you. Do not fear; you shall not die” (Judges 6:23). Then Gideon believed the Lord; and although the battle had not yet been fought and no victory had yet been seen, by faith he saw peace already secured. He built an altar to the Lord and called it “The LORD Is Peace” (Judges 6:24). Of all the needs of the human heart, none is greater than the need for peace, and none is more fully promised in the gospel. “Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you… Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid” (John 14:27). And again, “I have said these things to you, that in me you may have peace. In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). We often think peace must come from outward calm—that all enemies must disappear and all troubles must end. But the Lord speaks of an inner peace that can exist even in the middle of turmoil and rise above it. The foundation of this peace is not that we have overcome the world, or ever could, but that Christ has overcome it. Only the conqueror can declare peace, and those for whom He has fought can only enter into it. They cannot create it or destroy it. But they can refuse to believe it, and so fail to let it rule in their hearts. You may hesitate to believe that Christ has made peace for you, and so continue in a restless state of conflict; yet He has already done it, and your continued struggle is unnecessary. The Bible tells us that Christ Himself is our peace (Ephesians 2:14). Therefore, whether I feel peaceful or not, peace is already mine in Him, and I must take hold of it by faith. Faith simply believes and declares what God has said. If He says there is peace, faith affirms it and enters into it. If He has declared peace in Scripture, I must declare it in my own heart, regardless of appearances. “For the kingdom of God is not a matter of eating and drinking but of righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans 14:17), and anyone who has not entered into peace has not yet fully entered into this kingdom. In practice, we can always enter into peace by simply obeying Philippians 4:6–7: “do not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your minds in Christ Jesus”. The steps are very clear, and there are only two: first, give up all anxiety; second, hand your cares over to God. Then remain firmly there— peace must come. It must, because nothing else can take its place. The name Jehovah-tsidkenu, meaning “The Lord our righteousness,” was revealed by the Lord through the prophet Jeremiah when he spoke of the coming of Christ: “Behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when I will raise up for David a righteous Branch… And this is the name by which he will be called: ‘The LORD is our righteousness’” (Jeremiah 23:5–6). Greater than any other need is our need for righteousness. Most of the struggles and conflicts in our Christian life come from our battles with sin and our efforts to become righteous. And it hardly needs to be said how often we fail. As long as we try to overcome sin or gain righteousness by our own efforts, we are bound to fail. But if we discover that the Lord is our righteousness, we will have found the secret of victory. In the Lord Jesus Christ we have a fuller revelation of this wonderful name of God. The apostle Paul, speaking as an ambassador for Christ, declares that “for our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God” (Holy Bible, 2 Corinthians 5:21). And again he says, “And because of him you are in Christ Jesus, who became to us wisdom from God, righteousness and sanctification and redemption” (1 Corinthians 1:30). I am afraid that very few Christians truly understand what this means. We repeat these words as part of our religious language, and in a vague way think of them as belonging to Christ’s salvation; but what they really mean, or how they apply in daily life, we scarcely understand. To me, this name of God—“The Lord our righteousness”—is of such practical importance that I want, if possible, to make it clear. It is not easy, and I cannot explain it theologically. But in experience, it seems to be like this: we are not meant to store up righteousness within ourselves, as if we could draw from it when needed. Instead, we are to receive a continual fresh supply as we need it from the righteousness that is stored up for us in Christ. In other words, if we need any kind of righteousness—patience, humility, love—it is useless to look within ourselves, hoping to find it there, for we never will. Instead, we must simply take it by faith, as something already given to us in Christ, who is our righteousness. I may not be able to explain exactly how this works, but I know from experience that it does, and that the results are real and powerful. I have seen gentleness and kindness poured like sunlight into hearts that were once bitter and dark, when faith reached out to take them as a present possession in Christ. I have seen harsh words become gentle, anxious hearts become calm, and restless spirits become quiet through this simple act of faith—taking the righteousness that is ours in Christ. The apostle, after showing in Romans chapter 3 that it is impossible for us to gain righteousness through the law—that is, through our own efforts—goes on to say: “But now the righteousness of God has been manifested apart from the law… the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. For there is no distinction” (Romans 3:21–22). It is faith, and faith alone, that receives this righteousness that is ours in Christ. Just as we receive forgiveness by faith, so we must also receive patience, gentleness, meekness, long-suffering, or any other virtue we need—by faith. Our own efforts cannot produce righteousness any more than they can produce forgiveness. And yet, how many Christians still try! Paul describes such people when he says: “For I bear them witness that they have a zeal for God, but not according to knowledge. For, being ignorant of the righteousness of God, and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to God’s righteousness. For Christ is the end of the law for righteousness to everyone who believes” (Romans 10:2–4). If only all such earnest souls could discover this wonderful name of God—“The Lord our righteousness”—and would stop trying to establish their own righteousness, and instead submit to the righteousness of God. The prophet tells us that even our best righteousness is like “a polluted garment” (Isaiah 64:6). And Paul expresses his desire to “be found in him, not having a righteousness of my own that comes from the law, but that which comes through faith in Christ, the righteousness from God that depends on faith” (Philippians 3:9). Do we truly understand what this means? And are we ready to embrace it with all our hearts? If so, our struggle to become righteous will come to an end. Jehovah-tsidkenu will meet every need. The name Jehovah-shammah, meaning “The Lord is there,” was revealed to the prophet Ezekiel when he was shown in a vision, in the twenty-fifth year of the captivity, what would be the future home of the children of Israel. He described the land and the city of Jerusalem, and ended by saying: “And the name of the city from that time on shall be, The LORD Is There” (Ezekiel 48:35). To me, this name includes all the others. Wherever the Lord is, everything must be right for His children. Where a good mother is, things go well for her children, as far as she is able to provide. How much more is this true of God. His presence alone is enough. We can all remember how, as children, the simple presence of our mother was enough for us. All the comfort, rest, and help we needed seemed assured just by her being there—sitting in her usual place with her work or her book—while we came to her with our troubles. If we could only realise that God’s presence gives the same assurance—only infinitely greater—a deep well of joy would open in our spiritual lives, driving out every trace of fear and distress. All through the Old Testament, the Lord’s answer to the fears and anxieties of Israel was simply this: “I will be with you” (Exodus 3:12). Nothing more needed to be said. His presence was a complete guarantee that all their needs would be met; and once they were sure of it, they were no longer afraid to face even the fiercest enemy. You may say, “Ah, yes, if the Lord would only say the same thing to me, I should not be afraid either.” Well, He has said it, and He has said it in unmistakable terms. When the “angel of the Lord” announced to Joseph the coming birth of Christ, he said: “‘Behold, the virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and they shall call his name Immanuel’ (which means, God with us)” (Matthew 1:23). In this short sentence is revealed to us the grandest fact the world can ever know—that God, the Almighty God, the Creator of Heaven and earth, is not a far-off God, dwelling in a Heaven of unapproachable glory, but has come down in Christ to dwell with us right here in this world, in the midst of our poor, ignorant, helpless lives, as close to us as we are to ourselves. If we believe in Christ at all, we are forced to believe this, for this is His name, “God with us.” Both these names then, Jehovah-shammah and Emmanuel, mean the same thing. They mean that God is everywhere present in His universe, surrounding everything, and sustaining everything, and holding all of us in His safe and blessed keeping. They mean that we can find no place in all His universe of which it cannot be said, “The Lord is there.” The psalmist says: “Where shall I go from your Spirit? Or where shall I flee from your presence? If I ascend to heaven, you are there! If I make my bed in Sheol, you are there! If I take the wings of the morning and dwell in the uttermost parts of the sea, even there your hand shall lead me, and your right hand shall hold me” (Psalm 139:7-10). I have made peace for you, and my peace I give to you.” Jehovah-tsidkenu, i.e., “I am your righteousness. In me you will find all you need of wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption.” Jehovah-shammah, i.e., “I am with you. I am your ever-present, all-encompassing God and Saviour. I will never leave you nor forsake you. Wherever you go, I am there, and there shall my hand hold you, and my right hand lead you.” All this is true, whether we know it and recognise it or not.
