With joy you will draw water from the wells of salvation” (Isaiah 12:2-3).

fields.title: The Lord is Good
fields.body_html:
“Oh, taste and see that the Lord is good! Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him!” (Psalm 34:8).

Have you ever asked yourself what you honestly think of God at the bottom of your heart— whether you believe Him to be a good God or a bad God? I expect the question will shock you, and you will be horrified at the suggestion that you could by any possibility think that God is a bad God. But before you have finished this chapter, I suspect some of you will be forced to acknowledge that, perhaps unconsciously but nonetheless truly, you have, by your doubts and your complaints, attributed to Him a character that you would be horrified to have attributed to yourself.

I shall never forget the hour when I first discovered that God was really good. I had, of course, always known that the Bible said He was good, but I had thought it only meant He was religiously good; and it had never dawned on me that it meant He was actually and practically good, with the same kind of goodness He has commanded us to have. The expression, “The goodness of God,” had seemed to me nothing more than a sort of heavenly statement, which I could not be expected to understand. And then one day I came across the words in my Bible reading, “Oh, taste and see that the Lord is good,” and suddenly they meant something.

The Lord is good, I repeated to myself. What does it mean to be good? What but this: living up to the best and highest that one knows. To be good is exactly the opposite of being bad. To be bad is to know the right thing and not do it, but to be good is to do the best we know. And I saw that, since God knows everything, He must know what is the best and highest good of all, and that therefore His goodness must necessarily be beyond question. I can never express what this meant to me. I had such a view of the real, actual goodness of God that I saw nothing could possibly go wrong under His care, and it seemed to me that no one could ever be anxious again.

And over and over, when appearances have been against Him, and when I have been tempted to question whether He had been unkind, or neglectful, or indifferent, I have been stopped in my tracks by the words, “The Lord is good”; and I have seen that it was simply unthinkable that a God who was good could have done the bad things I had imagined.

You shrink with horror, perhaps, from the suggestion that you could under any circumstances, even in the secret depths of your heart, attribute to God what was bad. And yet you do not hesitate to accuse Him of doing things which, if one of your friends did them, you would look upon as most dishonourable and unkind. For instance, Christians get into trouble; everything looks dark, and they have no sense of the Lord’s presence. They begin to question whether the Lord has abandoned them, and sometimes even accuse Him of indifference and neglect. They never realise that these accusations are the same as saying that the Lord does not keep His promises, and does not treat them as kindly and honourably as they expect all their human friends to treat them. If one of our human friends should abandon us because we were in trouble, we would consider such a friend to be very far from being good. How is it, then, that we can even for one moment accuse our Lord of such actions? No, dear friend, if the Lord is good—not just pious, but really good—it must be because He always, under every circumstance, acts up to the highest ideal of that which He Himself has taught us is goodness. Goodness in Him must mean, just as it does with us, living up to the best and highest He knows.

Practically, then, it means that He will not neglect any of His duties toward us, and that He will always treat us in the best possible way. This may sound like a cliché, and you may exclaim, “Why tell us this, for it is what we all believe?” But do you? If you did, would it be possible for you ever to think He was neglectful, or indifferent, or unkind, or self-absorbed, or inconsiderate?

Do not put on a righteous air and say, “Oh, but I never do accuse Him of any such things. I would not dare to.” Do you not? Have you never blamed Him for things you would be ashamed to do yourselves? How was it when that last painful disappointment came? Did you not feel as if the Lord had been unkind in permitting such a thing to happen to you, when you were trying so hard to serve Him? Do you never look upon His will as a tyrannical and bossy will that must be submitted to, of course, but that could not by any possibility be loved? Does it never seem to you a hard thing to say, “Your will be done”? But could it seem hard if you really believed that the Lord is good, and that He always does that which is good?

The Lord Jesus took great care to tell us that He was a good Shepherd, because He knew how often appearances would be against Him, and how tempted we would be to question His goodness. “I am the good shepherd,” He says in effect, “not a bad one. Bad shepherds neglect and abandon their sheep, but I am a good Shepherd, and never neglect nor abandon My sheep. I lay down My life for the sheep.” His ideal of goodness in a shepherd was that the shepherd must protect the sheep entrusted to his care, even at the cost of his own life; and He lived up to His own ideal. Now, can we not see that if we really believe that He is good—not in some mysterious, religious way, but in this common-sense, human way—we shall be brought into a place of great peace and comfort at once. If I am a sheep, and the Lord is a good Shepherd in the ordinary, common-sense definition of good, how utterly secure I am! How sure I may be of the best care in every respect! How safe I am for time and for eternity!

Let us be honest with ourselves. Have we never in our secret hearts accused the Lord of the characteristics that He has told us in Ezekiel are the marks of a bad shepherd? Have we not thought that He cared for His own comfort or glory more than He cared for ours? Have we not complained that He has not strengthened us when we were weak, or bound up our broken hearts, or searched for us when we were lost?

Have we not even actually looked upon our diseased, and helpless, and lost condition, as a reason why He would not any longer have anything to do with us? In what does this differ from if we should say out plump and plain, the Lord is a bad shepherd, and does not fulfill His duties to His sheep. You shrink in horror, perhaps, at this translation of your inward murmurings and complainings, but what else, I ask you, can they in all honesty mean? It is of vital importance now and then to drag out our secret thoughts and feelings about the Lord into the full light of the Holy Spirit, that we may see what our attitude about Him really is. It is fatally easy to get into a habit of wrong thoughts about God, thoughts which will insensibly separate us from Him by a wide gulf of doubt and unbelief.

More than anything else, more even than sin, wrong thoughts about God sap the foundations of our spiritual life, and grieve His heart of love. We can understand this from ourselves. Nothing grieves us so much as to have our friends misjudge and misunderstand us, and attribute to us motives we scorn. And nothing, I believe, so grieves the Lord. It is, in fact, idolatry. For what is idolatry but creating and worshipping a false God, and what are we doing but this very thing, when we allow ourselves to misjudge Him, and attribute to Him actions and feelings that are unkind and untrustworthy.

It is called in the Bible a speaking against God. “They spoke against God, saying, “Can God spread a table in the wilderness?” This seemed a very innocent question to ask. But God had promised to supply all their needs in the wilderness; and to ask this question implied a secret want of confidence in His ability to do as He had promised; and it was therefore, in spite of its innocent appearance, a real “speaking against” Him. A good God could not have led His people into the wilderness, and then have failed to “spread a table” for them; and to question whether He was able to do it was to imply that He was not good.

In the same way we are sometimes sorely tempted to ask a similar question. Circumstances often seem to make it so impossible for God to supply our needs, that we find ourselves tempted over and over to “speak against” Him by asking if He can. Often as He has done it before, we seem unable to believe He can do it again, and in our hearts we “limit” Him, because we do not believe His Word or trust in His goodness.

If our faith were what it ought to be, no circumstances, however untoward, could make us “limit” the power of God to supply our needs. The God who can make circumstances can surely control circumstances, and can, even in the wilderness, “furnish a table” for all who trust in Him.

There are many similar questions to be found in the Bible, each one throwing doubts upon the goodness of God, and each one, I am afraid, is a duplicate of questions asked by God’s children now.

“Is God among us or not?”

“Has God forgotten to be gracious?”

“Is God’s mercy clean gone forever?”

“Has God in anger shut up his tender mercies?”

“Do God’s promises fail forevermore?”

“O God, why hast thou cast us off forever?”

“Why have you made me this way?”

Let us consider these questions for a little, and see whether we can find any counterparts to them in our own secret questionings.

“Is God among us or not?”

He has declared to us in unmistakable terms, as He did to the children of Israel, that He is always with us, and will never forsake us; and yet when trouble comes, we begin, as they did, to doubt His Word and to question whether He really can be there. Moses called this, when the Israelites did it, “tempting the Lord,” and it deserves the same condemnation when we do it. No one can ask such a question without casting a doubt upon the truthfulness and trustworthiness of the Lord; and to ask it is, if we only knew it, to insult Him, and to libel His character. I know that it is, alas! a common question even among God’s own children, and I know also that many of them think it is only true humility to ask it, and that, for such unworthy creatures as they feel themselves to be, it would be the height of presumption to be sure of His presence with them.

But what about His own Word in the matter? He has declared to us in every possible way that He is with us, and will never leave us nor forsake us, and dare we “make him a liar” by questioning the truth of His Word? A good God cannot lie, and we must give up forever asking such a question as this. The Lord is with us as truly as we are with ourselves, and we have simply just got to believe that He is, no matter what the seeming may be.

“Has God forgotten to be gracious?”

To ask this question is to “speak against” Him as grievously as it would be to ask a good mother if she had forgotten her child. And yet the Lord Himself says: “Can a woman forget her sucking child? Yea, they may forget, yet will I not forget thee.” Those of us who are mothers know very well how grieved and insulted we should feel if anyone should suggest the possibility of our forgetting our children; and we mothers at least, if no one else does, should be able to understand how such questioning must grieve the Lord.

“Is God’s mercy clean gone forever?” “Has God in anger shut up his tender mercies?”

To ask these two questions of a good God is to insult Him. It would be as impossible for His tender mercies to be shut up toward us, or for His mercy to go from us forever, as it would be for the tender mercies of a mother come to an end. The psalmist says: “The Lord is good to all, and his tender mercies are over all his works.” In the very nature of things this must be, because He is a good God, and cannot do otherwise.

“Do God’s promises fail forevermore?”

There come times in every Christian’s life when we are tempted to ask this question. Everything seems to be going wrong, and all God’s promises seem to have failed. But if we remember that the Lord is good, we shall see that He would cease to be good if such a thing could be. A man who breaks his promises is looked upon as a dishonorable and untrustworthy man; and a God who could break His, if one could imagine such a thing, would be dishonorable and untrustworthy also. And to ask such a question is to cast a stigma on His goodness, that may well be characterised as “speaking against God.” No matter how affairs may look, we may be sure of this, that because God is good no promise of His has ever failed, or can ever fail.

Heaven and earth may pass away, but His Word never.

“O God, why have you cast us off forever?”

It will be impossible for a good God to cast us off as it would be for a good mother to cast off her child. We may be in trouble and darkness, and may feel as if we were cast off and forsaken, but our feelings have nothing to do with the facts, and the fact is that God is good, and could not do it. The good Shepherd does not cast off the sheep that is lost, and take no further care of it, but He goes out to seek for it, and He seeks until He finds it. To suspect Him of casting us off forever is to wound and grieve His faithful love, just as it would wound a good mother’s heart is she should be supposed capable of casting off her child, let that child have wandered as far as it may. The thing is impossible in either case, but far more impossible in the case of God than even in the case of the best mother that ever lived.

“Why have you made me this way?”

This is a question we are very apt to ask. There is, I imagine, hardly one of us who has not been tempted at one time or another to “reply against God” in reference to the matter of our own personal make-up. We do not like our peculiar temperaments or our especial characteristics, and we long to be like someone else who has, we think, greater gifts of appearance or of talent. We are discontented with our make-up, both inward and outward, and we feel sure that all our failures are because of our unfortunate temperaments; and we are inclined to blame our Creator for having “made us this way.”

I remember vividly a time in my life when I was tempted to be very rebellious about my own make-up. I was a plain-spoken, energetic sort of an individual, trying to be a good Christian, but with no especial air of piety about me. But I had a sister who was so saintly in her looks, and had such a pious manner, that she seemed to be the embodiment of piety; and I felt sure I could be a great deal better Christian if only I could get her saintly looks and manner. But all my struggles to get them were useless.

My natural temperament was far too energetic and outspoken for any appearance of saintliness, and many a time I said upbraidingly in my heart to God, “Why hast thou made me thus?” But one day I came across a sentence in an old mystic book that seemed to open my eyes. It was as follows: “Be content to be what thy God has made thee”; and it flashed on me that it really was a fact that God had made me, and that He must know the sort of creature He wanted me to be; and that if He had made me a potato vine, I must be satisfied to grow potatoes, and must not want to be a rosebush and grow roses; and if He had fashioned me for humble tasks, I must be content to let others do the grander work. We are “God’s workmanship,” and God is good, therefore His workmanship must be good also; and we may securely trust that before He is done with us, He will make out of us something that will be to His glory, no matter how unlike this we may as yet feel ourselves to be.

The psalmist seemed to delight in repeating over and over again this blessed refrain, “for the Lord is good.” It would be worthwhile for you to take your concordances and see how often he says it. And he exhorted everyone to join him in saying it. “Let the redeemed of the Lord say so,” was his earnest cry. We must join our voices to his—The Lord is good—The Lord is good. But we must not say it with our lips only, and then by our actions give the lie to our words. We must “say” it with our whole being, with thought, word, and action, so that people will see we really mean it, and will be convinced that it is a tremendous fact.

A great many things in God’s divine providences do not look like goodness to the eye of sense, and in reading the Psalms we wonder perhaps how the psalmist could say, after some of the things he records, “for his mercy endureth forever.” But faith sits down before mysteries such as these, and says, “The Lord is good, therefore all that He does must be good, no matter how it looks, and I can wait for His explanations.”

A housekeeping illustration has often helped me here. If I have a friend whom I know to be a good housekeeper, I do not trouble over the fact that at housecleaning time things in her house may seem to be more or less upset, carpets up, and furniture shrouded in coverings, and even perhaps painting and decorating making some rooms uninhabitable. I say to myself, “My friend is a good housekeeper, and although things look so uncomfortable now, all this upset is only because she means in the end to make it far more comfortable than ever it was before.”

This world is God’s housekeeping; and although things at present look grievously upset, yet, since we know that He is good, and therefore must be a good Housekeeper, we may be perfectly sure that all this present upset is only to bring about in the end a far better state of things than could have been without it. I dare say we have all felt at times as though we could have done God’s housekeeping better than He does it Himself, but, when we realize that God is good, we can feel this no longer. And it comforts me enormously, when the world seems to me to be going all wrong, just to say to myself, “It is not my housekeeping, but it is the Lord’s; and the Lord is good, therefore His housekeeping must be good too; and it is foolish for me to trouble.”

A deeply taught Christian was asked by a despairing child of God, “Does not the world look to you like a wreck?

“Yes,” was the reply, in a tone of cheerful confidence; “yes, like the wreck of a bursting seed.”

Any of us who have watched the first sproutings of an oak tree from the heart of a decaying acorn will understand what this means. Before the acorn can bring forth the oak, it must become itself a wreck. No plant ever came from any but a wrecked seed.

Our Lord uses this fact to teach us the meaning of His processes with us. “Truly, truly, I say to you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit.” John 12:24.

The whole explanation of the apparent wreckage of the world at large, or of our own personal lives in particular, is here set forth. And, looked at in this light, we can understand how it is that the Lord can be good, and yet can permit the existence of sorrow and wrong in the world He has created, and in the lives of the human beings He loves. It is His very goodness that compels Him to permit it. For He knows that, only through such apparent wreckage, can the fruition of His glorious purposes for us be brought to pass. And we whose hearts also long for that fruition will, if we understand His ways, be able to praise Him for all His goodness, even when things seem hardest and most mysterious.

The apostle tells us that the will of God is “good and acceptable, and perfect.” The will of a good God cannot help being “good”—in fact, it must be perfect’; and, when we come to know this, we always find it “acceptable”; that is we come to love it. I am convinced that all trouble about submitting to the will of God would disappear, if once we could see clearly that His will is good.

We struggle and struggle in vain to submit to a will that we do not believe to be good, but when we see that it is really good, we submit to it with delight. We want it to be accomplished. Our hearts spring out to meet it.

I worship thee, sweet Will of God!

And all thy ways adore; And, every day I live, I seem To love thee more and more.

I love to kiss each print where thou Hast set thine unseen feet: I cannot fear thee, blessed Will!

Your empire is so sweet.

Space fails me to tell all that I might of the infinite goodness of the Lord. Each one must “taste and see” for himself. And if he will but do it honestly and faithfully, the words of the psalmist will become true of him: “They shall pour forth the fame of your abundant goodness and shall sing aloud of your righteousness.” Psalm 145:7
fields.body_text: “Oh, taste and see that the Lord is good! Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him!” (Psalm 34:8). Have you ever asked yourself what you honestly think of God at the bottom of your heart— whether you believe Him to be a good God or a bad God? I expect the question will shock you, and you will be horrified at the suggestion that you could by any possibility think that God is a bad God. But before you have finished this chapter, I suspect some of you will be forced to acknowledge that, perhaps unconsciously but nonetheless truly, you have, by your doubts and your complaints, attributed to Him a character that you would be horrified to have attributed to yourself. I shall never forget the hour when I first discovered that God was really good. I had, of course, always known that the Bible said He was good, but I had thought it only meant He was religiously good; and it had never dawned on me that it meant He was actually and practically good, with the same kind of goodness He has commanded us to have. The expression, “The goodness of God,” had seemed to me nothing more than a sort of heavenly statement, which I could not be expected to understand. And then one day I came across the words in my Bible reading, “Oh, taste and see that the Lord is good,” and suddenly they meant something. The Lord is good, I repeated to myself. What does it mean to be good? What but this: living up to the best and highest that one knows. To be good is exactly the opposite of being bad. To be bad is to know the right thing and not do it, but to be good is to do the best we know. And I saw that, since God knows everything, He must know what is the best and highest good of all, and that therefore His goodness must necessarily be beyond question. I can never express what this meant to me. I had such a view of the real, actual goodness of God that I saw nothing could possibly go wrong under His care, and it seemed to me that no one could ever be anxious again. And over and over, when appearances have been against Him, and when I have been tempted to question whether He had been unkind, or neglectful, or indifferent, I have been stopped in my tracks by the words, “The Lord is good”; and I have seen that it was simply unthinkable that a God who was good could have done the bad things I had imagined. You shrink with horror, perhaps, from the suggestion that you could under any circumstances, even in the secret depths of your heart, attribute to God what was bad. And yet you do not hesitate to accuse Him of doing things which, if one of your friends did them, you would look upon as most dishonourable and unkind. For instance, Christians get into trouble; everything looks dark, and they have no sense of the Lord’s presence. They begin to question whether the Lord has abandoned them, and sometimes even accuse Him of indifference and neglect. They never realise that these accusations are the same as saying that the Lord does not keep His promises, and does not treat them as kindly and honourably as they expect all their human friends to treat them. If one of our human friends should abandon us because we were in trouble, we would consider such a friend to be very far from being good. How is it, then, that we can even for one moment accuse our Lord of such actions? No, dear friend, if the Lord is good—not just pious, but really good—it must be because He always, under every circumstance, acts up to the highest ideal of that which He Himself has taught us is goodness. Goodness in Him must mean, just as it does with us, living up to the best and highest He knows. Practically, then, it means that He will not neglect any of His duties toward us, and that He will always treat us in the best possible way. This may sound like a cliché, and you may exclaim, “Why tell us this, for it is what we all believe?” But do you? If you did, would it be possible for you ever to think He was neglectful, or indifferent, or unkind, or self-absorbed, or inconsiderate? Do not put on a righteous air and say, “Oh, but I never do accuse Him of any such things. I would not dare to.” Do you not? Have you never blamed Him for things you would be ashamed to do yourselves? How was it when that last painful disappointment came? Did you not feel as if the Lord had been unkind in permitting such a thing to happen to you, when you were trying so hard to serve Him? Do you never look upon His will as a tyrannical and bossy will that must be submitted to, of course, but that could not by any possibility be loved? Does it never seem to you a hard thing to say, “Your will be done”? But could it seem hard if you really believed that the Lord is good, and that He always does that which is good? The Lord Jesus took great care to tell us that He was a good Shepherd, because He knew how often appearances would be against Him, and how tempted we would be to question His goodness. “I am the good shepherd,” He says in effect, “not a bad one. Bad shepherds neglect and abandon their sheep, but I am a good Shepherd, and never neglect nor abandon My sheep. I lay down My life for the sheep.” His ideal of goodness in a shepherd was that the shepherd must protect the sheep entrusted to his care, even at the cost of his own life; and He lived up to His own ideal. Now, can we not see that if we really believe that He is good—not in some mysterious, religious way, but in this common-sense, human way—we shall be brought into a place of great peace and comfort at once. If I am a sheep, and the Lord is a good Shepherd in the ordinary, common-sense definition of good, how utterly secure I am! How sure I may be of the best care in every respect! How safe I am for time and for eternity! Let us be honest with ourselves. Have we never in our secret hearts accused the Lord of the characteristics that He has told us in Ezekiel are the marks of a bad shepherd? Have we not thought that He cared for His own comfort or glory more than He cared for ours? Have we not complained that He has not strengthened us when we were weak, or bound up our broken hearts, or searched for us when we were lost? Have we not even actually looked upon our diseased, and helpless, and lost condition, as a reason why He would not any longer have anything to do with us? In what does this differ from if we should say out plump and plain, the Lord is a bad shepherd, and does not fulfill His duties to His sheep. You shrink in horror, perhaps, at this translation of your inward murmurings and complainings, but what else, I ask you, can they in all honesty mean? It is of vital importance now and then to drag out our secret thoughts and feelings about the Lord into the full light of the Holy Spirit, that we may see what our attitude about Him really is. It is fatally easy to get into a habit of wrong thoughts about God, thoughts which will insensibly separate us from Him by a wide gulf of doubt and unbelief. More than anything else, more even than sin, wrong thoughts about God sap the foundations of our spiritual life, and grieve His heart of love. We can understand this from ourselves. Nothing grieves us so much as to have our friends misjudge and misunderstand us, and attribute to us motives we scorn. And nothing, I believe, so grieves the Lord. It is, in fact, idolatry. We may be in trouble and darkness, and may feel as if we were cast off and forsaken, but our feelings have nothing to do with the facts, and the fact is that God is good, and could not do it. I am convinced that all trouble about submitting to the will of God would disappear, if once we could see clearly that His will is good. We struggle and struggle in vain to submit to a will that we do not believe to be good, but when we see that it is really good, we submit to it with delight. We want it to be accomplished. Our hearts spring out to meet it. I worship thee, sweet Will of God! And all thy ways adore; And, every day I live, I seem To love thee more and more. I love to kiss each print where thou Hast set thine unseen feet: I cannot fear thee, blessed Will! Your empire is so sweet. Space fails me to tell all that I might of the infinite goodness of the Lord. Each one must “taste and see” for himself. And if he will but do it honestly and faithfully, the words of the psalmist will become true of him: “They shall pour forth the fame of your abundant goodness and shall sing aloud of your righteousness.” Psalm 145:7

fields.title: The Lord Our Dwelling Place
fields.body_html:
“Lord, you have been our dwelling place in all generations” (Psalm 90:1).

The comfort or discomfort of our outward lives depends largely on where our bodies live; similarly, the comfort or discomfort of our inward life depends on the dwelling place of our souls.

Our dwelling place is the place where we actually live, not just a place we visit. It is our home.

All the interests of our earthly lives are tied up in our home, and we do everything we can to make it attractive and comfortable. But our souls need a comfortable dwelling place even more than our bodies do. Inward comfort is far more important than outward comfort; when the soul is full of peace and joy, our physical surroundings matter very little.

It is vital, then, that we find out exactly where our souls are living. The Lord declares that He has been our dwelling place throughout history, but the question is: Are we actually living in our dwelling place? The psalmist says of the children of Israel that “they wandered in desert wastes, finding no way to a city to dwell in; hungry and thirsty, their soul fainted within them” (Psalm 107:4-5). I am afraid there are many wandering souls in the church today whom this description fits perfectly. All their Christian lives they have been wandering in a spiritual wilderness, finding no permanent home, and their souls have fainted from hunger and thirst. Yet all the while, the dwelling place of God has been standing wide open, inviting them to come in and stay forever.

Our Lord Himself urges this invitation upon us: “Abide in me, and I in you” (John 15:4). He goes on to tell us the blessed results of staying there and the sad consequences of leaving.

The truth is, our souls were made for God. He is our natural home, and we can never be at rest anywhere else. “My soul longs, yes, faints for the courts of the Lord; my heart and flesh sing for joy to the living God” (Psalm 84:2). We will always hunger and faint for the courts of the Lord as long as we fail to make our home there.

God only is the creature’s home; Though rough and straight the road, Yet nothing else can satisfy The soul that longs for God.

How shall we describe this living dwelling place? David describes it when he says: “The Lord is my rock and my fortress and my deliverer, my God, my rock, in whom I take refuge, my shield, and the horn of my salvation, my stronghold and my refuge, my savior; you save me from violence” (2 Samuel 22:2-3). So we see that our dwelling place is also our fortress, our high tower, our rock, and our refuge. We all know what a fortress is. It is a place of safety where the weak and helpless can be hidden from the enemy and kept secure. When we are told that God is our fortress, it can only mean one thing: if we live in Him, we shall be perfectly safe from every possible enemy.

“For he will hide me in his shelter in the day of trouble; he will conceal me under the cover of his tent; he will lift me high upon a rock” (Psalm 27:5). “He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty” (Psalm 91:1). “In the cover of your presence you hide them from the plots of men; you store them in your shelter from the strife of tongues” (Psalm 31:20). In the “cover of God’s tent,” no enemy can find us and no troubles can reach us. Human pride and gossip find no entrance into the “shelter” of God. The “cover of His presence” is a more secure refuge than a thousand Gibraltars. I do not mean that no trials come.

They may come in abundance, but they cannot penetrate the sanctuary of the soul. We can dwell in perfect peace even in the midst of life’s fiercest storms.

But alas, how few of us know this! We might use David’s language, but to us, it is only a figure of speech with no reality. We say the words in a formal, religious tone. “Oh yes, I know the Lord is my dwelling place, and I have committed myself to His keeping, as every Christian should.

But—” and here the normal tone returns— “but I can’t forget that I am a poor, good-for-nothing person with no strength to conquer temptation. I can hardly expect to be kept in the perfect security David speaks of.” Then follows a story of fears and anxieties, exactly as if the dwelling place of God had never been heard of, and as if the soul were wandering alone and unprotected in a world of danger.

There is a psalm that I call the “Dwelling Place of God.” It is the Ninety-first Psalm, and it gives a wonderful description of what this home is. “He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty. I will say to the Lord, ‘My refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust’” (Psalm 91:1-2). Our idea of a fortress is usually a hard, stone building where one is safe but also very uncomfortable. But there are other types of fortresses that are soft, tender, and full of comfort. This psalm describes them: “He will cover you with his pinions, and under his wings you will find refuge” (Psalm 91:4), just as a mother hen covers her helpless chicks with her warm wings. The fortress of a mother’s heart—whether human, a bird, or even a tiger—is the strongest fortress the world knows, yet it is the tenderest. This is the kind of fortress the Lord is. “He will tend his flock like a shepherd; he will gather the lambs in his arms; he will carry them in his bosom” (Isaiah 40:11).

“The eternal God is your dwelling place, and underneath are the everlasting arms” (Deuteronomy 33:27). Wings, bosom, arms! What blessed fortresses these are! Everything enfolded by them is safe. Nature is full of such examples. Consider what one writer says of a mother tiger. When her cubs are born, a power teaches her to be gentle—a spirit she cannot resist, for it is the spirit of her Creator. It is a tiger’s instinct to resent an injury. If you were to pull her hair or strike her, she would rend you. But resenting injury is not her strongest impulse. Watch those helpless kittens playing with her. They are so weak that a careless movement of her giant paw would destroy them, but she makes no careless movement. They cause her more pain than a blow would, yet she does not return evil for evil. She strokes them with love in her eyes and licks her little tormentors.

Love transforms her groans of physical pain into sounds of delight. She moves her massive head in a way that shows the same God who told you to “turn the other cheek” created her. When she is strong enough to rise, she goes out to sacrifice herself for her own. She will starve so they may thrive. She is terrifying for the sake of her little ones, just as God is terrifying for the sake of His.

We have seen these “mother fortresses” hundreds of times and called them God-like. One would think the sight would make us fly to our refuge in God and leave all fear outside! But the trouble is, we flatly refuse to believe the Bible means such good news. Not in words, perhaps, but in practice we say, “The Lord’s arms are not as dependable as a human mother’s; the Lord’s heart is not as tender as a tiger’s; the Lord’s wings are not as protective as a mother hen’s.” We know He made these earthly fortresses, but we cannot believe He is equal to them. Having Him as our fortress does not feel half as safe or tender to us as having a mother as our fortress. And so, mothers are trusted, but God is not!

Yet look how safe the psalmist declares this divine dwelling place to be. He says we who are in this home shall be afraid of nothing—not the terror of night, nor the arrow by day, nor the pestilence in darkness, nor destruction at noonday. Thousands may fall around us, but no evil shall happen to the soul hidden in God. No plague shall come near those who have made God their “habitation.”

All the terrors that have made our religious lives so uncomfortable are provided for here. We shall be delivered from them all if we make the Lord our home. This does not mean we will have no outward trials. Plagues may attack your body or your possessions, but those things are not you. Nothing can come near the real, interior you while you are dwelling in God.

A large part of life’s pain comes from the haunting “fear of evil.” Our lives are full of “what-ifs.”

Suppose this happens, or that happens—what would we do? How could we bear it? But if we are living in the “high tower” of God, all these “what-ifs” drop out of our lives. We shall be “at ease, without dread of disaster” (Proverbs 1:33), for no threats of evil can penetrate God’s tower. Even when walking through the valley of the shadow of death, the psalmist could say, “I will fear no evil” (Psalm 23:4); if we are dwelling in God, we can say it too.

But you may ask how to get into this divine dwelling place. My answer is: simply move in. If a friend rented a house for us and said it was ready, and the lease was signed and legal, we wouldn’t ask how to get in—we would just pack up and move. We must do the same here. God says He is our dwelling place. The Bible contains all the necessary papers, signed and witnessed.

Our Lord invites us—actually, He commands us—to enter and stay. He is saying, “God is your home; make sure you take up your residence there. Move in.”

How do you move in? By faith. God has said He is your dwelling place; now you must say it too.

“I will say to the Lord, ‘My refuge and my fortress, my God, in whom I trust’” (Psalm 91:2).

Faith takes the Word of God and asserts that it is true. Christ says, “Abide,” and we must say, “I will abide.” We make Him our “habitation” by believing He is our home and by constantly declaring it. As the poet Coleridge said: Faith is an affirmation and an act, That bids eternal truth be present fact.

We must make the eternal truth that the Lord is our dwelling place a present fact by affirming it with our faith and by adopting the thoughts and actions that come from living in God’s presence.

One of the first things we would have to do is give up worry and anxiety forever. It is unthinkable that worry could enter God’s dwelling place; when we enter, we must leave it behind.

We talk about obeying the Lord’s commands and focus on outward duties, while ignoring commands about the inward life that are a thousand times more important. “Let not your hearts be troubled, neither let them be afraid” (John 14:27) is a command of our Lord that is almost universally disobeyed. Yet I doubt any other disobedience hurts His heart quite as much. I am certain that I would be far more hurt if my child mistrusted me and felt her interests were unsafe in my care than if she disobeyed me in a moment of temptation. I am convinced we don’t realise how much it wounds our Lord when His people do not feel safe with Him.

We can understand this from our own lives. Suppose a friend gave us something to keep for them, and we gave every assurance it would be safe. Then the friend went away and worried over it, expressing to others the same anxieties we express about the things we’ve given to God.

How would we feel? We would be deeply hurt. Eventually, we might say, “Since you obviously don’t trust me, you’d better take care of your things yourself.” It is amazing that God’s children dare to be anxious after committing a matter to Him; it is such a slight against His character.

Outsiders see this and think that having the Lord as a dwelling place must not mean much, otherwise we wouldn't be so troubled.

He who cares for sparrows and numbers the hairs on our heads cannot possibly fail us. He is an unbreakable fortress where no evil or enemy can enter. I hold it as an obvious truth: the moment I have really committed anything to this divine dwelling place, all anxiety should stop. While I keep things in my own care, I have reason to tremble, for they are unsafe. but in God’s care, security is absolute.

“The name of the Lord is a strong tower; the righteous man runs into it and is safe” (Proverbs 18:10). The only goal, then, is to “run into” this tower and stay there forever. It would be foolish to stand outside a fortress while an enemy surrounds you, crying out for safety. If I want to be safe, I must go inside.

“O Jerusalem, Jerusalem... How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Matthew 23:37). If a chick wants to be safe, it must run to the mother’s wings. Many people stay outside of God’s dwelling place because they feel too unworthy or weak to go in. What would we think of a chick that saw a hawk coming, heard its mother calling, but stayed outside trembling and saying, “Oh, I am such a weak, helpless little chick that I’m not worthy to go under those wings”? If the mother hen could speak, she would say, “You silly thing, it is because you are weak and helpless that I want you here. If you were a big, strong rooster able to take care of yourself, I wouldn’t need to gather you at all.” Do I need to explain the point?

But we must not only “run into” our dwelling place. “Let me dwell in your tent forever! Let me take refuge under the shelter of your wings!” (Psalm 61:4). We must do the same. Staying in His tent forever is, I admit, sometimes very hard. It is relatively easy to take a step of faith, but much harder to stay in that place. Many people run into God’s fortress on Sunday and come out again as soon as Monday morning arrives. Some run into it when they kneel for evening prayers and come out five minutes later when they get into bed. This is total foolishness. You wouldn’t imagine a refugee running into a fortress one day and running back out to the enemy the next.

We would think they had lost their mind. But isn't it even more foolish for the soul? Are our enemies less active on Monday? Are we better able to handle them while sleeping than while praying?

The question is: Do we want to just visit God, or do we want to live there? Do we want to take refuge today and be exposed to enemies tomorrow? No one would choose that deliberately, but too many drift into it. Staying in Christ is entirely a matter of faith, but we fail to realise this. We think our intense struggles or hard work are the main part of it; when these fade, our faith weakens. But the Christian life is lived by faith. Without faith it is impossible to please God. It is useless to waste time on our own efforts that achieve nothing.

We must put our willpower and energy into our faith. We must be determined to move into God’s dwelling place and stay there, regardless of temptations to doubt or feel discouraged.

“He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty” (Psalm 91:1). “Abiding” and “trusting” are effectively synonyms; they mean the same thing.

While I trust the Lord, I am staying in Him. If I trust Him consistently, I am staying in Him consistently. If I trust Him only now and then, I am running in and out. I used to think there was a mystery to “abiding,” but I see now it just means trusting Him fully. Once you understand this, it is the simplest thing in the world. We sometimes say of two people that they “live in each other’s hearts.” This just means they have perfect love and confidence in each other, and doubt is impossible. If my trust in the Lord’s fortress is absolute, I am abiding in that fortress. That is the whole story.

The practical thing to do, therefore, since God is declared to be our fortress and our high tower, is to put ourselves and all our interests into this divine dwelling place by a definite act of surrender and faith, and then dismiss all care or anxiety about them from our minds. Since the Lord is our dwelling place, nothing committed to His care can possibly come to any harm. As long as we believe this, our affairs remain in His care; the moment we begin to doubt, we take our affairs back into our own hands, and they are no longer in the divine fortress.

Things cannot be in two places at once. If they are in our own care, they cannot be in God’s care; and if they are in God’s care, they cannot be in our own. This is as clear as daylight, yet for want of a little common sense, people often get mixed up over it. They try to put their affairs into God’s fortress while keeping them in their own at the same time, and then wonder why they are not taken care of. This is foolish. Either trust the Lord completely, or trust yourself completely; but do not try to mix the two, for they will not mix.

It will help you practically if you put your trust into words. Say definitely, “God is my dwelling place, and I am going to stay in Him forever. It is all settled; I am in this divine home, I am safe here, and I am not going to move out again.” You must meet every assault of doubt and discouragement with the simple assertion that you are there and that you know you will not be put to shame. Let others do as they may, but you must declare that you, at least, are going to stay in your divine dwelling place forever. Having taken this stand, you must utterly refuse to reconsider the matter. It is settled; there is nothing more to be said.

By all this, I do not mean that we should stay in bed and let things go. I am talking about the inward aspect of our affairs, not the outward. Outwardly, we may have to be very active and careful, but it must all come from the inward basis of a soul that has hidden itself and its interests in God, and is therefore “anxious for nothing” (Philippians 4:6) in the beautiful Bible sense of having no worried thoughts. To be without inward care is the surest foundation for successful outward care. The soul hidden in God is the soul that can triumphantly bear earth’s greatest trials and conquer its strongest foes.

There is one point I must mention. When we move into a new house, we do not just move in ourselves; we take all our belongings and, above all, our family. No one would be so foolish as to leave someone they loved outside. Yet I am afraid some of God’s children move into His dwelling place themselves but, through a lack of faith, leave those they love best outside—often their children. We would be horrified at a father who fled into a fortress for safety during danger but left his children outside; yet many Christians do this very thing. Every anxious thought we have about our children proves we have not really taken them with us into the dwelling place of God.

If we trust for ourselves, we must trust for our loved ones too. God is more their Father than any earthly father is, and if they are dear to us, they are far dearer to Him. We cannot do anything better for them than to trust them to His care, and hardly anything worse than trying to keep them in our own. I knew a mother who trusted peacefully for her own salvation but was racked with anxiety about her sons, who seemed indifferent to religion. One evening, she heard about putting loved ones into the fortress of God by faith. She saw how inconsistent it was to hide herself in God while leaving her sons outside.

At once, her faith took them into the fortress with her. She abandoned them to God’s care so completely that her anxiety vanished. She told me she felt her sons were God’s sons now—no longer hers—and that He loved them better and would care for them more wisely than she ever could. She stayed ready to do whatever the Lord suggested for them, but she was content to leave the matter in His hands. She went home and told her sons, “I’ve been so worried about you and have probably annoyed you with my preaching. But I have learned to trust. I have put you into the fortress of God and left you in His care. He will save you in His own way. My anxieties are over.”

A year later, she told me with joy, “Rejoice with me! My boys have been safe in God's fortress ever since, and all of them are good Christians today.”

The conclusion is simple: move into your dwelling place in God and take everything you own and everyone you love with you. Hide yourself in Him, away from yourself and others, and lose sight of everything outside of Him—except as you see it through His eyes. God’s eyes are the only windows in His house; seen through them, everything looks different. We shall see trials as blessings and enemies as friends in disguise. We shall be calm in the face of life’s worries. “My people will abide in a peaceful habitation, in secure dwellings, and in quiet resting places” (Isaiah 32:18).

While I keep things in my own care, I have reason to tremble, for they are unsafe. but in God’s care, security is absolute. “The name of the Lord is a strong tower; the righteous man runs into it and is safe” (Proverbs 18:10). The only goal, then, is to “run into” this tower and stay there forever. It would be foolish to stand outside a fortress while an enemy surrounds you, crying out for safety. If I want to be safe, I must go inside. “O Jerusalem, Jerusalem... How often would I have gathered your children together as a hen gathers her brood under her wings, and you were not willing!” (Matthew 23:37). If a chick wants to be safe, it must run to the mother’s wings. Many people stay outside of God’s dwelling place because they feel too unworthy or weak to go in. What would we think of a chick that saw a hawk coming, heard its mother calling, but stayed outside trembling and saying, “Oh, I am such a weak, helpless little chick that I’m not worthy to go under those wings”? If the mother hen could speak, she would say, “You silly thing, it is because you are weak and helpless that I want you here. If you were a big, strong rooster able to take care of yourself, I wouldn’t need to gather you at all.” Do I need to explain the point? But we must not only “run into” our dwelling place. “Let me dwell in your tent forever! Let me take refuge under the shelter of your wings!” (Psalm 61:4). We must do the same. Staying in His tent forever is, I admit, sometimes very hard. It is relatively easy to take a step of faith, but much harder to stay in that place. Many people run into God’s fortress on Sunday and come out again as soon as Monday morning arrives. Some run into it when they kneel for evening prayers and come out five minutes later when they get into bed. This is total foolishness. You wouldn’t imagine a refugee running into a fortress one day and running back out to the enemy the next. We would think they had lost their mind. But isn't it even more foolish for the soul? Are our enemies less active on Monday? Are we better able to handle them while sleeping than while praying? The question is: Do we want to just visit God, or do we want to live there? Do we want to take refuge today and be exposed to enemies tomorrow? No one would choose that deliberately, but too many drift into it. Staying in Christ is entirely a matter of faith, but we fail to realise this. We think our intense struggles or hard work are the main part of it; when these fade, our faith weakens. But the Christian life is lived by faith. Without faith it is impossible to please God. It is useless to waste time on our own efforts that achieve nothing. We must put our willpower and energy into our faith. We must be determined to move into God’s dwelling place and stay there, regardless of temptations to doubt or feel discouraged. “He who dwells in the shelter of the Most High will abide in the shadow of the Almighty” (Psalm 91:1). “Abiding” and “trusting” are effectively synonyms; they mean the same thing. While I trust the Lord, I am staying in Him. If I trust Him consistently, I am staying in Him consistently. If I trust Him only now and then, I am running in and out. I used to think there was a mystery to “abiding,” but I see now it just means trusting Him fully. Once you understand this, it is the simplest thing in the world. We sometimes say of two people that they “live in each other’s hearts.” This just means they have perfect love and confidence in each other, and doubt is impossible. If my trust in the Lord’s fortress is absolute, I am abiding in that fortress. That is the whole story. The practical thing to do, therefore, since God is declared to be our fortress and our high tower, is to put ourselves and all our interests into this divine dwelling place by a definite act of surrender and faith, and then dismiss all care or anxiety about them from our minds. Since the Lord is our dwelling place, nothing committed to His care can possibly come to any harm. As long as we believe this, our affairs remain in His care; the moment we begin to doubt, we take our affairs back into our own hands, and they are no longer in the divine fortress. Things cannot be in two places at once. If they are in our own care, they cannot be in God’s care; and if they are in God’s care, they cannot be in our own. This is as clear as daylight, yet for want of a little common sense, people often get mixed up over it. They try to put their affairs into God’s fortress while keeping them in their own at the same time, and then wonder why they are not taken care of. This is foolish. Either trust the Lord completely, or trust yourself completely; but do not try to mix the two, for they will not mix. It will help you practically if you put your trust into words. Say definitely, “God is my dwelling place, and I am going to stay in Him forever. It is all settled; I am in this divine home, I am safe here, and I am not going to move out again.” You must meet every assault of doubt and discouragement with the simple assertion that you are there and that you know you will not be put to shame. Let others do as they may, but you must declare that you, at least, are going to stay in your divine dwelling place forever. Having taken this stand, you must utterly refuse to reconsider the matter. It is settled; there is nothing more to be said. By all this, I do not mean that we should stay in bed and let things go. I am talking about the inward aspect of our affairs, not the outward. Outwardly, we may have to be very active and careful, but it must all come from the inward basis of a soul that has hidden itself and its interests in God, and is therefore “anxious for nothing” (Philippians 4:6) in the beautiful Bible sense of having no worried thoughts. To be without inward care is the surest foundation for successful outward care. The soul hidden in God is the soul that can triumphantly bear earth’s greatest trials and conquer its strongest foes. There is one point I must mention. When we move into a new house, we do not just move in ourselves; we take all our belongings and, above all, our family. No one would be so foolish as to leave someone they loved outside. Yet I am afraid some of God’s children move into His dwelling place themselves but, through a lack of faith, leave those they love best outside—often their children. We would be horrified at a father who fled into a fortress for safety during danger but left his children outside; yet many Christians do this very thing. Every anxious thought we have about our children proves we have not really taken them with us into the dwelling place of God. If we trust for ourselves, we must trust for our loved ones too. God is more their Father than any earthly father is, and if they are dear to us, they are far dearer to Him. We cannot do anything better for them than to trust them to His care, and hardly anything worse than trying to keep them in our own. I knew a mother who trusted peacefully for her own salvation but was racked with anxiety about her sons, who seemed indifferent to religion. One evening, she heard about putting loved ones into the fortress of God by faith. She saw how inconsistent it was to hide herself in God while leaving her sons outside. At once, her faith took them into the fortress with her. She abandoned them to God’s care so completely that her anxiety vanished. She told me she felt her sons were God’s sons now—no longer hers—and that He loved them better and would care for them more wisely than she ever could. She stayed ready to do whatever the Lord suggested for them, but she was content to leave the matter in His hands. She went home and told her sons, “I’ve been so worried about you and have probably annoyed you with my preaching. But I have learned to trust. I have put you into the fortress of God and left you in His care. He will save you in His own way. My anxieties are over.” A year later, she told me with joy, “Rejoice with me! My boys have been safe in God's fortress ever since, and all of them are good Christians today.” The conclusion is simple: move into your dwelling place in God and take everything you own and everyone you love with you. Hide yourself in Him, away from yourself and others, and lose sight of everything outside of Him—except as you see it through His eyes. God’s eyes are the only windows in His house; seen through them, everything looks different. We shall see trials as blessings and enemies as friends in disguise. We shall be calm in the face of life’s worries. “My people will abide in a peaceful habitation, in secure dwellings, and in quiet resting places” (Isaiah 32:18).

fields.title: Much More Versus Much Less
fields.body_html:
“But where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20).

A great deal of the comfort in our religious lives depends on the view we take of things. Our view doesn't change reality, but it changes how we experience it. Our safety comes from what is real, but our comfort comes from what we believe to be real.

There is an expression used repeatedly in the Bible to describe the salvation of Jesus Christ: “much more.” It tells us that there is no human need that cannot be “much more” than met by His salvation. Yet we are often tempted to think “much less” would be a truer term—that in actual experience, salvation is much less than our needs. This “much less” view makes our spiritual lives miserable.

If what we have learned about the fullness of God’s salvation is true, “much more” should be the only language we use. Because some Christians act as though “much less” is more realistic, let’s look at what the Bible actually says. If God says His salvation is more than enough and we insist it is less, we are calling Him untrustworthy and creating our own misery.

“Much less” is the language of what we can see; “much more” is the language of the unseen.

“Much less” seems more reasonable because our weakness is visible, while God’s strength is invisible. Our needs are right in front of us, while God’s supply is hidden and must be realised by faith.

To see unseen things, we need our “interior eye” opened—the ability to see below the surface.

This eye looks not at the temporary things we see, but at the eternal things we cannot see. The vital question is: has that eye been opened in you?

Consider the story in 2 Chronicles 32:1-15. An enemy had threatened to overwhelm Judah. This enemy had been successful everywhere else and was sure he would conquer Israel too. But King Hezekiah looked at the unseen God and saw He was stronger. He told the people: “Be strong and courageous. Do not be afraid or dismayed before the king of Assyria and all the horde that is with him, for there are more with us than with him. With him is an arm of flesh, but with us is the Lord our God, to help us and to fight our battles” (2 Chronicles 32:7-8). On one side was human strength; on the other, the Lord our God! No wonder the people felt encouraged.

When the enemy king, Sennacherib, saw their faith, he mocked them. He asked, “How much less shall your God deliver you out of my hand?” since no other god had saved any other nation.

“How much less”—what a temptation to doubt! It looked impossible. But Hezekiah kept the people’s eyes on the unseen, and the Lord sent a great deliverance. The “much less” of the enemy became a “much more” victory.

Do we ever feel like God is “much less” able to deliver us than He promised? Does it feel like trusting the Lord alone is a desperate last resort? I once heard a Christian in great trouble say despairingly, “Well, there is nothing left for me now but to trust the Lord.” His friend replied in shock, “Is it possible it has come to that?”

We might be horrified by that, but honestly, we often feel the same. Yet God's “much mores” of grace are equal to any emergency. The apostle tells us that God is “able to do far more abundantly than all that we ask or think” (Ephesians 3:20). This is what “much more” means. We can think of wonderful blessings, but God can do far more than even those.

We are told that “no eye has seen, nor ear heard, nor the heart of man imagined, what God has prepared for those who love him” (1 Corinthians 2:9). If He has prepared more than we can even imagine, surely we can trust Him for the things we can imagine, and much more besides.

Let’s decide that our language will be the “much more” of faith. “For if many died through one man's trespass, much more have the grace of God and the free gift by the grace of that one man Jesus Christ abounded for many” (Romans 5:15). This reaches the depths of human need.

We know for a fact that death is real; are we just as sure that grace abounds much more? Do we believe the remedy is greater than the disease?

One of our deepest needs is to be saved. Is there a “much more” for this? “But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Since, therefore, we have now been justified by his blood, much more shall we be saved by him from the wrath of God. For if while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son, much more, now that we are reconciled, shall we be saved by his life” (Romans 5:8-10).

The question of salvation is settled by these “much mores.” Since Christ did the hard part— dying for us while we were enemies—He will certainly do the “lesser” part of keeping us now that we are His friends. Having done the greater, much more will He do the rest.

Now the practical point for us in all this is: Do we really believe it? Have we got rid of all doubts regarding our salvation? Can we speak with assurance of forgiveness and of eternal life? Do we say with the timidity of unbelief, “I hope I am a child of God”; or do we lift up our heads with joyous confidence in God as our Father, and say with John, “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are”? Is it in this respect “much more” with us, or “much less”?

We long and pray for the gift of the Holy Spirit, but it seems all in vain. We feel that our prayers are not answered. But our Lord gives faith a wonderful “much more” to hold onto for this: “If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” There is not one of us who does not know how thankful and eager good parents are to give good gifts to their children—how they often press them upon the children before the child is even ready to receive them, or even knows that it has a need. And yet, which of us really believes that God is actually “much more” eager to give the Holy Spirit to those who ask Him? Is it not rather that many feel secretly that He is “much less” willing, and that we will have to beg, and plead, and wrestle, and wait for this desperately needed gift? If we could only believe this “much more,” how full of faith our asking would be. We should then truly be able to believe that we actually did receive that for which we had asked, and would find that we were in actual possession of the Holy Spirit as our present and personal Helper and Guide; and all our weary struggles and agonising prayers for this promised gift would be over.

Sorer, perhaps, than any other need is our need of victory over sin and over circumstances. Like unstoppable vehicles, they roll over us with irresistible power and crush us into the dust. And the language of “much less” seems the only language that our souls dare speak. But God has given us for this a most triumphant “much more”: “For if, because of one man’s trespass, death reigned through that one man, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and the free gift of righteousness reign in life through the one man Jesus Christ.”

We have known the reigning of that spiritual death which comes by sin, and have groaned under its power. But how much do we know of that “much more” reigning in life by Jesus Christ of which the apostle speaks? That is, do we now have greater victories than we used to have defeats? Do we reign over things “much more” than they once reigned over us?

I mean this: that in the Gospel it is promised that we shall be “more than conquerors” over the very things that once conquered us, and the question is whether we really are. We have been reigned over by thousands of things: by the fear of man, by our peculiar temperaments, by our outward circumstances, by our irritable tempers, even by bad weather, by our environment of every kind. We have been slaves where we ought to have been kings. We have found our reigning to be “much less” rather than “much more.” Why is this? Simply because we have not “received” enough of the abundance of grace that is ours in Christ. We have let unbelief cheat us out of our rightful possessions.

We are called to be kings and were created to have dominion, but here God declares that it shall be “much more” of a dominion than it was formerly a bondage; have we found it to be so? If not, why not? The lack cannot possibly be on God’s side. He has not failed to provide the “much more” of victory. It must be that we have in some way failed to make use of it. And I cannot help but believe that our failure arises from the fact that we have substituted our “much less” for God’s “much more”; and in our heart of hearts have not believed there really is a sufficiency in the gift of righteousness in Christ to enable us to reign. We have failed through our unbelief to “receive the abundance of grace” that is necessary for reigning.

What then is our remedy? Only this—to abandon forever our “much less” of unbelief, and to accept as true God’s declaration of “much more,” and to claim at once the promised victory. And according to our faith it must and will be done for us.

But these assurances of the “much mores” of God’s salvation are not for our spiritual needs only, but for our temporal needs as well. Do not be anxious, He says, about earthly things, for “But if God so clothes the grass of the field, which today is alive and tomorrow is thrown into the oven, will he not much more clothe you, O you of little faith?”

I know that to many Christians this passage and others like it are so familiar that they have almost lost all meaning. But they do mean something, and something almost too wonderful for belief. They tell us that God cares for us human beings “much more” than He cares for the universe around us, and that He will watch over and provide for us much more than He will even for it.

Incredible, yet true! How often we have marvelled at the orderly working of the universe, and have admired the great creative Power that made it and now controls it! But none of us, I suppose, has ever felt it necessary to take the burden of the universe upon our own shoulders. We have trusted the Creator to manage it all without our help. Although I must confess, from the way some people find fault with the Creator’s management of things, and the advice they seem to feel it necessary to give Him in their prayers, one would think the whole burden was resting upon them!

But even where we have fully recognised that the universe is altogether in God’s care, we have failed to see that we also are there, and have never dreamed that it could be true that “much more” than He cares for the universe will He care for us. We have looked at the visible things of our circumstances and our surroundings, and at the greatness of our need and our own helplessness, and have been anxious and afraid. We have burdened ourselves with the care of ourselves, feeling in our unbelief that, instead of being of “much more” value than the birds of the air or the lilies of the field, we are in reality of infinitely “much less”; and it seems to us that the God who cares for them is not at all likely to care for us. We say with the psalmist: “When I look at your heavens, the work of your fingers, the moon and the stars, which you have set in place, what is man that you are mindful of him, and the son of man that you care for him?” Man seems so puny, so insignificant, of so little account when compared with the great, wide universe; what is he, we ask, that God should care for him? And yet God declares that He does care for him, and that He even cares for him much more than He cares for the universe. Much more, remember, not much less. So that every thought of anxiety about ourselves must be immediately crushed with the common-sense reflection that, since we are not so foolish as to be anxious about the universe, we must not be so much more foolish as to be anxious about ourselves.

In the Sermon on the Mount, our Lord gives us the crowning “much more” of all. “Or which one of you, if his son asks him for bread, will give him a stone? Or if he asks for a fish, will give him a serpent? If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will your Father who is in heaven give good things to those who ask him!”

In this “much more” we have a guarantee for the supply of every need. Whatever our Father sees to be good for us is here abundantly promised. And the illustration used to convince us is one of universal application. In all ranks and conditions of life, among all nations, and even in the hearts of birds and beasts, the mother instinct never fails to provide for its offspring the best it can manage.

Under no conditions of life will a mother, unless she is wicked beyond compare, give a stone when asked for bread, or a serpent when asked for fish. And could our God, who created the mother heart, be worse than a mother? No, no, a thousand times no! What He will do is “much more,” oh, so much more than even the tenderest mother could do. And if mothers “know how,” as surely they do, to give good things to their children, “how much more” does He. But do we really believe this “much more”? Our hours of anxious tossing on our beds must answer. If God is actually much more willing and able to give good things to us than parents are to give good things to their children, then all possibility of doubt or anxiety as to our prayers being answered must vanish forever. All “good things” must be given to us when we ask, as inevitably as the mother who is able feeds her child when it asks her for bread. As inevitably, do I say? Ah, dear friends, far more inevitably. For it is “how much more shall your Father which is in heaven.”

Which of us has fathomed the meaning of this “how much more”? But at least this it must mean, that all human readiness to hear and answer the cry of need can only be a faint picture of God’s readiness, and that, therefore, we can never dare to doubt again. And if parents would not give a stone for bread, neither would He; so that when we ask, we must be absolutely sure that we do receive the “good thing” for which we asked, whether what we receive looks like it or not.

The mother of St. Augustine, in her longing for the conversion of her son, prayed that he might not go to Rome, as she feared its temptations. God answered her by sending him to Rome to be converted there. Things we call good are often God’s evil things, and our evil is His good. But, however things may look, we always know that God must give the best because He is God and could do no other.

“He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all, how will he not also with him graciously give us all things?” Since He has done the supreme thing by giving us Christ, “much more” will He do the lesser thing by giving us all things with Him. And yet we continually hear God’s own children complaining about their spiritual poverty and their state of spiritual starvation. Sometimes, it even seems they think this is a pious thing to do and a sign of true humility. But what is this other than glorying in the “much less” of their unbelief, instead of in the “much more” of God?

“Oh, I am such a poor creature,” I heard a child of God say once with actual complacency when urged toward a victory of faith; “I am such a poor creature that I cannot expect to reach the heights you great Christians reach.” “Poor creature,” indeed; of course you are, and so are we all!

But God is not poor, and it is His part to supply your needs, not your part to supply His. He is able, no matter what unbelief may say, to “make all grace abound to you, so that having all sufficiency in all things at all times, you may abound in every good work.” “All,” “always,” “every”—what all-embracing words these are! They include our needs to their absolute limit and leave no room for any question. How can we, how dare we, in the face of such declarations, ever doubt or question again?

We have only touched upon the wonders of grace hidden in these “much mores” of God. We can never exhaust their meaning in this life. But let us at least resolve from now on to lay aside every “much less” of unbelief regarding all aspects of salvation. Out of the depths of our utter weakness, sinfulness, and need, let us assert with a conquering faith, always and everywhere, the mighty “much more” of the grace of God!
