fields.title: A Word to the Wavering Ones
fields.body_html:
“But let him ask in faith, with no doubting, for the one who doubts is like a wave of the sea that is driven and tossed by the wind. For that person must not suppose that he will receive anything from the Lord” (James 1:6-7).

It would be difficult to find anything that produces more discomfort in the religious life than a wavering faith. The image given to us by the Apostle James describes it exactly: “a wave of the sea... driven and tossed”. Just as it is impossible for a traveller to reach a destination by moving forward one day and retracing their steps the next, it is equally impossible for the wavering soul to reach a place of settled peace while it continues to waver.

In our last chapter, we considered the shakings of God. It might be thought that our wavering is similar to his shaking, but they are very different. God’s shakings are caused by his love for our blessing; they always lead to rest and peace. Our waverings are caused by our lack of faith; they always lead to discomfort and turmoil.

A wavering Christian is someone who trusts in the love of God one day and doubts it the next, and is alternately happy or miserable as a result. They climb to the hilltop of joy at one time, only to descend into the valley of despair the next. They are driven back and forth by every “wind of doctrine,” always striving but never attaining. They are a victim of every changing influence—whether it is their physical health, the people around them, or even the weather.

You would suppose that even the most inexperienced child of God would know that this sort of experience is wrong. Wavering in one's faith in such a way is deeply dishonouring to the Lord, as it questions his truth and faithfulness. Yet, many Christians are so blinded that they actually think this tendency to waver is a sign of humility. They treat every new attack of doubt as if it were a pious virtue.

A wavering Christian might say complacently, “Oh, but I know I am so unworthy that I'm sure it's right for me to doubt.” They often imply that if their listener were truly humble, they would doubt as well. I once knew a devoted Christian whose religious life was a constant torment of doubt. After I urged him to have more faith, he said in all seriousness, “My dear friend, if I were ever so arrogant as to feel sure that God loved me, I would be certain I was on the direct road to hell.”

He clearly thought that such assurance could only come from feeling he was “good enough” to deserve God’s love. He was right that thinking we are worthy of God’s love is arrogant.

However, the ground for our assurance does not come from our own goodness, but from the goodness of God. While we should never be satisfied with our own goodness, there can be no question—for anyone who believes the Bible—regarding the total sufficiency of his.

To see how absurd this position of doubt is, consider how it would work in human relationships.

Imagine a marriage, or the relationship between a child and a parent—both of which the Lord uses as symbols for our relationship with him. If a wife or husband had a “wavering experience” of confidence in their spouse—trusting one day and doubting the next—would that be seen as a sign of humility or a virtue to be cherished? Similarly, if children wavered in their confidence toward their parents the way Christians do with their heavenly Father, what word would be harsh enough for such unfilial conduct? In human relationships, such wavering might be excused if one person were actually untrustworthy. But with God, there is no such excuse. The wavering faith of his children may even lead outsiders to conclude that he isn't worthy of much confidence.

So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief” (Hebrews 3:18-19). It wasn't that God wouldn't let them in as a punishment; they simply could not enter. It was an impossibility. You can shut the door against every suggestion of doubt that comes and, by faith, declare exactly the opposite. The process I believe to be most effective is to lay our doubts—just as we lay our other sins— upon God's altar and make a total surrender of them. Let nothing shake your faith. Should even sin unhappily overtake you, you must not let it make you doubt. At once, upon discovering any sin, act on the truth that “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9).

To allow sin to cause your faith to waver is only to add a new sin to the one already committed. Return at once to God in the way the Bible teaches and let your faith hold steadfastly to his word. Believe it, not because you feel it or see it, but because he says it. Believe it actively and steadfastly, through dark and light, through ups and downs, through times of comfort and times of despair, and I can promise you that your wavering experience will be ended.

fields.title: Discouragement
fields.body_html:
“The soul of the people was much discouraged because of the way” (Numbers 21:4).

The Church of Christ abounds in people who are “discouraged because of the way.” Whether inwardly or outwardly—and often both—things look wrong, there seems to be no hope of escape, and their religious lives are full of discomfort. There is nothing that paralyses effort like discouragement, and nothing that more successfully invites defeat. The secret of failure or success lies far more in the soul's interior attitude than in any other cause. It is a law of our being that the “inward man” counts for far more in every conflict than anything the outward man may do or possess.

Nowhere is this truer than in the spiritual life. The Bible declares from beginning to end that faith is the law of the spiritual life, and “according to your faith be it done to you” (Matthew 9:29).

Since faith and discouragement cannot exist together, discouragement is an absolute barrier to faith. Where discouragement rules, it shall be to us not according to our faith, but according to our discouragement.

In fact, just as courage is a faith in good, discouragement is a faith in evil. While courage opens the door to good, discouragement opens it to evil. An allegory I heard early in my Christian life has always remained in my memory as a warning, like those signs for cyclists at the top of a hill: “This hill is dangerous.”

The allegory tells of a council Satan called to decide how to entrap a devoted Christian worker.

One imp offered to paint the pleasures of sin in glowing colours. Satan shook his head: “The man has tried sin and knows it leads to ruin.” Another offered to picture the trials and self-denials of a righteous life to make him eager to escape them. “No,” said Satan, “he knows that the paths of righteousness are paths of peace.” Then a third imp started up: “I will discourage his soul.” “That will do!” exclaimed Satan. “You will be successful.”

An old Quaker once said, “All discouragement is from the devil.” I believe this is a deep truth.

Discouragement cannot have its source in God. The religion of Jesus is one of faith, good cheer, and hope. “Be discouraged,” says our lower nature, “for the world is a place of temptation.” “In the world you will have tribulation. But take heart; I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).

There is no room for discouragement in a world Christ has overcome.

We must settle it, then: discouragement always comes from an evil source. We often persuade ourselves that being discouraged is a “pious” state of mind or evidence of humility, but the causes we think are legitimate are often just short-sightedness.

The most common cause is our own incapacity. We think it is right to be cast down because we are “good-for-nothing” creatures. Moses is a perfect illustration of this. When God called him to lead Israel out of Egypt, Moses looked at his own infirmities: “Oh, my Lord, I am not eloquent...

but I am slow of speech and of tongue” (Exodus 4:10). Naturally, we think Moses had cause for discouragement. But notice God's answer. He did not try to convince Moses that he was actually eloquent. He simply said: “Who has made man's mouth? Who makes him mute, or deaf, or seeing, or blind? Is it not I, the Lord? Now therefore go, and I will be with your mouth and teach you what you shall speak” (Exodus 4:11-12).

When the word of the Lord came to Jeremiah, he felt unequal to the work: “Ah, Lord God!

Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am only a youth” (Jeremiah 1:6). But the Lord answered: “Do not say, 'I am only a youth'; for to all to whom I send you, you shall go... Do not be afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you” (Jeremiah 1:7-8).

Gideon is another example. Called to deliver Israel from the Midianites, the Lord told him: “Go in this might of yours and save Israel... Do not I send you?” (Judges 6:14). Gideon looked at his lack of status: “Please, Lord, how can I save Israel? Behold, my clan is the weakest in Manasseh, and I am the least in my father's house” (Judges 6:15). How familiar this sounds to victims of discouragement! But the Lord simply said: “But I will be with you, and you shall strike the Midianites as one man” (Judges 6:16).

God never gives us “encouragement” regarding our own capacities. He gives us the bare statement: “I will be with you.” This answer precludes all argument. I, your Creator, your strength, and your wisdom, will be with you.

Even so, discouragement is subtle. We think our “temperament” makes it right for us to be discouraged. We think we are too weak to grapple with enemies. And we would be right—if we were fighting the battles ourselves. But if the Lord is to fight them for us, our lack of ability becomes an advantage. “For when I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10).

The children of Israel provide a warning here. At the borders of the promised land, Moses urged them: “Do not fear or be dismayed” (Deuteronomy 1:21). But they felt helpless and murmured that God must hate them. They said: “Where are we going up? Our brothers have made our hearts melt, saying, 'The people are greater and taller than we. The cities are great and fortified up to heaven'” (Deuteronomy 1:28). This is the voice of discouragement—looking at the “giants” instead of the God who is with us. When we read the report of the spies, we cannot be surprised at their discouragement. In fact, we might even feel that courage under such circumstances would have been foolhardiness. “The land, through which we have gone to spy it out, is a land that devours its inhabitants,” the spies declared, “and all the people that we saw in it are of great height. And there we saw the Nephilim... and we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers, and so we seemed to them” (Numbers 13:32-33).

Nothing could have seemed more humble than for them to look upon themselves as poor, good-for-nothing grasshoppers; true humility would have seemed to teach that it would be the height of presumption for grasshoppers to try to conquer giants. We also often feel ourselves to be but grasshoppers in the face of the giants of temptation and trouble that assail us, and we think ourselves justified in being discouraged. But the question is not whether we are grasshoppers, but whether God is; for it is not we who have to fight these giants, but God.

In vain Moses reminded the Israelites of this. In vain he assured them that they had no need to be afraid of even the sons of the Anakim, for “The Lord your God who goes before you will himself fight for you” (Deuteronomy 1:30). He even reminded them of past deliverances, asking if they did not remember how “in the wilderness... the Lord your God carried you, as a man carries his son, all the way that you went” (Deuteronomy 1:31). But they were still too discouraged to believe. The result was that not one of that “evil generation” was allowed to see the promised land, except for Caleb and Joshua, who had steadfastly believed that God could and would lead them in.

Such are the fruits of giving way to discouragement, and such is the reward of a steadfast faith.

The Apostle, in commenting on this story, asks: “And to whom did he swear that they would not enter his rest, but to those who were disobedient? So we see that they were unable to enter because of unbelief” (Hebrews 3:18-19).

Is there no parallel here to our own case? Do we not look at our weakness instead of looking at the Lord's strength? Have we not sometimes become so discouraged as to sink into such “anguish of spirit” (Exodus 6:9) that we cannot even hearken to the Lord's own declarations that he will fight for us and give us the victory? Our souls long to enter into the rest the Lord has promised, but giants and cities “fortified up to heaven” seem to stand in our pathway, and we are afraid to believe. So we too, like the Israelites, cannot enter in because of unbelief.

How different it would be if we only had faith enough to say with the Psalmist: “Though an army encamp against me, my heart shall not fear; though war arise against me, yet I will be confident...

For he will hide me in his shelter in the day of trouble; he will conceal me under the cover of his tent; he will lift me high upon a rock” (Psalm 27:3, 5). How joyfully and triumphantly would we be able to enter into rest if this were our language.

Another very subtle cause for discouragement is found in the “fear of man.” There seems to exist in this world a company of beings called “they” who lord it over life with an iron hand of control.

What will “they” say? What will “they” think? These are among the most frequent questions that assail the timid soul. At every turn, this ubiquitous “they” stands in our way to discourage us.

This form of discouragement often wears the disguise of “due consideration for others,” but it is especially dangerous because it exalts “they” into the place of God. The only remedy is the constant reminder that God is with us. “Be not afraid of them, for I am with you to deliver you, declares the Lord” (Jeremiah 1:8). “The Lord is my helper; I will not fear; what can man do to me?” (Hebrews 13:6).

There is, however, one sort of discouragement that is very common and seems as if it must be right: the discouragement arising from our own failures. This is what the children of Israel suffered after their defeat at Ai. They had “broken the covenant” and “therefore the people of Israel cannot stand before their enemies” (Joshua 7:11-12). Their discouragement was so great that “the hearts of the people melted and became as water,” and Joshua “fell on his face to the earth before the ark of the Lord until the evening” (Joshua 7:5-6).

When God's people “turn their backs before their enemies,” one might think they ought to lie on their faces in despair. But the Lord thought otherwise, for he said to Joshua, “Get up! Why have you fallen on your face?” (Joshua 7:10). The proper thing to do after a failure is not to abandon ourselves to discouragement, humble as that may appear, but to face the evil, get rid of it, and immediately reconsecrate ourselves to the Lord. “Up, consecrate the people” (Joshua 7:13) is always God's command. “Lie down and be discouraged” is always our temptation.

You may ask whether a sense of sin produced by the Holy Spirit ought not to cause discouragement. If I see myself as a sinner, how can I help it? To this I answer that the Holy Spirit does not convict us of sin to discourage us, but to encourage us. He shows us our sin not so we may lie down in despair, but so we may get rid of it. A good mother points out her children's faults to help them correct them. Conviction is a privilege; it means deliverance is coming.

A good housewife discovers stains on her linen not to throw it away, but to have it cleansed. If she has a good laundress, she won't be discouraged by the worst of stains. Surely then, when God says, “though your sins are like scarlet, they shall be as white as snow” (Isaiah 1:18), it is pure unbelief to be discouraged by our failures. God's “washing of regeneration” is more effective than any human effort.

Fénelon says: “It is of great importance to guard against discouragement on account of our faults.

Discouragement is not a fruit of humility, but of pride... It springs from a secret love of our own excellence. We are hurt at feeling what we are... Poor nature longs from self-love to behold itself perfect; it is vexed that it is not so; it is impatient, haughty, and out of temper with itself and everybody else.”

Discouragement leads people to “murmur” and “speak against God.” When the Israelites were “discouraged because of the way,” they “spoke against God” (Numbers 21:4-5). Discouragement is, in its essence, a claim that God has failed to keep his promises. The Psalmist says: “They spoke against God, saying, 'Can God spread a table in the wilderness?'” (Psalm 78:19). Even our “reasonable” questions about God's willingness to help are a “speaking against God” because they reveal that we “did not believe in God and did not trust his saving power” (Psalm 78:22).

Another grievous quality of discouragement is its contagiousness. Nothing is more catching.

When the spies sent out by Moses brought back an “evil report” of the promised land and spoke of the giants there, they so “made the heart of the people melt” (Joshua 14:8) that the people “lifted up their voices and cried” (Numbers 14:1) and utterly refused to enter the land the Lord had given them. The “evil report” that so many Christians bring of their failures and disappointments is one of the most discouraging things in our fellowship. The hearts of young Christians are far too often discouraged by older believers who have little idea of the harm they do with their doleful accounts of the trials of the way.

I can never look back without shame to a time when I “discouraged the heart” of a young friend by the “evil report” I gave of the “giants” of doubt I had met. Later, when a stronger faith delivered me from those fears, I found my former report had so effectively discouraged her that it took a long time before she would listen to the good report I then had to bring.

So important did the Lord feel it to be that no one should discourage another, that he gave this law for warfare: “What man is there who is fearful and fainthearted? Let him go back to his house, lest he make the heart of his fellows melt like his own” (Deuteronomy 20:8). Discouraged people, if they must be discouraged, should at least keep it to themselves, hidden in the privacy of their own bosoms.

We know that courage is contagious; one brave soul can save a crowd from panic. But we forget that one fainthearted person can infect a crowd with fear. We even, strange to say, sing our discouragements in our hymns: “Where is the blessedness I knew When first I saw the Lord?

...But now I find an aching void, The world can never fill.”

Or this: “And shall we then for ever live At this poor dying rate...

Hosannas languish on our tongues, And our devotion dies.”

To sing such hymns seems a travesty of worship. If there are “aching voids” in our experience, let us keep it to ourselves. Surely it cannot please God to hear complainings exalted into the place of hosannas. What would we think of wives who met together to sing such things about their husbands? They would not be tolerated for a single day.

If the Church would expurgate all hymns of discouragement and allow only songs of courage and good cheer, the faith of Christians would go up with a mighty bound. “Take heart,” is the Lord's command, founded on the fact that “I have overcome the world” (John 16:33).

Which would you rather have been? The spies who brought an evil report, or Caleb and Joshua, who “stilled the people before Moses and said, 'Let us go up at once and occupy it, for we are well able to overcome it'” (Numbers 13:30)? Moses spoke of Caleb as one who “wholly followed the Lord” (Deuteronomy 1:36). This “wholly following” consisted simply in the fact that Caleb gave a good report.

How different it would be if discouragement were seen in its true light—as a “speaking against God.” In Isaiah’s prophecy, he describes God’s people: “Everyone helps his neighbor and says to his brother, 'Be strong!' The craftsman strengthens the goldsmith, and he who smooths with the hammer him who strikes the anvil” (Isaiah 41:6-7). Shall we follow their example?

If asked how to get rid of discouragement, I can only say: give it up. It is never worth while to argue with it. When David found his city burned and his men spoke of stoning him, “David strengthened himself in the Lord his God” (1 Samuel 30:6). The result was a magnificent victory.

The Psalmist asked himself: “Why are you cast down, O my soul, and why are you in turmoil within me?” (Psalm 42:11). He answered with the argument of God: “Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God.” He did not analyse his disquietude; he turned to the Lord and began to praise. Faith flies when discouragement appears, and discouragement flies where faith appears. You must choose between them.

He answered with the argument of God: “Hope in God; for I shall again praise him, my salvation and my God.” He did not analyse his disquietude; he turned to the Lord and began to praise. Faith flies when discouragement appears, and discouragement flies where faith appears. You must choose between them.

fields.title: The Shout of Faith
fields.body_html:
“And as soon as you hear the sound of the trumpet, then all the people shall shout with a great shout, and the wall of the city will fall down flat” (Joshua 6:5).

The shout of a steadfast faith is in direct contrast to the moans of a wavering faith or the wails of a discouraged heart. In the history of Israel, they often indulged in wailing to their own undoing; but on one occasion, they gave a magnificent shout that brought a glorious victory.

This took place after they had crossed the Jordan. God had said to Joshua: “Every place that the sole of your foot will tread upon I have given to you” (Joshua 1:3). They entered the land expecting possession, but were immediately brought face to face with Jericho—a city “great and walled up to heaven.” To the eye of sense, there was no possibility of conquering it.

But the Lord said: “See, I have given Jericho into your hand” (Joshua 6:2). He did not say “I will give,” but “I have given.” It belonged to them already; they were simply called to take possession. God’s plan was strange: after marching and blowing trumpets, “all the people shall shout with a great shout; and the wall of the city shall fall down flat.”

It came to pass just as the Lord said. Joshua told the people, “Shout, for the Lord has given you the city” (Joshua 6:16). When they shouted, the walls fell down flat. No one supposes the noise of the shout caused the walls to fall. The secret lay in the fact that it was the shout of a faith which dared, on the authority of God's word alone, to claim a victory while as yet there were no signs of it.

Faith reckoned God's word to be true. Unbelief might have said, “Wait to shout until the walls actually fall, lest we look foolish.” But faith laughed at such “prudence” and gave a shout of victory while the walls were still standing. “By faith the walls of Jericho fell down after they had been encircled for seven days” (Hebrews 11:30).

“Faith, mighty faith, the promise sees And looks at that alone; Laughs at impossibilities, And cries, It shall be done.”

Jehoshaphat is another example. A great multitude came against him, and he realized he had “no might” and did not know “what to do.” He did not waste time on engines of warfare; he “set his face to seek the Lord” (2 Chronicles 20:3). He stood before the people and prayed: “We are powerless against this great horde... we do not know what to do, but our eyes are on you” (2 Chronicles 20:12).

The Lord answered: “Do not be afraid and do not be dismayed at this great horde, for the battle is not yours but God's... You will not need to fight in this battle. Stand firm, hold your position, and see the salvation of the Lord” (2 Chronicles 20:15, 17).

Without a thought of doubt, Jehoshaphat and the children of Israel believed the word of the Lord and began at once to praise him beforehand for the victory they were sure was coming. The next morning they rose early and went out to meet their enemy. Jehoshaphat, instead of exhorting them to look to their arms and be brave in battle as an ordinary General would have done, simply called upon them to have a courageous faith. “Hear me, Judah and inhabitants of Jerusalem!

Believe in the Lord your God, and you will be established; believe his prophets, and you will succeed” (2 Chronicles 20:20).

Jehoshaphat then consulted with the people; and their faith proving equal to his own, they appointed singers to go out before the army to sing praises as they went forward to meet the enemy. And it came to pass that when they began to sing and to praise, the Lord set an ambush against the enemy, so that they struck one another down. When the children of Israel came to a watchtower in the wilderness, from which they could see the great multitude that had come up against them, “behold, there were dead bodies lying on the ground; none had escaped” (2 Chronicles 20:24).

By this wonderful method of warfare they were made even “more than conquerors”; for they were “three days in taking away the spoil, for it was so much” (2 Chronicles 20:25).

David’s fight with Goliath is another example of this method of victory. To the eye of sense, David had no chance whatever of conquering the mighty giant who had been defying the armies of Israel. But David, looking with the eye of faith, could see the unseen divine forces fighting on his side. When Saul said to him, “You are not able to go against this Philistine to fight with him, for you are but a youth, and he has been a man of war from his youth,” David stood firm in his faith. After recounting his past deliverances, he said calmly, “The Lord who delivered me from the paw of the lion and from the paw of the bear will deliver me from the hand of this Philistine” (1 Samuel 17:33, 37).

Saul, partly convinced by this strong faith, said, “Go, and the Lord be with you!” He could not, however, quite give up all trust in his own accustomed armour; he armed David with a bronze helmet, a coat of mail, and his own powerful sword. David “tried in vain to go,” for he was not used to them. He put them off and took instead the simple weapons the Lord had blessed before: his staff, his sling, and five smooth stones from the brook. Thus equipped, he drew near to the giant.

When the giant saw the youth who had come to fight him, he disdained him and said contemptuously, “Come to me, and I will give your flesh to the birds of the air and to the beasts of the field” (1 Samuel 17:44). To the eye of sense, it looked as though this must necessarily be the end of such an unequal battle. But David’s faith triumphed, and he shouted a shout of victory before the battle had even begun. “You come to me with a sword and with a spear and with a javelin,” he said, “but I come to you in the name of the Lord of hosts, the God of the armies of Israel, whom you have defied. This day the Lord will deliver you into my hand... that all the earth may know that there is a God in Israel, and that all this assembly may know that the Lord saves not with sword and spear. For the battle is the Lord's, and he will give you into our hand” (1 Samuel 17:45-47).

In the face of such faith, what could even a giant do? Every word of that triumphant shout of victory was fulfilled, and the mighty enemy was delivered into the hands of the youth he had disdained. And so it will always be. Nothing can withstand the triumphant faith that links itself to omnipotence. For “this is the victory that has overcome the world—our faith” (1 John 5:4).

The secret of all successful warfare lies in this shout of faith. It is a secret incomprehensible to those who know nothing of the unseen divine power that waits on the demands of faith; a secret that must always seem the height of folly to those who do not understand it.

We are all called to be “a good soldier of Christ Jesus” (2 Timothy 2:3) and to “fight the good fight of the faith” (1 Timothy 6:12) against worse enemies than those which attacked the Israelites. Our enemies are interior, and the giant that defies us is the strength of our temptations and the powerlessness of our own strength to resist. It is a hard and often discouraging fight.

Many of God's children have sinned, repented, and resolved so often that they see no hope of victory. They hate sin and love righteousness, but “the good I want to do, I do not do, but the evil I do not want to do—this I keep on doing” (Romans 7:19). In the language of the Apostle, they find a law in their members warring against the law of their mind. They know they ought to conquer, but they do not know how. It is for these people that this chapter is written. If they can discover the secret of this shout of faith, they will know how, for it never fails to bring victory.

In John 16:33, our Lord reveals the ground of this triumphant shout: “Take heart; I have overcome the world.” Not “I will overcome,” but “I have overcome.” It is already done; we only need to enter into the power of it. Joshua did not say, “Shout, for the Lord will give you the city,” but “Shout, for the Lord has given you the city” (Joshua 6:16). It must have required all of Joshua's will to make such a statement while the walls of the city were still standing as massive as ever. But God was a reality to Joshua, and he was not afraid to proclaim the victory before it was visible.

There is a great difference between saying “The Lord will give” and “The Lord has given.” A victory promised in the future may be hindered by a thousand things, but a victory already accomplished cannot be undone. When our Lord assures us that he has already overcome the world, he gives an assured foundation for a triumphant shout. Henceforward, the forces of sin are a defeated foe. If we believe the words of Christ, we can meet them without fear, since we have been made “more than conquerors through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37).

It is a well-known fact that as long as a defeated army can keep its defeat a secret, it can still show some resistance. But the moment it finds out that its defeat is known, it loses all heart and has no resource left but to retreat. The secret lies in this: we must meet sin not as a foe yet to be conquered, but as one that has already been conquered. When Rahab helped the spies escape, she confessed: “I know that the Lord has given you the land... and that all the inhabitants of the land melt away before you” (Joshua 2:9). If we had eyes to see the unseen kingdom of evil, I believe we would find that a terror has fallen upon all the forces of that region, and that they see in every person of faith a triumphant conqueror.

A Christian I know, who had been fearfully beset by temptation, was told this secret. It brought conviction at once, and she went forth to a fresh battle with the assurance of an already accomplished victory. She said afterwards it seemed as if she could hear the tempter saying as he slunk away, “Alas! She has found out the secret. She knows that I am an already conquered foe!”

We are told that “The reason the Son of God appeared was to destroy the works of the devil” (1 John 3:8); and again, “he appeared in order to take away sins” (1 John 3:5); and “he has appeared once for all at the end of the ages to put away sin by the sacrifice of himself” (Hebrews 9:26).

We must accept it as a fact that sin is for us a conquered foe. If our faith will lay hold of this and “consider yourselves dead to sin” (Romans 6:11), and will dare to raise the shout of victory when temptation comes, we shall find that every wall will fall down flat!

Our enemies are “giants” now just as they were in Israel's day, and cities as great as Jericho confront us. Like the Israelites, we have no human weapons with which to conquer. Our armour must be the “armor of God” (Ephesians 6:11). Our shield is the same invisible shield of faith, and our sword is the “sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6:17). But how different is our usual method of warfare! Instead of a triumphant shout, we meet temptations with feeble resolutions, futile arguments, or despairing prayers. “O Lord, save me!” we cry.

When no deliverance seems to come and we are defeated, we cry out that God has failed us. But what we ought to do is recognise sin as a conquered foe and meet it with a shout of victory.

Where we prayed before that the Lord would save us, we must now make the assertion that he does save us, and that he saves us now. We must add the letter “s” to the word “save” and make it the present tense.

The walls may look as high as ever, and prudence may say it is not safe to shout until the victory is won. But the faith that can shout in the midst of temptation, “Jesus saves me; he saves me now!” is a faith that will win a glorious and speedy victory.

Many of God's children have tried this plan and found it to work far beyond their expectations.

Temptations have come in like a flood—temptations to irritability, wicked thoughts, bitterness of spirit, or a thousand other things. They have seen the danger, and their feelings declared there was no hope of escape.

But their faith laid hold of the grand fact that Christ has conquered. They fixed their gaze on the unseen power of God's salvation and gave their shout of victory: “The Lord saves! He saves me now! I am more than a conqueror through him who loved us” (Romans 8:37). The result is always a glorious victory.

It may sometimes seem so impossible that the Lord can save that the words will not “say themselves” inside. They have to be said aloud, forcing one's lips to utter them over and over, shutting one's eyes and ears against every suggestion of doubt. These declarations of faith often seem “untrue” at first because the reasons for discouragement appear so real. But the unseen facts are truer than the seen. If faith is steadfastly persisted in, these facts never fail to prove themselves. “According to your faith be it done to you” (Matthew 9:29). When we shout the shout of faith, the Lord invariably gives the victory of faith.

I once knew a Christian carman (a driver) who had a naturally violent temper. In his daily work among ungodly companions, he was sorely tempted to give way to it. He struggled valiantly but in vain. One morning, he told his minister in despair, “Can you tell me of any short road to victory—something I can lay hold of at the needed moment?”

“Yes,” the minister replied. “When the temptation comes, at once lift up your heart and claim the promised victory. Shout the shout of faith, and the temptation will flee.”

The carman understood that sin is an already conquered foe. That day at the station, his fellow-drivers taunted him and jostled him out of his rightful place. The temptation to anger was overwhelming. But, folding his arms, he said inwardly over and over, “Jesus saves me; he saves me now!” At once his heart was filled with peace. Later, a heavy box fell on his foot, causing great pain. Again he folded his arms and repeated his shout of victory, and all was calm. Night found him more than a conqueror, and even his companions were forced to own the reality of a religion that could so triumph over their assaults.

The Psalmist, after telling of the enemies who tried to swallow him up, declared: “Then my enemies will turn back in the day when I call. This I know, that God is for me” (Psalm 56:9).

Do you know what the Psalmist knew? Do you know that God is for you? If you do, then go out to meet your temptations singing a song of triumph. At the first approach of temptation, begin to give thanks for the victory. Claim that you are more than a conqueror. Shout the shout of faith with Joshua, Jehoshaphat, David, and Paul. When you shout, the Lord will “set ambushments,” and your enemies shall fall.

fields.title: Thanksgiving Versus Complaining
fields.body_html:
“Give thanks in all circumstances; for this is the will of God in Christ Jesus for you” (1 Thessalonians 5:18).

Thanksgiving and complaining are two contrastive attitudes. The soul that gives thanks can find comfort in everything; the soul that complains can find comfort in nothing.

God’s command is, “In everything give thanks.” It is a positive command. If we want to obey God, we simply must give thanks in everything. There is no getting around it. Yet many Christians look upon this as a “counsel of perfection” that mere flesh and blood could never reach. Unconsciously, they change the wording to “be resigned” instead of “give thanks,” and “in a few things” instead of “in everything.”

They argue, “If everything came direct from God, I might do it, but most things come through human sources or sin.” To this I answer: we cannot always give thanks for the things themselves, but we can always give thanks for God’s love in the things. He is in them somewhere, compelling even the most grievous to work together for our good. Faith never sees “second causes” (the people or mistakes that hurt us); it sees only the hand of God behind them. By the time the effects of a trial reach us, they have become God's will for us and must be accepted from his hands.

The story of Joseph is an illustration. Nothing could have seemed more contrary to God’s will than being sold into slavery by his brothers. Yet, if he had known the end from the beginning, he would have been filled with thanksgiving. His slavery was the direct doorway to the greatest blessings of his life. At the end, Joseph could say, “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). To the eye of sense, his brothers sent him to Egypt; to the eye of faith, “God sent me” (Genesis 45:7).

I remember a trial in my own life brought upon me by another person. I was filled with bitter rebellion and saw nothing to be thankful for. But that very trial worked out the richest blessings of my life. If only I had had faith enough to give thanks at first, how much sorrow I would have been spared.

I am afraid the highest many Christians reach is “striving after resignation” to things they cannot alter. Thanksgiving is almost an unknown exercise. In the world, it is considered discourteous to receive a benefit and fail to say thank you; I cannot see why it is not just as discourteous toward God. We wouldn't dream of omitting a thank-you note to a human friend for a trifling gift, yet we fail to thank God for the innumerable benefits he showers on us.

Worse still, many allow themselves to complain and murmur. We are told that “the people complained in the hearing of the Lord about their misfortunes, and when the Lord heard it, his anger was kindled” (Numbers 11:1). We are tempted to think our “spiritual” complaining doesn't displease him—that it is a sign of zeal or deep insight. But complaining is the opposite of the faith that pleases God.

But complaining is always alike, whether it is on the temporal or the spiritual plane. It always contains the element of fault-finding. Webster says to complain means “to make a charge or an accusation.” It is not merely disliking the thing we have to bear; it is finding fault with the agency that lies behind it. If we carefully examine the inwardness of our complainings, we shall generally find they are founded on a subtle fault-finding with God. We secretly feel as if He were to blame, and we make mental charges against Him.

On the other hand, thanksgiving always involves praise of the Giver. Have you ever noticed how much we are urged in the Bible to “praise the Lord”? It was the principal part of Israel's worship: “Praise the Lord, for the Lord is good; sing to his name, for it is pleasant!” (Psalm 135:3). I believe if we counted them, we would find more commands to give thanks “always for all things” than for any other act. It is evident that the Lord loves to be thanked and praised just as much as we do. It gives Him real pleasure, and our failure to thank Him for His “good and perfect gifts” (James 1:17) wounds His heart, just as ours are wounded when loved ones fail to appreciate what we bestow upon them.

When the Apostle exhorts us to be “imitators of God, as beloved children,” he includes this: “giving thanks always and for everything to God the Father in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Ephesians 5:1, 20). “Always for all things” is a sweeping expression. It must mean that there is nothing in our lives—no matter the channel—that does not contain a hidden blessing from God.

The Apostle tells us that “everything created by God is good, and nothing is to be rejected if it is received with thanksgiving” (1 Timothy 4:4). But it is hard to believe things are good when they do not look so. Often, God’s gifts look like curses to those who only see the surface.

How many “good and perfect gifts” have we looked upon as curses? For how many have we thanked ourselves, our friends, or our circumstances, without looking behind the earthly givers to the Heavenly Giver? It is as if we thanked the messenger but never sent word to the friend who sent the gift.

Even when we realize things come from God, it is hard to thank Him for what hurts. Yet, we thank a skillful physician for a treatment, even if it is severe. Should we not likewise thank our Divine Physician when He gives us bitter medicine to cure a spiritual disease, or performs a painful operation to rid us of something harmful?

Instead of thanking Him, we complain. We usually direct our complaints not against the Physician, but against the “bottle” in which He sent the medicine. This “bottle” is usually a human being whose unkindness or neglect caused our suffering—but they are only the “second cause” God used for our healing. Common sense tells us it is folly to rail against the medicine bottle; it is equal folly to rail against the “second causes” meant to teach our souls.

When the Israelites wandered, they “murmured against Moses and Aaron” (Exodus 16:2). But in reality, their complaining was against God, for He had brought them there. The Psalmist calls this “speaking against God” (Psalm 78:19). Divine history takes no account of second causes; it goes directly to the real Cause behind them.

We may settle it, then: all complaining is “speaking against God.” Second causes are powerless to act except by God’s permission; what He permits becomes His arranging. The Lord was wroth with the complainers “because they did not believe in God and did not trust his saving power” (Psalm 78:22). At the bottom, all complaining means we do not trust His salvation.

The Psalmist says, “I will praise the name of God with a song; I will magnify him with thanksgiving. This will please the Lord more than an ox or a bull” (Psalm 69:30-31). Many are willing to offer a great sacrifice, but a little genuine praise would please Him more.

The Bible calls it a “sacrifice of thanksgiving” (Leviticus 7:12). It is an act of worship. “Let them offer sacrifices of thanksgiving, and tell of his deeds in songs of joy!” (Psalm 107:22). It is an easy thing to offer, yet if the prayers of Christians were noted for a single day, I fear we would find—as with the ten lepers—that nine out of ten offered no genuine thanks.

Our Lord was grieved by those ungrateful lepers: “Were not ten cleansed? Where are the nine?

Was no one found to return and give praise to God except this foreigner?” (Luke 17:17-18). Will He ask the same of us? We wonder at their ingratitude, but what of our own? Do we not pass by innumerable blessings and fix our eyes on our “losses” until our whole horizon is filled with them?

We can judge how this must grieve the Lord by our own feelings. A child who complains about the provision a parent has made wounds that parent's heart often beyond words. We all know people who are always complaining—nothing pleases them, and no kindness is ever appreciated.

We know how uncomfortable their society makes us, and, conversely, how life is brightened by one who finds something to be pleased with in all that comes. I believe far more misery is caused in human hearts by the grumblings of those they love than we imagine; and I believe woundings we never dream of are given to the heart of our Father in Heaven by the continual murmuring of His children.

How often is it said of fretful spirits, “Will nothing ever satisfy them?” And how often must God turn away, grieved by our complainings, when His love has been lavished upon us in untold blessings. I have sometimes thought that if we realized this, we would check our inordinate grief even over the loss of those we love, and try, for His sake, to be cheerful and content even in our lonely condition.

I remember hearing of a girl who underwent a very painful medical treatment. The doctors dreaded her outcries, but to their amazement, not even a moan escaped her. She simply smiled at her father. When asked how she did it, she said: “I knew how much my father loved me, and I knew how he would suffer if he saw that I suffered, so I tried to hide it; and I smiled to make him think I did not mind.” Can any of us do this for our Heavenly Father?

Job was a great complainer, and we might think he had good cause. He said, “I loathe my very life; therefore I will give free utterance to my complaint and speak out of the bitterness of my soul” (Job 10:1). We can hardly wonder at him. Yet, could he have seen the divine side, he would have known his troubles were permitted in the tenderest love to bring him a revelation of God he could have had by no other means. If he had seen the end from the beginning, thanksgiving would have taken the place of complaining.

The children of Israel were always complaining. They complained when they had no water, and when water was supplied, they complained it was bitter. We do the same when our spiritual “water” seems bitter—when religious exercises seem dull and unsatisfying. We turn from the “fountain of living waters” and then complain because the “broken cisterns” we hewed for ourselves hold no water (Jeremiah 2:13).

The Israelites complained about their food, fearing starvation, and then complained when manna was provided because they “loathed this worthless food” (Numbers 21:5). We also complain about our spiritual food—that our preacher doesn't “feed” us or that we lack the privileges others have. We ask for bread and then complain that He has given a stone. But our Divine Master knows what food and drink are best for us. The amazing thing is that we cannot believe, without waiting for the end, that the Shepherd knows which pasture is best.

Jonah provides a wonderful illustration. His prayer of thanksgiving came from the “belly of Sheol”: “I called out to the Lord, out of my distress, and he answered me... But I with the voice of thanksgiving will sacrifice to you” (Jonah 2:2, 9). No depth of misery is too great for the sacrifice of thanksgiving. We do not thank God for the misery, but in the misery, knowing He is there to help and bless.

It is not because things are good that we thank the Lord, but because He is good. We aren't wise enough to judge if a circumstance is a joy or a sorrow in its essence, but we know His goodness makes it certain that what He permits must be for our ultimate good.

In the tract “Mrs. Pickett's Missionary Box,” a woman who had complained all her life was challenged to put a penny in a box for every benefit she discovered. She said: “'Great benefits I have!' says I... 'Guess the heathen won't get much out of me.' I made up my mind I would keep count, jest to show myself how little I did have.”

But sitting on her steps, hearing about women in other lands who were starved and abused, she blurted out: “Well, if I be a widow, I'm thankful I'm where I can earn my own living!” Her niece told her that was her first benefit. She dropped in a penny. Then she put in another because she wasn't Chinese. Then she sold some eggs—a “penny sellin' eggs”—and when she tried to say it wasn't the Lord's benefit, her niece sang: “God's grace is the only grace, And all grace is the grace of God.”

Soon, she was searching for things to be thankful for, and the box didn't rattle near so much when she shook it.

There is a Psalm which I call our Benefit Psalm. It is the 103rd, and it recounts some of the benefits the Lord has bestowed upon us, and urges us not to forget them. “Bless the Lord, O my soul, and forget not all his benefits” (Psalm 103:2). Our dear sister’s Benefit box had taught her something of the meaning of this Psalm. All her life she had been forgetting the benefits the Lord had bestowed upon her, but now she was beginning to remember them.

Have we begun to remember ours?

If during the past year we had kept count of those benefits for which we had actually given thanks, how many pennies, I wonder, would our boxes have contained?

We sometimes sing at mission meetings a hymn of thanksgiving, with the chorus, “Count your many blessings, name them one by one, and it will surprise you what the Lord has done.” And sometimes I have wondered whether any of us who were singing it so heartily had ever kept the slightest record of our blessings, or even in fact knew that we had any.

For the trouble is that very often God’s gifts come to us wrapped up in such rough coverings that we are tempted to reject them as worthless; or the messengers who bring them come in the guise of enemies, and we want to shut the door against them, and not give them entrance. But we lose far more than we know when we reject even the most unlikely.

“Evil is only the slave of good, And sorrow the servant of joy: And the soul is mad that refuses food From the lowest in God’s employ.”

We are commanded to enter into His gates with thanksgiving, and into His courts with praise, and I am convinced that the giving of thanks is the key that opens these gates more quickly than anything else. Try it, dear reader. The next time you feel dead, and cold, and low-spirited, begin to praise and thank the Lord. Enumerate to yourself the benefits He has bestowed upon you, and thank Him heartily for each one, and see if your spirits do not begin to rise, and your heart get warmed up. Sometimes, it may be, you feel too disheartened to pray; then try giving thanks instead; and, before you know it, you will find yourself “glad” in the multitude of His loving-kindnesses and His tender mercies.

One of my friends told me that her little boy one night flatly refused to say his prayers. He said there was not a single thing in all the world he wanted, and he did not see what was the use of asking for things that he did not want. A happy thought came to his mother, and she said, “Well, Charlie, suppose then we give thanks for all the things you have got.” The idea pleased the child, and he very willingly knelt down, and began to give thanks. He thanked God for his marbles, and for a new top that had just been given him, and for his strong legs that could run so far, and that he was not blind like a little boy he knew, and for his kind father and mother, and for his nice bed, and for one after another of his blessings, until the list grew so long that at last he said he believed he would never be finished. And when finally they rose from their knees, he said to his mother, with his face shining with happiness, “Oh, mother, I never knew before how perfectly splendid God is!” And I believe, if we sometimes followed the example of this little boy, we too would find out, as never before, the goodness of our God.

It is very striking to notice how much thanksgiving had to do with the building of the Temple.

When they had collected the treasures for the Temple, David gave thanks to the Lord for enabling them to do it. When the Temple was finished, they gave thanks again. And then a wonderful thing happened, for it came to pass as the trumpeters and singers were as one, to make one sound to be heard in praising and thanking the Lord . . . that then the house was filled with a cloud, even the house of the Lord, so that the priests could not stand to minister by reason of the cloud; for the glory of the Lord had filled the house of God. When the people praised and gave thanks, then the house was filled with the glory of the Lord. And we may be sure that the reason our hearts are not more often filled with the “glory of the Lord,” is because we do not often enough make our voices to be heard in praising and thanking Him.

If the giving of thanks is the way to open the gates of the Lord, complaining, on the other hand, closes these gates. Jude quotes a prophecy of Enoch's concerning murmurers: “to execute judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly of all their deeds of ungodliness that they have committed in such an ungodly way, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him. These are grumblers, malcontents, following their own sinful desires” (Jude 1:15-16). People who are “grumblers” and “complainers” make, in their complainings, more “harsh speeches” against the Lord than they would like to admit, or than they will care to face at the last day. And it is not to be wondered at that the judgment of God, instead of the “glory of God,” is the result.

I wish I had room to quote all the passages in the Bible about giving thanks and praises to the Lord. It is safe to say that there are hundreds and hundreds of them; and it is an amazing thing how they can have been so persistently ignored. I beg of you to read the last seven Psalms, and see what you think. They are simply full to overflowing with a list of the things for which the Psalmist calls upon us to give thanks; all of them things relating to the character and the ways of God, which we dare not dispute. They are not for the most part private blessings of our own, but are the common blessings that belong to all humanity, and that contain within themselves every private blessing we can possibly need. But they are blessings which we continually forget, because we take them for granted, and hardly notice their existence, and never give thanks for them.

But the Psalmist knew how to “count his many blessings, and name them one by one,” and he would have us do the same. Try it, dear reader, and you will indeed be surprised to see what the Lord has done. Go over these Psalms verse by verse, and blessing by blessing, and see if, like the little boy of our story, you are not made to confess that you never knew before “how splendid God is.”

The last verse of the Book of Psalms, taken in connection with the vision of John in the Book of Revelation, is very significant. The Psalmist says, “Let everything that has breath praise the Lord!” (Psalm 150:6). And, in the Book of Revelation, John, who declares himself to be our brother and our partner in the tribulation, tells us that he heard this being done: “And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying, 'To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!'” (Revelation 5:13). The time for universal praise is sure to come some day. Let us begin to do our part now.

I heard once of a discontented, complaining man, who, to the great surprise of his friends, became bright and happy, and full of thanksgiving. After watching him for a little while, and being convinced that the change was permanent, they asked him what had happened. “Oh,” he replied, “I have changed my residence. I used to live in Grumbling Lane, but now I have moved into Thanksgiving Square, and I find that I am so rich in blessings that I am always happy.”

Shall we each one make this move now?

And then a wonderful thing happened, for it came to pass as the trumpeters and singers were as one, to make one sound to be heard in praising and thanking the Lord . . . that then the house was filled with a cloud, even the house of the Lord, so that the priests could not stand to minister by reason of the cloud; for the glory of the Lord had filled the house of God. When the people praised and gave thanks, then the house was filled with the glory of the Lord. And we may be sure that the reason our hearts are not more often filled with the “glory of the Lord,” is because we do not often enough make our voices to be heard in praising and thanking Him. If the giving of thanks is the way to open the gates of the Lord, complaining, on the other hand, closes these gates. Jude quotes a prophecy of Enoch's concerning murmurers: “to execute judgment on all and to convict all the ungodly of all their deeds of ungodliness that they have committed in such an ungodly way, and of all the harsh things that ungodly sinners have spoken against him. These are grumblers, malcontents, following their own sinful desires” (Jude 1:15-16). People who are “grumblers” and “complainers” make, in their complainings, more “harsh speeches” against the Lord than they would like to admit, or than they will care to face at the last day. And it is not to be wondered at that the judgment of God, instead of the “glory of God,” is the result. I wish I had room to quote all the passages in the Bible about giving thanks and praises to the Lord. It is safe to say that there are hundreds and hundreds of them; and it is an amazing thing how they can have been so persistently ignored. I beg of you to read the last seven Psalms, and see what you think. They are simply full to overflowing with a list of the things for which the Psalmist calls upon us to give thanks; all of them things relating to the character and the ways of God, which we dare not dispute. They are not for the most part private blessings of our own, but are the common blessings that belong to all humanity, and that contain within themselves every private blessing we can possibly need. But they are blessings which we continually forget, because we take them for granted, and hardly notice their existence, and never give thanks for them. But the Psalmist knew how to “count his many blessings, and name them one by one,” and he would have us do the same. Try it, dear reader, and you will indeed be surprised to see what the Lord has done. Go over these Psalms verse by verse, and blessing by blessing, and see if, like the little boy of our story, you are not made to confess that you never knew before “how splendid God is.” The last verse of the Book of Psalms, taken in connection with the vision of John in the Book of Revelation, is very significant. The Psalmist says, “Let everything that has breath praise the Lord!” (Psalm 150:6). And, in the Book of Revelation, John, who declares himself to be our brother and our partner in the tribulation, tells us that he heard this being done: “And I heard every creature in heaven and on earth and under the earth and in the sea, and all that is in them, saying, 'To him who sits on the throne and to the Lamb be blessing and honor and glory and might forever and ever!'” (Revelation 5:13). The time for universal praise is sure to come some day. Let us begin to do our part now. I heard once of a discontented, complaining man, who, to the great surprise of his friends, became bright and happy, and full of thanksgiving. After watching him for a little while, and being convinced that the change was permanent, they asked him what had happened. “Oh,” he replied, “I have changed my residence. I used to live in Grumbling Lane, but now I have moved into Thanksgiving Square, and I find that I am so rich in blessings that I am always happy.” Shall we each one make this move now?

fields.title: Conformed to the Image of Christ
fields.body_html:
“For those whom he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, in order that he might be the firstborn among many brothers” (Romans 8:29).

God’s ultimate purpose in our creation was that we should finally be “conformed to the image of Christ.” Christ was to be the firstborn among many brothers, and His brothers were to be like Him. All the discipline and training of our lives is with this end in view; and God has implanted in every human heart a longing, however unformed and unexpressed, after the best and highest it knows.

Christ is the pattern of what each one of us is to be when finished. We are “predestined” to be conformed to His image, in order that He might be the firstborn among many brothers. We are to be “partakers of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4) with Christ; we are to be filled with the spirit of Christ; we are to share His resurrection life, and to walk as He walked. We are to be one with Him, as He is one with the Father; and the glory God gave to Him, He is to give to us. And when all this is brought to pass, then, and not until then, will God’s purpose in our creation be fully accomplished, and we stand forth “in His image and after His likeness.”

Our likeness to His image is an accomplished fact in the mind of God, but we are, so to speak, in the factory as yet, and the great Master Workman is at work upon us. “Beloved, we are God's children now, and what we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

And so it is written: “Thus it is written, 'The first man Adam became a living being'; the last Adam became a life-giving spirit. But it is not the spiritual that is first but the natural, and then the spiritual. The first man was from the earth, a man of dust; the second man is from heaven. As was the man of dust, so also are those who are of the dust, and as is the man of heaven, so also are those who are of heaven. Just as we have borne the image of the man of dust, we shall also bear the image of the man of heaven” (1 Corinthians 15:45-49).

It is deeply interesting to see that this process, which was begun in Genesis, is declared to be completed in Revelation, where the one like a son of man gave to St. John this significant message to the overcomers: “The one who conquers, I will make him a pillar in the temple of my God. Never shall he go out of it, and I will write on him the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God, the new Jerusalem, which comes down from my God out of heaven, and my own new name” (Revelation 3:12). Since name always means character in the Bible, this message can only mean that at last God’s purpose is accomplished, and the spiritual development of man is completed, and he has been made, what God intended from the start, so truly into His likeness and image, as to deserve having written upon him the name of God!

Words fail before such a glorious destiny as this! But our Lord foreshadows it in His wonderful prayer, when He asks for His brothers “that they may all be one, just as you, Father, are in me, and I in you, that they also may be in us, so that the world may believe that you have sent me.

The glory that you have given me I have given to them, that they may be one even as we are one, I in them and you in me, that they may become perfectly one” (John 17:21-23). Could oneness be closer or more complete?

Paul also foreshadows this glorious completion when he declares, that, if we suffer with Christ, we shall also be glorified together with Him; and when he asserts that “the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us” (Romans 8:18).

The whole creation waits for the revealing of this glory; for Paul goes on to say that “the creation waits with eager longing for the revealing of the sons of God” (Romans 8:19). And he adds finally, “And not only the creation, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies” (Romans 8:23).

In view of such a glorious destiny, at which I dare not do more than hint, shall we not cheerfully welcome the processes, however painful they may be, by which we are to reach it? And shall we not strive eagerly and earnestly to be “working together with him” (2 Corinthians 6:1) in helping to bring it about? He is the great Master-builder, but He wants our cooperation in building up the structure of our characters, and He exhorts us to take care how we build. We are all of us at every moment of our lives engaged in this building. Sometimes we build with gold, silver, and precious stones, and sometimes we build with wood, hay, and straw. And we are solemnly warned that “each one's work will become manifest, for the Day will disclose it, because it will be revealed by fire, and the fire will test what sort of work each one has done” (1 Corinthians 3:13). There is no escaping this. We cannot hope, when that day comes, to conceal our wood, hay, and straw, however successfully we may have managed to do so beforehand.

To my mind, there is no more solemn passage in the whole Bible than the one in Galatians which says: “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap. For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life” (Galatians 6:7-8). It is the absolute certainty of this that is so awe-inspiring. It is far more serious than any arbitrary punishment; for punishment can sometimes be avoided, but there is no possibility of altering the working of a natural law such as this.

In a Catechism I saw lately were the following questions and answers: Q: What is the reward for generosity?

A: More generosity.

Q: What is the punishment for meanness?

A: More meanness.

No Catechism ever spoke more truly. We all know it for ourselves. In the parable of the talents, our Lord illustrates this inevitable law. The condemnation of the unfaithful servant may have sometimes seemed unfair to us, but it was only the reaping of what that servant had sown. “So take the talent from him and give it to him who has the ten talents. For to everyone who has will more be given, and he will have an abundance. But from the one who has not, even what he has will be taken away” (Matthew 25:28-29). This is no arbitrary statement, but is simply a revelation of the inherent nature of things, from which none of us can escape.

But in order to be labourers together with God, we must not only build with His materials, but also by His processes, and we are often very ignorant of these. Our idea of building is of hard, laborious work, done by the sweat of our brow; but God’s idea is very different. Paul tells us what it is: “And we all, with unveiled face, beholding the glory of the Lord, are being transformed into the same image from one degree of glory to another. For this comes from the Lord who is the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18). Our work is to “behold,” and, as we behold, the Lord carries out the marvellous transformation, and we are “changed into the same image by the Spirit of the Lord.” This means, of course, to behold, not in our earthly sense of merely looking at a thing, but in the divine sense of really seeing it. We are to behold the glory of the Lord with our spiritual eyes, and we are to keep beholding it. The glory of the Lord does not mean a great shine or a halo, however. The real glory of the Lord is the glory of what He is and of what He does—the glory of His character. And it is this we are to behold.

Let me give an illustration. Someone offends me, and I am tempted to get angry and strike back.

But I look at Christ, and think of what He would have done, and dwell upon the thought of His gentleness and meekness, and His love for the person who offended me. As I look, I begin to want to be like Him, and I ask in faith that I may be made a “partaker of the divine nature” (2 Peter 1:4), and anger and revenge die out of my heart. I love my enemy and long to serve him.

It is by this sort of beholding Christ that we are to be changed into His image; and the closer we keep to Him, the more rapid the change will be.

I have heard of a wonderful mirror known to science called the parabolic mirror. It is a hollow cone lined with a mirror all over its inside surface. It has the power of focusing rays of light in different degrees of intensity, in proportion to how close they get to the meeting point at the top end of the cone; the power becomes more and more intense as the end point is approached. It has been discovered by science that at a certain stage in this movement toward the interior point— where all the sides of the mirror meet in absolute oneness—the power of the focus concentrates all the light-giving properties of the sun’s rays into such an intense brilliancy that it makes visible things never before seen by the human eye. It even makes flesh transparent, enabling us to see through the outer covering of our bodies to the inner operations beneath.

Moving a little further into the interior of our mirror, the heat properties of the sun’s rays are so concentrated that they generate enough heat to melt iron in sixteen seconds, and to clear away the alloy from gold, leaving only the solid bead of pure metal, in fourteen seconds.

Moving further still, the photographing properties of the sunlight are so concentrated that they impress a permanent image of the mirror upon anything that is passed through the focus for only one second.

Moving still further, nearly to the point of oneness, the magnetising powers of light are so concentrated that anything exposed to it for a single instant becomes a powerful magnet, drawing all things to itself afterwards.

Whether all this is scientifically correct or not, I am not scientist enough to know, but at least it will serve as an allegory to show the progress of the soul, as it is changed from glory to glory, in its development “into His image.”

First, as we behold as in a mirror the glory of the Lord, we come to the light focus, which reveals our sinfulness and our need. “Again Jesus spoke to them, saying, 'I am the light of the world.

Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life'” (John 8:12).

Second, as we draw closer, we reach the heat focus, where all our dross and worthless silver is burned up. For He is like a refiner’s fire and like fullers' soap: “He will sit as a refiner and purifier of silver, and he will purify the sons of Levi and refine them like gold and silver, and they will bring offerings in righteousness to the Lord” (Malachi 3:2-3).

Third, as we draw closer still, we come to the photographing focus, where the image of Christ is permanently impressed upon our souls, and we are made like Him because we see Him as He is.

“We know that when he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

Fourth and finally, as we come to the point of oneness, we reach the magnetic focus, where our character is so shaped like Christ’s that people, seeing it, will be irresistibly drawn to “give glory to your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

If we would be shaped into the image of Christ, then, we must live closer and ever closer to Him.

We must become better and better acquainted with His character and His ways; we must look at things through His eyes and judge all things by His standards. It is not by effort or by struggling that this likeness is to be accomplished; it is by assimilation. According to a natural law, we grow like those we spend time with, and the stronger character always exerts the controlling influence. And, as divine law is all one with natural law—only working in a higher sphere and with more unhindered power—it should not seem mysterious to us that we should become like Christ by a spiritual union with Him.

But again I must repeat, that this union with Christ cannot come by our own efforts, no matter how strenuous they may be. Christ is to “dwell in your hearts through faith” (Ephesians 3:17), and He can dwell there in no other way. Paul, when he tells us that he was crucified with Christ, says: “I have been crucified with Christ. It is no longer I who live, but Christ who lives in me.

And the life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself for me” (Galatians 2:20).

“Christ lives in me”—this is the transforming secret. If Christ lives in me, His life must, in the very nature of things, be shown in my physical body, and I cannot fail to be changed from glory to glory into His image. Our Lord’s teaching about this is very clear: “Abide in me, and I in you.

As the branch cannot bear fruit by itself, unless it abides in the vine, neither can you, unless you abide in me. I am the vine; you are the branches. Whoever abides in me and I in him, he it is that bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:4-5).

This is literally true. If we abide in Him, and He in us, we can no more help bringing forth much fruit than the branches of a healthy vine can. In the very nature of things, the fruit must come.

But we cannot take the “old man” into Christ. We must put off the old self with its deeds before we can “put on the Lord Jesus Christ” (Romans 13:14). The Apostle Paul, in writing to the Colossians, bases his encouragement to live a holy life on the fact that they had already done this: “Do not lie to one another, seeing that you have put off the old self with its practices and have put on the new self, which is being renewed in knowledge after the image of its creator” (Colossians 3:9-10).

Sin must disappear when Christ enters; no soul that is not prepared to surrender everything contrary to His will can hope to welcome Him. The “old man” must be set aside if the new man is to reign. But both the putting off and the putting on must be done by faith. There is no other way. As I have tried to explain elsewhere, we must move our personality, our ego, and our will out of ourselves and into Christ. We must consider ourselves dead to self and alive only to God.

“So you also must consider yourselves dead to sin and alive to God in Christ Jesus. Let not sin therefore reign in your mortal body, to make you obey its passions. Do not present your members to sin as instruments for unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as those who have been brought from death to life, and your members to God as instruments for righteousness” (Romans 6:11-13).

The same kind of faith that allows us to grasp the forgiveness of sins also brings about this union with Christ. To those who do not understand the law of faith, this will no doubt be as great a mystery as the secrets of gravity were before the law of gravity was discovered. However, to those who do understand it, the law of faith works as unerringly and as definitely as the law of gravity, and produces its results just as certainly. No one can read the eleventh chapter of Hebrews and fail to see that faith is an all-conquering force. I believe myself it is the creative force of the universe. It is the higher law that controls all the lower laws beneath it; what looks like a miracle is simply the working of this higher controlling law.

Faith is, as I say, the law of creation: “By faith we understand that the universe was created by the word of God, so that what is seen was not made out of things that are visible” (Hebrews 11:3). We are told that God spoke and it was done, He commanded and it stood fast. And our Lord tells us that if we have faith, we can do the same: “And Jesus answered them, 'Have faith in God. Truly, I say to you, whoever says to this mountain, “Be taken up and thrown into the sea,” and does not doubt in his heart, but believes that what he says will come to pass, it will be done for him. Therefore I tell you, whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you have received it, and it will be yours'” (Mark 11:22-24).

Faith, we are told, “calls into existence the things that do not exist” (Romans 4:17). By calling them, it brings them into being. Therefore, although we cannot see any physical sign of change when by faith we put off the old self—which is corrupt according to deceitful desires—and by faith put on the new self—which is created after the likeness of God in true righteousness and holiness—it has nevertheless really been done. Faith has accomplished it. I cannot explain this theologically, but I can fearlessly assert that it is a massive practical reality. Those souls who abandon the life of self and give themselves up to the Lord to be fully possessed by Him find that He takes possession of the inner springs of their being, and “works in you, both to will and to work for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13).

Paul prayed for the Ephesians “that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith” (Ephesians 3:17), and this is the whole secret of being shaped into His image. If Christ is dwelling in my heart, I must necessarily be Christ-like. I cannot be unkind, irritable, self-seeking, or dishonest; instead, His gentleness, sweetness, tender compassion, and loving submission to the will of His Father must be shown in my daily walk and conversation.

We shall not be fully changed into the image of Christ until He appears and we “see him as he is” (1 John 3:2). But meanwhile, to our own extent, the life of Jesus is to be “manifested in our mortal flesh” (2 Corinthians 4:11). Is it manifested in ours? Are we so “conformed to the image” of Christ that people, in seeing us, see a glimpse of Him as well?

A Methodist minister's wife told me that at one time, when they had moved to a new place, her little boy came in after his first afternoon of play and exclaimed joyfully, “Oh, mother, I have found such a lovely, good little girl to play with here that I never want to go away again.” “I am very glad, darling,” said the loving mother, happy for her child's happiness; “what is the little girl's name?” “Oh,” replied the child with a sudden solemnity, “I think her name is Jesus.” “Why, Frank!” exclaimed the horrified mother, “what do you mean?” “Well, mother,” he said defensively, “she was so lovely that I did not know what she could be called but Jesus.”

Are our lives so Christ-like that anyone could have such a thought about us? Is it obvious to everyone around us that we have been with Jesus? Is it not, sadly, often just the opposite? Are not some of us so grumpy and difficult in our living that exactly the opposite would have to be said about us?

Paul says we are to be “a letter from Christ... written not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts” (2 Corinthians 3:3). I firmly believe that if every child of God, all over the world, would begin from this day forward to be a “letter from Christ,” living a truly Christ-like life at home and abroad, it would not be a month before the churches would be crowded with people wanting to know more, coming in to see what religion could so transform human nature into something divine.

The world is full of people who do not believe in the reality of the Christian religion, and nothing will convince them except facts they cannot disprove. We must meet them with transformed lives. If they see that whereas once we were angry, now we are sweet; once we were proud, now we are humble; once we were worried, now we are patient and calm; and if we are able to testify that it is the religion of Christ that has caused this change, they cannot help but be impressed.

A Christian man who had gained a great reputation for piety because of his hard work unfortunately also had a reputation for a bad temper and a sharp tongue.
